 Inspiration 

 Managing multiple vendors during a home renovation is difficult, especially for homeowners balancing a project alongside full-time work. OpenPlan was inspired by the need to centralise renovation information and make everyday updates or queries quick and simple. 

 What it does 

 OpenPlan provides one shared place to manage renovation projects, floors, spaces, budgets, tasks, notes, and timelines. Its WebMCP integration lets homeowners use natural language in ChatGPT to read, create, update, and delete project information while the interface remains the central source of truth. 

 How we built it 

 We built OpenPlan with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and Cloudflare D1 for shared persistent data. Browser-native WebMCP and an unauthenticated Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint connect the same renovation data and tools to ChatGPT. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP fits OpenPlan because it lets homeowners manage complex renovation projects through simple natural-language requests while keeping the visual interface as the central source of truth. People and AI agents can now work together to create, review, update, and delete projects, floors, spaces, budgets, renovation items, notes, and timelines.

title: Ttrialbridge
pitch: Evidence-based clinical trial matching that explains eligibility, identifies missing information, and highlights trials patients may qualify for now or later.
about_excerpt: Evidence-based clinical trial matching that explains eligibility, identifies missing information, and highlights trials patients may qualify for now or later. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Finding a clinical trial is only the first step. The harder question is: Is this trial actually suitable for this patient, and why? Clinical trial eligibility criteria are long and complex, while the information needed to evaluate them is scattered across diagnoses, biomarkers, treatments, laboratory results, and clinical notes. We built TrialBridge to turn clinical trial discovery into a transparent, evidence-based eligibility workflow for both humans and AI agents. What it does TrialBridge helps users discover cancer clinical trials and evaluate eligibility at the individual criterion level . Instead of generating a single match score, TrialBridge breaks eligibility criteria into structured checks and classifies each one as: Matched Unmatched Missing information Requires clinical review Every assessment is linked to the original trial criterion and the corresponding patient evidence, making the reasoning independently reviewable. TrialBridge also identifies actionable eligibility gaps . A patient may need a biomarker test, updated laboratory result, completion of a treatment washout period, or clinician confirmation. This means TrialBridge can distinguish between: Not eligible now ≠ Not enough information ≠ Potentially eligible later How we built it We designed TrialBridge as a structured eligibility engine rather than a conventional semantic-search system. Trial criteria are decomposed into individual inclusion and exclusion requirements. Patient information is normalized into structured clinical facts including diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, treatment history, laboratory values, performance status, and relevant dates. AI helps interpret unstructured clinical language, while deterministic rules evaluate conditions such as numerical thresholds, dates, treatment history, washout periods, and explicit exclusions. We also implemented WebMCP , allowing compatible browser agents to discover and invoke TrialBridge capabilities directly from the website. Public trial-search tools can be discovered through the browser's model context. Patient-context tools are dynamically exposed only after explicit permission, allowing the available agent capabilities to change with the application's state. This makes TrialBridge not just an AI-powered website, but an agent-ready clinical trial workspace . Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was uncertainty . Clinical eligibility criteria contain ambiguous language, temporal conditions, nested logic, and requirements that ultimately depend on clinical judgment. Patient information may also be missing, outdated, or conflicting. A naive matching system can easily mistake missing information for either eligibility or ineligibility. We therefore created explicit uncertainty states and separated AI-assisted interpretation from deterministic eligibility checks . We also needed a safe way for AI agents to interact with clinical workflows. Instead of exposing every capability by default, our WebMCP implementation makes tool availability dependent on explicit user permission and application state. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working prototype that connects: Trial discovery → Criterion-level matching → Evidence → Eligibility gaps → Agent interaction TrialBridge does more than rank trials. It explains why a patient may qualify, which evidence supports the assessment, what information is missing , and what could make the patient eligible later . We are especially proud of: Criterion-level explainability with traceable patient evidence Explicit uncertainty handling instead of forcing binary decisions Future eligibility reasoning for potentially resolvable barriers Actionable missing-data identification WebMCP-native tools that browser agents can discover and execute Permission-aware tool exposure for patient-context workflows These features transform TrialBridge from a trial search engine into an explainable, agent-ready clinical trial eligibility workspace . What we learned We learned that clinical trial matching is not simply a search or ranking problem. Reliable matching requires structured clinical facts, temporal reasoning, uncertainty management, deterministic validation, and human oversight . We also learned that explainability must be built into the architecture. A clinically useful system should not only answer: “Which trial matches?” It should also answer: “Why?” — “Based on what evidence?” — “What is missing?” — “What happens next?” Building TrialBridge with WebMCP also showed us a new way for AI agents to interact with clinical software: instead of giving an agent unrestricted access, the application itself can control which tools are discoverable based on user permission and context. What's next for TrialBridge Next, we plan to expand TrialBridge from a working prototype toward prospective clinical validation. We plan to integrate real-time trial registry data, improve automated eligibility parsing, and connect with structured EHR data through standards such as FHIR . We also want to add: Site-level recruitment verification Multilingual patient-friendly explanations Automated missing-data checklists More advanced temporal eligibility reasoning Prospective evaluation with clinical trial coordinators Expanded WebMCP workflows for agent-assisted screening Our long-term goal is for TrialBridge to become the bridge between patients, clinical evidence, trial teams, and AI agents —while keeping final eligibility and enrollment decisions with the responsible clinical trial team. title: Dominaitrix
pitch: Dominaitrix teaches the old web new tricks: a Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters, turning unsupported sites into reliable tools for people and their agents.
about_excerpt: Dominaitrix teaches the old web new tricks: a Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters, turning unsupported sites into reliable tools for people and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web was built for people clicking buttons, not agents trying to complete tasks. When agents rely on screenshots, coordinates, and brittle selectors, even simple workflows become slow and unreliable. WebMCP offers a better interface—but most existing websites do not support it yet. Dominaitrix was inspired by a practical question: what if we could teach the web we already have to speak WebMCP? What it does Dominaitrix is a sideloadable Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters on supported websites. Each adapter translates a site’s live interface into structured tools that agents can discover and invoke directly. Our adapters currently support: Managing a live ESPN Fantasy Football draft Exploring Domino’s menus and building a cart Reading Hacker News stories and discussions Searching and navigating Wikipedia articles The difference is dramatic. In two ESPN drafts using the same prompt, ordinary browser control successfully drafted only 3 of 16 intended players and followed 1 of 5 roster instructions. With Dominaitrix, the agent drafted 16 of 16 players and followed 5 of 5 instructions. Dominaitrix does not provide the agent. It gives WebMCP-capable agents a faster, safer, and more reliable way to use existing websites. How we built it Dominaitrix consists of three main pieces: A Chrome extension that installs adapters through chrome.userScripts A shared runtime that registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() A static adapter registry containing versioned metadata, compatibility information, tool descriptions, and SHA-256 source digests The extension periodically checks the registry, verifies each adapter’s integrity, and installs or updates it on matching pages. Adapters run in an isolated user-script world by default and expose narrowly scoped tools with structured inputs, outputs, and errors. Every adapter is reviewed and tested in the repository before publication. The project includes an adapter template, automated registry generation, integrity validation, and a browser-like test harness for exercising tools without depending entirely on live sites. We also built privacy-conscious local diagnostics. Dominaitrix records minimized health events—such as the adapter version, tool name, outcome, and broad error category—but never records tool arguments, page content, cookies, tokens, or response bodies. Nothing is uploaded automatically. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was translating dynamic, human-oriented interfaces into stable agent tools. ESPN’s draft room uses virtualized tables, changing position filters, a live clock, and controls whose meaning changes when the user is on the clock. A delayed instruction could accidentally draft a player during the wrong pick. We addressed this by using stable player IDs, requiring the expected pick number for consequential actions, detecting stale state, and verifying the result after every selection. We faced similar issues across sites: hidden application state, asynchronous UI updates, undocumented APIs, route changes, and actions that can return success before the visible interface has actually updated. Distribution created another challenge. Downloadable adapters make rapid compatibility fixes possible, but they also create a trust boundary. We designed a curated registry with no public upload path, exact source digests, restrictive match patterns, explicit execution worlds, and automated consistency checks. Finally, WebMCP and Chrome’s user-script support are still experimental. We had to handle missing APIs, disabled browser settings, unsupported pages, and partial initialization without leaving users with mysterious failures. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that Dominaitrix demonstrates a measurable improvement rather than merely registering demo tools. The ESPN experiment showed that structured tools can turn a fragile, time-sensitive workflow into one an agent completes accurately and with time to spare. The agent could inspect the draft, manage autopick, search available players, maintain a queue, and make validated selections while following a multi-part strategy. We are also proud that the adapter system is reusable. The same runtime supports experiences as different as drafting a fantasy team, configuring a pizza, exploring a discussion tree, and navigating an encyclopedia. What we learned We learned that agents do not need unrestricted access to a website’s internals. They need a small set of well-designed capabilities with stable identifiers, precise descriptions, bounded results, and actionable errors. We also learned that successful execution must be verified. A click or HTTP response is not proof that the intended state changed—especially during live, asynchronous workflows. Most importantly, WebMCP is valuable even before websites adopt it natively. An adapter layer can provide an immediate bridge while showing site owners what an agent-native interface for their product could look like. What's next for Dominaitrix Next, we want to expand the curated adapter library and make adapters easier to develop, review, test, and maintain. We plan to add stronger compatibility monitoring, richer local diagnostics, safer confirmation patterns for consequential actions, and tooling that detects when a site change breaks an adapter. Longer term, we hope Dominaitrix can serve two purposes: make today’s web useful to agents now, and provide working prototypes that help websites design native WebMCP support of their own. title: WebMCPify
pitch: Give any existing website an agent interface — without rebuilding it.
about_excerpt: Give any existing website an agent interface — without rebuilding it. Like Comment Story Updates home demo Inspiration Most websites were built for people clicking around. Agents are bad at that. They guess at buttons, and that’s a terrible idea when money is involved. WebMCP is the right fix: the page exposes real tools. But the site has to add them. Shopify can. Almost nobody else will. I wanted something in between. Paste a URL. Keep the original site. Agents still get tools. What it does Paste a public URL. WebMCPify crawls it, GPT-5.6 writes tools as recipes (click this, fill that — not page JavaScript), we run them on the live site, and a small script registers them with document.modelContext.registerTool . You get an agent-ready URL (Cloudflare proxy, no change to the original site) or a one-line script for you to update it in code. Humans keep the same UI. Agents call named tools. How I built it Playwright crawls the site (this runs on Render). GPT-5.6 writes the tools. We try them on the live site. If one fails, a second model ( gpt-5.6-terra ) tries to fix it. A Cloudflare Worker serves the page and injects the script. Or you drop in a script tag. GPT never writes code that runs in the browser. If a tool would pay, order, delete, or send something, we mark it sensitive and show a confirm dialog. Results stay small so the agent doesn’t get a wall of HTML. What I learned Don’t let the model write page JavaScript. Recipes are boring and that’s the point. They’re easy to check and they can’t eval anything. OpenAI structured outputs hate nested schemas. My first recipe format used a union type per step and the API just rejected it. I flattened the schema and generate started working. ChatGPT only sees tools on the top-level page. A bookmarklet or an iframe doesn’t count. The proxy keeps the shop UI and the tools on one origin, which is what the in-app browser needs. Netlify doesn’t have a real filesystem. Site state lives in Redis. The dashboard is a WebMCP page too. You can ask it to analyze a site and hand back the agent-ready URL. Challenges Sites you don’t own. A script tag is clean, but most sites won’t add one. The Worker proxy injects the same bridge with no deploy on their side. I shipped both. Same origin, or it doesn’t count. Tools have to sit on the top-level document. That’s a proxy problem, not a prompt problem — rewrite HTML, patch fetch/history, keep the UI. Don’t trust the model with money. Pay / order / delete / send is marked sensitive in code and gets an on-page confirm. The agent can still call place_order . A human has to click Confirm. Structured outputs. Nested step types died at the API. One flat step object, unused fields null , and the pipeline runs. What’s next Tighter locators on messy SPAs. Confirm as a hard rule in the interpreter, not only in the recipe. More navigation than fetch / history . Then more of the public web. The web isn’t getting rebuilt. It can still grow an agent interface. title: WebMCP Guardrail Labs
pitch: Prototype risky browser-agent actions with visible human approval and deterministic proof.
about_excerpt: Prototype risky browser-agent actions with visible human approval and deterministic proof. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Giving an AI agent a structured web action is easy. Making a consequential action understandable, reviewable, and verifiable is harder. Teams exploring agentic commerce, deployment operations, or incident workflows need to see exactly what an agent intends to change before connecting it to production. What it does WebMCP Guardrail Labs is an open-source sandbox for designing that boundary. An agent can inspect page state, prepare a typed action, and explain the result through WebMCP. A consequential call stops at CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED ; only the visible page can record the human decision. Deterministic code then rechecks the action and creates a local receipt. The primary Promotion Regression Lab compares PROMO-20 v1, which starts at $120, with a proposed v2 starting at $100. Four boundary carts reveal exactly two changed customer outcomes: $100 and $119. Supporting labs apply the same pattern to a synthetic deployment rollback and a mock incident case. The reusable interaction contract is: agent prepares, human decides, code verifies . Why WebMCP The page already knows its business operations, schemas, state, and safety checks. WebMCP exposes those semantics as page-scoped tools, so an agent does not have to infer them from visual layout or raw DOM interaction. The ordinary interface remains fully usable. People and agents divide the work cleanly: the agent gathers state and prepares evidence; the person makes the consequential decision in context; deterministic code verifies the result. This makes sensitive browser-agent workflows clearer and more auditable without giving the agent hidden authority. How we built it Each selected lab registers strict imperative WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Agent and visible-UI calls enter the same state machine in src/domain.mjs , so validation, ordering, stale-state handling, plan matching, redaction, idempotency, and receipt rules cannot drift between surfaces. Module-private decision provenance prevents JSON arguments from manufacturing approval. The dependency-free Node server serves native HTML, CSS, and browser JavaScript. No application data is sent to an external model or API. Key features Four boundary carts expose two promotion regressions immediately. Strict schemas, annotations, discovery, and execution through WebMCP. Agent-supplied approval cannot commit consequential actions. Deterministic verification precedes each idempotent local receipt. Promotion, rollback, and incident labs share one four-stage interaction model. The complete workflow remains available through the ordinary UI. Evidence distinguishes verified Chrome runs from checks that were not run. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled. In Promotion, ask: "Inspect PROMO-20 and preview v2 with a $100 threshold. Tell me which carts change. Do not approve it." Confirm that $100 and $119 are marked as regressions and an agent approval attempt returns CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED . Use Approve and verify v2 on the visible page; confirm 4/4 assertions and receipt PROMO-20-v2-r2 . Open ?id=D2 and ?id=B2 for the synthetic rollback and mock incident journeys. From a Node.js 20+ checkout, run npm test , npm run evaluate:chrome , and npm run evaluate . The deterministic suite passes all 64 checks. Hosted Chrome journeys pass for E2-R, D2, and B2. Interactive ChatGPT and assistive-technology checks are honestly marked not run. AI and Codex usage OpenAI Codex assisted with official-source research, product scoping, implementation, accessibility review, tests, Chrome DevTools Protocol automation, Render packaging, evidence capture, and submission preparation under human review. The participant selected the concept, key product decisions, public deployment, and review checkpoints. Links Live app: https://webmcp-guardrail-labs.onrender.com Source: https://github.com/procloudkim/webmcp-guardrail-labs Demo video: https://youtu.be/a1ZVDmXYohQ Known limitations This is a deterministic proof of concept, not production authorization infrastructure. It has no authentication, durable audit store, tenant isolation, rate limiting, validated DLP, real commerce/deployment/regulator integrations, user study, legal guidance, or production-security claim. All demonstrated data and effects are synthetic. title: Forsyningsdata Danmark – WebMCP
pitch: An AI-agent-ready address platform for exploring Danish property and infrastructure data through WebMCP — turning fragmented public datasets into clear, interactive answers.
about_excerpt: An AI-agent-ready address platform for exploring Danish property and infrastructure data through WebMCP — turning fragmented public datasets into clear, interactive answers. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Public property and infrastructure information is valuable, but it is fragmented across national registries, map services, municipal portals and local utility sources. For a homeowner, contractor or adviser, the difficult part is often not knowing the address — it is knowing which authority, dataset or portal to search next. Forsyningsdata Danmark was created around a simple idea: The user should know the address, not the public-data bureaucracy behind it. The WebMCP Challenge made it possible to take that idea further by allowing an AI agent to work with the same application and the same evidence as the person using it. What it does Forsyningsdata Danmark is an address-first platform for exploring Danish property, utility and environmental information. The workflow begins with one address. From there, WebMCP tools can help an agent: resolve and verify the address retrieve property and parcel context retrieve utility information perform environmental screening identify available map layers surface relevant original and local sources open the visible address profile move the interface directly to the section being discussed change interface language while preserving Denmark as the active data country The important part is that the AI does not replace the website. The agent can retrieve structured evidence, while the person can still see the same address profile, inspect the information and follow the original sources when an exact drawing, permit, pipe location or authority decision is required. How it is built Forsyningsdata Danmark is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript and uses Danish public data sources including Dataforsyningen and other property, planning and geospatial sources. The application already existed before the challenge as an unfinished public-data product. During the challenge period, it was meaningfully extended with a WebMCP integration exposing 10 structured tools through the browser's WebMCP interface. These tools cover interface context, language control, address search, property overview, utility overview, environmental screening, map-layer discovery, follow-up sources and visible interface actions. The map remains useful as part of the human interface, but WebMCP gives the agent a structured contract instead of forcing it to infer actions from buttons, text and map controls. Why WebMCP Property and infrastructure research is a strong example of why WebMCP matters. Without WebMCP, an AI agent has to interpret a presentation-oriented webpage and guess how to search, navigate and connect information. With WebMCP, the application can expose explicit actions and structured results while preserving sources, limitations and human-visible context. For example, an agent can retrieve sewer information and then move the visible address profile directly to the sewer and stormwater section. The human and the agent are therefore working with the same evidence in the same workflow. Trust and human control Not every public-data result has the same level of certainty. Forsyningsdata Danmark deliberately separates documented information from screening and orientation. Environmental screening is not presented as a laboratory result. Utility information is not presented as excavation-safe pipe geometry. Missing data is not treated as proof that no risk exists. When greater certainty is required, the workflow points the user back to the relevant original source. Challenge and learning The main challenge was not simply registering browser tools. It was deciding what each tool should return, where the trust boundaries should be, how structured agent output should relate to visible UI state, and how to keep sources and limitations attached to the result. WebMCP also introduced a different way of thinking about web applications: not just as interfaces designed for people, but as shared workspaces where people and AI agents can cooperate without hiding the underlying evidence. That is the direction Forsyningsdata Danmark is now built around. about_excerpt:
A human-controlled WebMCP workspace that helps people and agents organize verified funding applications without losing oversight.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for PrizePilot WebMCP 

 Inspiration 

 Funding and hackathon applications are repetitive, deadline-driven, and easy to lose track of. Existing trackers are passive: they store records, while browser agents often rely on brittle screen scraping. PrizePilot WebMCP explores a better contract—structured tools that let a person and an agent work from the same verified record without giving away control. 

 What it does 

 PrizePilot WebMCP turns opportunities into a prioritized, evidence-led queue. The live page exposes four WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_opportunities finds verified local records by project, organizer, tag, or status. 
 build_application_plan produces a five-step, evidence-led checklist without changing data. 
 stage_status_change proposes a local status update for human review. 
 record_verified_submission requires an HTTPS receipt before it can stage Submitted status. 
 

 Every tool call is visible in the activity log. Any state-changing request opens a clear confirmation card. Nothing is submitted to an external form automatically. 

 How we built it 

 The prototype is a responsive React and TypeScript application built with Next.js-compatible components and vinext, hosted on ChatGPT Sites. It registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool with bounded JSON schemas, length limits, read-only annotations, and explicit human-confirmation semantics. Demo records are stored locally in the browser, so the experience remains useful without an account or external database. 

 A progressive fallback detects browsers without WebMCP and keeps the full dashboard usable. The same interface supports normal manual interaction, a safe built-in agent-plan demo, and real WebMCP calls from compatible agents. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is an emerging standard, so we designed for uncertain browser support and made every capability progressively enhanced. The hardest product decision was not how much the agent could do, but where it should stop. We treated submission claims and consequential status changes as evidence-backed proposals rather than silent automation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A working public prototype with four registered WebMCP tools. 
 A shared visual activity log for people and agents. 
 Receipt-gated submission records and visible confirmation before local mutations. 
 A complete no-login fallback that preserves the product experience. 
 Clear separation between organizing work and submitting external applications. 
 

 What we learned 

 Structured page tools are more reliable and understandable than screen scraping. More importantly, WebMCP can make agent behavior easier to inspect: the interface, schemas, annotations, and confirmation state become a shared contract between the site, the user, and the agent. 

 What's next for PrizePilot WebMCP 

 Next steps are official-source synchronization, reusable evidence libraries, team review, receipt exports, deadline alerts, and connectors that can prepare—but never silently submit—applications across funding platforms.

title: Schedule-Rank-WebMCP-Adapter
pitch: A reusable WebMCP adapter that normalizes contractor availability and ranks it by scheduling-evidence reliability.
about_excerpt:
A reusable WebMCP adapter that normalizes contractor availability and ranks it by scheduling-evidence reliability.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Contractor scheduling data is fragmented. One provider exposes explicit slots, another has business hours and calendar events, and another only has workforce information. Agents need a consistent way to find suitable appointments without pretending that every availability answer is equally reliable. 

 What it does 

 Schedule-Rank-WebMCP-Adapter gives service-provider websites a shared WebMCP scheduling interface. An agent can discover a provider's services and service areas, request available times, and make an appointment request through predictable tools. 

 The adapter also assigns an evidence tier to availability: 

 
 CONFIRMED — explicit bookable slots 
 DERIVED — calculated from business hours and existing appointments 
 INFERRED — based on partial structured data such as workforce schedules 
 UNCERTAIN — based primarily on formatted free text 
 UNAVAILABLE — insufficient scheduling evidence 
 

 The tier measures the reliability of the scheduling evidence, not the quality or reputation of the contractor. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Scheduling is an action-oriented workflow. Visual page scraping forces agents to reinterpret every provider website and can hide the difference between a real slot and a plausible time. WebMCP lets each page expose structured, typed capabilities directly. 

 This creates a better experience for both people and agents: customers can compare relevant providers without repeatedly searching and filling forms, while businesses can keep their existing scheduling backend and expose only the capabilities they already support. 

 How it works 

 The shared JavaScript scheduler registers three tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 get_business_services 
 find_times_for_appointment 
 book_appointment 
 

 Provider-specific adapters supply their own backend data and functions. The shared layer normalizes those different representations and classifies their evidence strength. Three hosted examples demonstrate explicit-slot, calendar-derived, and workforce-inferred scheduling systems. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 An agent can discover which providers offer the requested service, discard providers outside the customer's postcode, query suitable times, and explain the evidence behind each result. The person retains control over the final provider and appointment choice, particularly before a booking action. 

 Testing 

 The three public provider demos were tested in ChatGPT's Codex in-app browser. Each registered all three WebMCP tools with valid JSON Schemas and no console errors. get_business_services was invoked successfully for every provider and returned provider-specific services, service areas, and timezone information.

 Codex assisted with JavaScript development, provider examples, documentation, debugging tool registration and schema problems, live WebMCP browser verification, and preparing the hackathon materials. 

 Limitations 

 This is a prototype using demonstration provider data rather than live contractor systems. Availability confidence is deterministic and based on exposed scheduling capabilities. Production-grade holds, release, revalidation, idempotency, and externally sourced contractor reputation remain future work.

title: Toolsmith
pitch: An agent can only press the buttons a website gives it. Toolsmith lets it build the one that's missing — and lets you decide whether it keeps it.
about_excerpt: An agent can only press the buttons a website gives it. Toolsmith lets it build the one that's missing — and lets you decide whether it keeps it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An AI agent can only press the buttons a website gives it — and those were decided by whoever built the site, months ago. When the button you need isn't one of them, the agent does what agents do: it guesses from the DOM, it scrapes, or it hands you a snippet of Python and hopes you run it. Adding a real one today means leaving the conversation entirely: write an MCP server, host it, edit a config file, restart the client. Minutes to days of work, and a permanent new attack surface, for a function you might call once. WebMCP already moved the button surface into the page — where the user's data and session already live, and where a human is already watching. That's enough to close the loop without leaving. (A note on vocabulary: we say "button" in the interface because that's what it is to the person looking at the screen. The spec calls the same thing a tool, and so does our code.) What it does Toolsmith registers five permanent tools on document.modelContext . One of them, forge_tool , takes a name, a JSON Schema and a JavaScript body, and turns them into a real WebMCP tool the same agent can call seconds later — but only after a human grants it. The loop: the agent calls read_workbench to learn your real column names → calls forge_tool to build the button that isn't there → the page renders it as pending , code on screen and editable, not registered → you press Test run to execute it against your real data before it exists → you press Grant it , which calls registerTool with its own AbortController → the agent presses its new button in the same conversation → Take it back aborts that signal and the button leaves the registry immediately. The count in the header — "buttons the agent can press" — is the honest answer to what can this agent do right now? And a person decided every one of them. How WebMCP is used This is not a wrapper around an existing app; the spec's lifecycle is the product. Every built button is registered via registerTool(tool, { signal }) with its own AbortController . Unregistration isn't a side feature here — aborting that signal is the revocation mechanism the entire safety argument rests on. The tool surface is genuinely dynamic and authored at runtime by the agent talking to the page. getTools() and the toolchange event drive the live count in the header. annotations.untrustedContentHint on every built button, because its output is computed by code an agent wrote minutes ago. annotations.readOnlyHint on the two read-only tools. forge_tool accepts the child tool's inputSchema as a JSON string, validates it, and passes it to registerTool as a real JSON Schema object — schema round-tripping through a tool call. Native document.modelContext when present; otherwise a vendored @mcp-b/global polyfill. The header pill says which one you got. A button you didn't read is not a button you granted Self-extension is only acceptable if refusing is as cheap as granting. So: nothing registers before a human approves; the schema and function body stay on screen and editable, with a Test run that executes against real data before registration; each call spawns a fresh Web Worker with fetch , XMLHttpRequest , WebSocket , EventSource , importScripts , storage and navigator deleted from the global scope before the code is compiled (verified: built code sees typeof fetch === "undefined" ); a 3-second leash terminates runaway loops; editing a granted button unregisters it and sends it back for re-approval; reloading returns every button to pending, never to granted; and every call, with arguments and results, lands in the activity log. This is defence in depth, not a security boundary — a Worker shares the origin, and the README says so plainly. It's enough friction that a button written thirty seconds ago can't quietly drain your data while you're still reading the diff. Challenges we ran into The hard part wasn't generating code — it was revocation. A page that lets an agent extend itself is only defensible if taking the capability back is instant and obvious. WebMCP's AbortSignal -based registration turned out to be exactly the right primitive: one controller per button made grant, edit, take-back and page-reload all collapse into the same mechanism. The second hard part was language. Our first build talked about "dynamic tool lifecycles," which is accurate and means nothing to anyone. Calling it a button — something a person already knows they can be given, and can have taken away — made the same code explain itself. What we learned That the interesting part of WebMCP isn't that a page can expose tools. It's that the set of tools is mutable at runtime , and that mutation can be put in a human's hands. Most of the spec's power lives in the { signal } argument that's easy to skim past. What's next for Toolsmith Cross-origin granting via exposedTo , so one page can hand a vetted button to another. Signed button sets, so a team can publish a reviewed collection instead of each person approving their own. And an output schema, so built buttons can declare structuredContent rather than text. title: tripcanvas
pitch: One trip itinerary on a live map, co-edited by you and your browser agent through WebMCP — the agent plans, you drag, both see the same trip.
about_excerpt: One trip itinerary on a live map, co-edited by you and your browser agent through WebMCP — the agent plans, you drag, both see the same trip. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case fits WebMCP Planning a trip with an AI today is a copy-paste loop: the model writes a text itinerary, the human re-enters it into a maps app, and neither side ever sees the other's current version. An itinerary is exactly the shared, structured, spatial state WebMCP was made for: the page holds one live map and one schedule, and document.modelContext.registerTool hands the agent the same editing operations the human's buttons call. No server, no API keys — the page is the interface for both actors. How it improves the user experience One truth. Agent tool calls mutate the same store the human edits, so the map and timeline always show the current trip. Reviewable AI. Every agent change is applied-but-pending — amber highlight, per-edit Revert, Accept all; editing a pending stop accepts it implicitly, so review never blocks flow. One undo history covers both. Real schedules, not wish lists. The page computes place resolution, walk/drive matrices, day clustering, ordering and timed schedules deterministically; the agent contributes names and judgment ( get_planning_guide ), never arithmetic. The agent sees the collaboration. get_itinerary returns the timed trip plus what the human changed since its last read plus which of its edits are still pending; get_changes is a revision feed with per-edit fates (pending / accepted / reverted). What people and agents can now do together — that was difficult or impossible before Before: the model writes a text itinerary, the human re-types it into a maps app, and every correction is another paste. Now: one live map and schedule that both edit through the same operations, with the agent's changes reviewable in place and its next read showing what the human did. Ask it to plan 3 days in Tokyo and watch pins drop ( plan_trip , ≤12 names, one atomic pending batch). Drag a stop or kick one out — the agent reads your correction and fills the gap ( add_place ). Tell it you won't have a car and it switches every non-walkable leg to live transit, naming the line and the stop to get off at ( set_leg_mode , MOTIS routes — including the ride back to your hotel). Compare a leg by walk / drive / transit before committing ( get_leg_options ), anchor a different hotel per night ( set_lodging ), rebalance days ( arrange_days , the same function as the human's button), fix an overpacked evening ( set_times ), or let it clean up after itself ( revert_pending ) — while you keep dragging, searching and undoing on the same canvas. How WebMCP was implemented Imperative registration only , once, at module scope in the top-level document before React mounts — StrictMode/HMR-safe, feature-detected as typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool === "function" . Without WebMCP the page runs as a plain manual planner with a notice. Twelve tools ( get_itinerary , get_changes , get_leg_options , plan_trip , add_place , move_stop , set_times , set_leg_mode , set_lodging , arrange_days , revert_pending , get_planning_guide ), all inside Chrome's recommended budgets — names ≤30, descriptions ≤500, param descriptions ≤150, results ≤1,500 chars — enforced by an automated audit test. readOnlyHint on the read tools; untrustedContentHint marks exactly the tools whose results carry external text (Nominatim names, MOTIS headsigns). Every tool execute is a thin adapter: zod-parse → the same exported store action the UI button imports → result string. Failures are explanatory ERROR: ... strings; tools are never unregistered. 30-second budget respected: plan_trip resolves ≤12 names serially through one app-wide Nominatim queue (≥1.1 s spacing, geocache, 8 s timeout clipped to the deadline) under a 22 s wall-clock deadline that the OSRM phases share. Pure static site: Nominatim, OSRM and transitous/MOTIS are called directly from the browser; every failure degrades to marked-approximate times or a soft error — the itinerary never blocks. Try it Open https://tripcanvas.tillmac.com in Chrome 149+ (the origin-trial token is shipped; or enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) or in the ChatGPT desktop browser with Site tools enabled, then ask your agent: "Plan 3 days in Tokyo — temples, museums, Shibuya and teamLab — we're staying at Hotel Gracery Shinjuku." The "What the agent sees" panel under the schedule prints the exact get_itinerary text live. Prior work vs. new work The pure itinerary math (schedule computation, best-insertion, geo, OSRM/MOTIS/Nominatim builders and parsers) and the Leaflet map pane are ported from my pre-challenge project intent-transition-mcp (a Claude-connector MCP server, June–July 2026) and live separated in src/ported/ . Everything WebMCP is new for this challenge (2026-08-25 →): the tool layer, the headless trip store with its by-id inverse log (= undo stack = change feed), the pending-edit model and [s#] / [c#] ids, day clustering + arrange, per-night lodging, the Nominatim queue, plan_trip orchestration, transit leg overrides, the handback renderer, and the co-editing canvas UI. title: Concierge
pitch: Your AI travel concierge that plans, compares, and books your entire trip across the web through WebMCP, with you staying in control.
about_excerpt:
Your AI travel concierge that plans, compares, and books your entire trip across the web through WebMCP, with you staying in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Concierge 

 Planning a trip today means becoming the API between five different websites. 

 You search for flights on one site, compare hotels on another, make a restaurant reservation somewhere else, book activities, then arrange transportation between everything. Even AI agents struggle with this because most websites expose information through interfaces designed for humans to click through, not structured capabilities that agents can reliably use. 

 Concierge explores a different future: a web where services are built for both people and agents. 

 With Concierge, a traveler can simply say: 

 
 “I’m going to Paris for 5 days next month. Find me a good flight, a hotel near the city center, two great dinners, a Louvre experience, and airport transportation. Keep the total under $2,500 and ask me before making any purchase over $200.” 
 

 Instead of manually operating each service, Concierge coordinates the trip across independent WebMCP-enabled services: 

 FlyNow → flights
 Stayly → hotels
 Dine → restaurants
 Explore → activities
 Ride → transportation 

 Each service exposes structured capabilities through WebMCP. Concierge can discover and use those capabilities rather than relying on fragile UI guessing. 

 The result is not another travel chatbot that simply recommends links. It is an experiment in an agent-native travel ecosystem , where specialized websites can become capabilities that an agent can compose into a complete real-world task. 

 The human remains in control. Concierge can present the complete itinerary, explain its decisions, compare alternatives, and request approval before consequential actions such as larger purchases. The traveler can intervene at any point. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 The important part of this project is not simply putting an AI chatbox on a travel website. 

 Each provider is independently useful to a human, but also exposes machine-readable tools for agents. This creates a composable ecosystem: 

 Human → Concierge → WebMCP services → Real-world task 

 A flight provider doesn't need to know about hotels. A hotel provider doesn't need to know about restaurants. Concierge composes their capabilities around the user's goal. 

 This demonstrates what becomes possible when websites stop being destinations that agents have to navigate and start becoming capabilities agents can use . 

 What we built 

 We created a lightweight ecosystem of WebMCP-enabled travel services and a Concierge interface that brings them together. 

 The provider applications intentionally resemble familiar travel products so the experience feels immediately understandable, while their underlying capabilities are exposed specifically for agent interaction. 

 The Concierge experience focuses on the difficult part: understanding a high-level travel goal, coordinating multiple services, maintaining context across them, handling dependencies, presenting the resulting plan to the human, and knowing when to ask for approval. 

 What we learned 

 Building this exposed an important distinction between an ordinary AI application and an agent-native web application. 

 An agent shouldn't have to interpret every button, infer every form field, or scrape every page. When a website explicitly exposes what an agent can do, the website becomes dramatically easier to compose with other services. 

 Concierge is our exploration of what happens when that principle is applied to an entire workflow rather than a single website. 

 The long-term vision is bigger than travel: a web where people state what they want, and interoperable websites provide the capabilities needed to make it happen.

title: Clear Dose
pitch: Transparent prescriptions. Agent-ready. Search, compare, understand, and complete simulated prescription-shopping workflows with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Transparent prescriptions. Agent-ready. Search, compare, understand, and complete simulated prescription-shopping workflows with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Cleardose main Inspiration Prescription shopping is a good example of a workflow where ordinary browser automation quickly becomes fragile. A user may need to search for a medication, identify the correct strength and form, compare fulfillment options, understand medication information, choose delivery, manage a cart, and move through checkout. An agent trying to accomplish that by visually reading a page has to continually reconstruct the application's state from text and pixels. I wanted to explore a different model: What if the website explicitly told the agent what it can do? That is what WebMCP enables. ClearDose turns the underlying actions of a prescription-shopping experience into structured tools that an agent can discover and call directly. What I built ClearDose is a local-first prescription reference and simulated commerce application. Users can: Search medications by generic or brand name Inspect structured medication information Choose exact form, strength, and quantity configurations Compare fictional pharmacy and delivery options Compare public medication reference information Create a prescription request summary Add and remove items from a cart Compare current cart savings Select delivery options Complete a simulated checkout Inspect simulated order status The same application capabilities are also exposed to WebMCP agents. For example, a user can ask: Find available sleep medications, compare the best options, add the selected option to my cart, and prepare checkout. The agent can translate that request into a sequence of structured application operations instead of visually navigating the interface. Why WebMCP ClearDose is a strong fit for WebMCP because medication and fulfillment comparisons depend on exact structured state. A meaningful comparison can depend on: medication active ingredient dosage form strength quantity fulfillment option delivery method WebMCP lets ClearDose expose those values through explicit JSON schemas rather than asking an agent to infer them from the rendered interface. ClearDose exposes tools for medication search, medication details, exact fulfillment comparison, selecting offers, cart management, delivery changes, simulated checkout, order status, medication comparison, and Drug Explorer workflows. The result is an application contract for agents instead of a collection of buttons they have to reverse-engineer. Human + Agent Collaboration One of the most important parts of the project is that there is not a separate "AI version" of the application. The normal Vue interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same underlying Pinia state and application services. If the agent adds an item to the cart, the user sees it. If the user changes the selection manually, the agent works with that new state. That allows control to move naturally between the human and the agent. The agent handles repetitive navigation and information gathering while the human remains responsible for decisions. ClearDose deliberately does not turn medication similarity into autonomous treatment recommendations. Public medication information is also kept separate from the fictional commerce layer used by the demo. How I Built It ClearDose is built with Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, browser-local storage, and WebMCP. I created a shared application action layer used by both normal UI components and WebMCP handlers. For example, the visible Add to Cart button and the add_to_cart WebMCP tool ultimately call the same underlying cart behavior. Medication information is normalized through a data layer that can work with sources including: RxNorm openFDA NADAC The application keeps public medication facts, cached data, fallback data, and fictional commerce information explicitly labeled. WebMCP tools use strict schemas, bounded results, runtime validation, state checks, and clear read/write behavior. I also built a WebMCP documentation and Agent Lab experience so the application's tool catalog, schemas, prompts, workflows, and recent tool calls can be inspected directly. Challenges I Faced One major challenge was handling a domain where two medications that look similar in a search result are not automatically interchangeable. That made exact state and provenance important throughout the application. Another challenge was keeping the WebMCP layer from becoming a second implementation of the product. I wanted the agent and the UI to share business logic instead of slowly diverging. Designing useful tool schemas was also more difficult than simply exposing JavaScript functions. Tool names, argument limits, outputs, recovery instructions, destructive actions, and context all affect how reliably an agent can use an application. What I Learned The biggest thing I learned is that making software "agent-ready" is much more than adding an AI chat box. Applications already contain useful domain operations. WebMCP provides a way to expose those operations explicitly. I also found that small composable tools work better than giant automation commands because an agent can inspect the result of each operation and decide what should happen next. What's Next ClearDose could be extended with additional verified public healthcare datasets and, where appropriate permissions and regulatory controls exist, real fulfillment integrations. More broadly, the same design applies to any complex commerce system where product configuration, provenance, comparisons, and human review matter. title: RE:PAIR
pitch: Take a photo of something broken and get clear, safe steps to fix it.
about_excerpt: Take a photo of something broken and get clear, safe steps to fix it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Cover Inspiration Most repairs begin with a broken object and a phone photo—not a service manual. People search for phrases like “lamp flickers” or “cup cracked at the base,” then receive generic advice that has never seen the object in front of them. WebMCP gave me a chance to rethink that experience. If a website can expose its capabilities as tools, a browser agent can do more than describe a page: it can work with the person inside a shared, visible workspace. That raised an important question: what should an agent be allowed to do when the outcome involves a real person holding a screwdriver? RE:PAIR is my answer. The agent can inspect evidence, operate the digital workspace, ask focused questions, and draft a cautious repair plan. It cannot feel a loose connection, smell burnt plastic, or decide that a mains-powered device is safe to open. I designed that boundary into the product instead of hiding it in a disclaimer. What it does RE:PAIR turns one photo of an everyday object into a collaborative repair workspace for a person and a browser agent. The experience can begin in three ways: The agent can select a bundled demo object, giving judges a completely agent-driven path with no manual setup. The agent can import an image from a public HTTPS URL when the source permits browser access. A person can choose a private image from their device. In that case, WebMCP prepares and focuses the uploader, then returns a successful awaiting_user handoff so the person can approve the operating-system file picker. Once an image is ready, OpenAI produces a structured visual assessment containing the likely object, visible condition, possible failure points, uncertainty, repair hotspots, clarifying questions, and safety category. The workspace then connects every view to the same state: Hotspots on the photo, the optional 3D model, the semantic hotspot list, and agent focus calls all select the same repair area. The agent can open the most useful clarifying question, but only the person can record a physical observation. The agent can draft guidance that separates evidence for a diagnosis, evidence against it, unknowns, limitations, stop conditions, and the safest next step. High-risk categories—including mains electricity, damaged batteries, gas, medical devices, structural systems, and unknown chemicals—trigger a deterministic professional-help stop. No repair instructions are generated in those cases. For suitable objects, an image-to-3D provider can generate a GLB that the user can orbit, zoom, and explode. The photo, hotspot controls, and repair guidance remain fully usable if 3D generation is unavailable, so 3D enhances the experience without becoming a single point of failure. Every browser-agent action appears in a compact, always-visible assistant panel. It shows the tool source, lifecycle state, timing, redacted input and result, and the visible change caused by the action. This makes the agent’s work inspectable instead of magical. The WebMCP contract is deliberately narrow. The agent can read workspace state, select a demo, import a public image, prepare the private-image uploader, start or cancel work, focus a hotspot, request a human observation, draft guidance, and undo its own changes. Only the person can grant access to a local file, report a physical observation, approve a repair, or mark the work complete. How I built it The frontend uses React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. Zustand manages session-only workspace state, Zod validates every boundary, and Three.js—through React Three Fiber and Drei—powers the optional 3D scene. The WebMCP runtime registers tools on the browser’s model-context API. Registration is stage-aware and diff-based: the agent only sees actions that are valid for the workspace’s current state, newly available tools are registered, and retired tools are removed. Every mutating tool receives an expected state version. If the page changes between the agent reading the workspace and taking an action, the tool returns a structured stale-state error instead of silently overwriting newer work. Registration refreshes also wait for in-flight calls to finish, allowing a mutation that changes its own availability to return cleanly. I designed the image tools around browser security rather than around a simulated success: Bundled samples give the agent a reliable, zero-click demo path. URL imports accept only HTTPS sources, reject embedded credentials, enforce supported image types and the 24 MB limit, and still respect the remote server’s CORS policy. Local file access remains user-controlled. The tool prepares the uploader and reports an awaiting_user state instead of pretending that an agent can bypass an operating-system permission boundary. The backend consists of stateless Vercel serverless routes for visual analysis, 3D generation, and plan drafting. It does not store user images or provider jobs. The server validates image bytes and dimensions, binds the image and analysis to a short-lived HMAC-signed session, wraps provider job identifiers in opaque signed tokens, and returns only validated public contracts. OpenAI analysis uses Structured Outputs with storage disabled. On the client, images are resized to a 2,048-pixel long edge and encoded below 2.9 MB before upload. Polling uses bounded exponential backoff, cancellation propagates through compression and network requests, and object URLs are revoked when an image is replaced, reset, or unmounted. My test suite covers the domain model and WebMCP runtime with Vitest, the interface with Testing Library, and end-to-end accessibility and real browser tool registration with Playwright and axe-core. Challenges I ran into The mock lied My first WebMCP mock behaved more conveniently than the browser. It passed an options object to execute , replaced duplicate registrations, and never interrupted an active tool call. The real API behaved differently: duplicate names could be rejected, execution received only its declared input, and registration changes could affect an in-flight call. The result was a classic integration trap: everything passed in unit tests and failed in the browser. I rebuilt registration as a state diff, handled duplicate-registration errors safely, deferred refreshes until active calls returned, and added real Chromium coverage so the mock could not drift again. A file picker is a permission boundary My first uploader tool highlighted the page correctly but reported HUMAN_ACTION_REQUIRED as a failure. That was technically honest but poor product semantics—and it made a successful WebMCP action look broken. I changed the contract. The tool now succeeds after preparing and focusing the uploader, returning awaiting_user with one clear instruction. For a completely autonomous demonstration, the agent can instead select a bundled sample or import a public image URL. This gives me both a smooth demo and a truthful privacy model. Serverless behavior differed from local development Routes that worked locally initially returned 500 and 504 responses on Vercel. I converted them to fetch-style handlers with ESM-safe imports and tightened the contracts at the deployment boundary. 3D generation was not reliable enough to own the critical path The image-to-3D provider sometimes returned generic failures and incomplete pending payloads. I separated authentication, payment, and request errors, accepted valid placeholder fields while a job is pending, and redesigned the product so the repair assessment always comes first. A failed 3D model no longer blocks the repair workflow. Drawing the authority line It was tempting to let the agent answer clarifying questions or approve a plan because that would make the demo faster. I decided that any action requiring physical presence should remain a human action. In RE:PAIR, those actions are either omitted from the tool surface or represented as explicit handoffs. Accomplishments that I’m proud of A real WebMCP experience verified through the browser’s actual tool API, not only through mocks. A fully agent-driven demo path: the agent can select a sample image, analyze it, focus the likely failure point, ask for missing physical evidence, and draft the safest plan. A truthful private-file flow that treats the operating-system picker as user consent and reports it as a successful handoff. An activity panel that makes every agent action legible without exposing image data, signed URLs, tokens, or hidden reasoning. Deterministic safety stops for high-risk repair categories, independent of model confidence. A workspace that remains usable when WebMCP, WebGL, or the 3D provider is unavailable. Keyboard-accessible camera controls and a semantic hotspot list, backed by automated accessibility checks. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools represent meaningful product actions rather than low-level clicks. A browser agent bec

title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

title: YallaQueue Agent Desk
pitch: WhatsApp booking meets an agent-native live queue for local service businesses.
about_excerpt: WhatsApp booking meets an agent-native live queue for local service businesses. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Many small service businesses manage appointments through WhatsApp and then manually transfer those bookings into a schedule or queue. This wastes time, creates booking conflicts, and makes it difficult to keep customers and staff working from the same information. I created YallaQueue to connect WhatsApp booking, a live business dashboard, and an AI agent. What it does YallaQueue converts natural WhatsApp messages into confirmed appointments. It can: Check whether an appointment time is available Prevent conflicting bookings Assign a queue number Save the appointment Send a WhatsApp confirmation Display the appointment on a live shop dashboard The signed-in shop owner can also use two WebMCP tools through a browser agent: get_queue_summary returns the current queue without exposing customer phone numbers. update_queue_status changes one appointment to confirmed, completed, cancelled, or no-show. For example, the owner can ask: “Summarize today’s queue.” “Mark queue 1 completed.” The dashboard immediately shows the updated state. How we built it YallaQueue uses Next.js and React for the dashboard, Supabase and PostgreSQL for authentication and appointment data, and n8n with the WhatsApp Cloud API for messaging automation. The dashboard registers two browser-native WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool calls a protected server route using the owner’s active login. The server checks authentication, shop membership, input validity, appointment ownership, and database row-level security before returning data or making a change. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was giving the agent useful access without bypassing security. The agent must only access appointments belonging to the signed-in owner’s shop. Customer phone numbers must not appear in tool results, and an appointment must not be changed without a clear user request. Another challenge was keeping WhatsApp, the database, the dashboard, and the agent synchronized so they all display the same queue state. Testing WebMCP also required enabling its experimental Chrome flag and using ChatGPT Work so the browser agent could discover the registered tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of Connected a real WhatsApp booking flow to a live dashboard Built and deployed two working WebMCP tools Used structured tool data instead of visual browser guessing Protected every tool route with server-side authorization Excluded customer phone numbers from agent responses Successfully tested both reading and updating the live queue through ChatGPT Work What we learned I learned how websites can provide structured tools for both humans and AI agents. I also learned that WebMCP does not replace application security. Agent actions must still pass normal authentication, authorization, input validation, ownership checks, and database security rules. What's next for YallaQueue The next steps are adding more carefully controlled tools for availability searches, creating appointments, rescheduling, and cancellations. I also plan to add clearer confirmation screens for sensitive actions, support multiple shops and staff members, and improve reporting for business owners.
