title: Spokes - a collaborative map to help with coordination
pitch: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you.
about_excerpt: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you. Like Comment Story Updates Social media banner for Spokes Spokes — Devpost submission Live: https://spokes.alainschlesser.com/ Inspiration Groups are bad at picking somewhere to go, and the reason is structural rather than social. The needs that decide the answer are scattered across people and arrive piecemeal: a dietary restriction here, a budget there, a veto that lands after everyone else has settled, and at least one reason nobody wants to say out loud. A search results page optimises a single query. A group chat collects messages. Neither keeps a shared model of what the group has actually asked for, and neither lets a sensitive constraint count toward the decision without being explained to everybody first. That last part is what made this worth building for WebMCP specifically. A personal agent already knows things about its user that the user would rather not broadcast to five friends. Until now the only way to put that knowledge to work was to hand it to a shared service. I wanted to find out whether an agent could advocate for someone inside a live page, as that person and within an authority they granted, while the reason itself never left their client. What it does Three people open one planning room from a link. They see the same live map and the same brief of what the group has asked for so far. Each person states what matters in a single composer bar and chooses who may see it before they speak . A need can be shared, private, or agent-only. The server evaluates a private need and peers see only its effect on the count. An agent-only need stays with your agent and never reaches the server at all. The app suggests the next thing worth asking about from the data itself, never from a built-in list of categories. Every need becomes a row you can set aside. Press and hold a row and the map shows the room without that need, live. The cost of a need becomes visible instead of argued about. The room recomputes which places still work after every move, and it counts what is merely unverified separately from what actually failed. Missing data is drawn as its own state rather than quietly dropping a place. When nothing satisfies everyone, Spokes does not name who is blocking. It privately offers each person a quantified way out. The organizer sees "widen the area from 800 m to 1.2 km, brings back 4 places". The person who stated a need sees "let this need be nice-to-have, +12 places". Consent is explicit and confirmed on the page. Once the group agrees, the composer gives way to arrival: a travel mode and a one-tap handoff to the map app everyone already has. Alongside all of it, your personal ChatGPT can act in the same session through WebMCP. It can catch up on what changed while you were away, inspect places, put one forward, rule one out, or grant an adjustment. Your agent can assist you, or negotiate for you outright. How I built it A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). Fastify and a Postgres event log sit behind a WebSocket realtime channel. The front end is React and Vite with MapLibre GL over keyless OpenFreeMap tiles. TypeBox contracts are shared by both sides behind a hashed contract-manifest gate. Place data is a one-time OpenStreetMap extract of Berlin Mitte. The WebMCP surface is 22 tools registered imperatively on document.modelContext at page load, 10 for negotiation and 12 spatial. Each is a narrow function with closed enum schemas, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and a capped result budget. The page works fully without WebMCP. The tools are an additional way in. Four decisions did most of the work. Two protocols over the WebMCP substrate. WebMCP itself only carries tool names and schemas. So the first sync_session call returns a capability manifest that teaches the agent a domain-independent negotiation protocol (identity, revision sync, privacy tiers, requirements, stances, adjustments, consent, agreement) and a spatial-destination domain layered on top. Server-owned identity and per-viewer projections. Actor identity comes only from the bearer token. No tool argument accepts an actor id. Every event is stored once and projected per viewer, so unauthorised fields never appear in another participant's HTTP body or WebSocket frame. The test suite asserts this at the wire, not at the function boundary. Revision discipline instead of pretend realtime. Every mutation carries the agent's last-seen revision. A stale one returns a structured sync_required with a delta instead of acting on old state. That fits an agent that participates in bursts far better than a subscription it never really holds. Consent an agent cannot forge. An agent may recommend a grant, but a change beyond what the user delegated only stages . Staging mints a single-use code delivered on the participant's own realtime channel. The applying command must carry it back, and the code never appears in any tool result. Eligibility, minimal-conflict-set detection and the impasse counterfactuals are all deterministic. No model is allowed to invent a feasibility fact. 364 automated tests across three lanes: 222 unit, 128 three-user API, and 14 Playwright specs driving three isolated browser contexts. Challenges I ran into Privacy that is neither a lie nor a hole. The rule I settled on is that a private need's effect is always public and its content never leaves its owner. Both halves matter. Hiding the effect would make the count inexplicable, and leaking the content is the whole thing I was avoiding. It took a real redesign to stop routing private predicates through shared state "just for rendering", and a wire-level test suite to prove I had. Proving a human consented, honestly. My first cut let a bearer token commit an agreement over plain HTTP without ever touching the page. The realtime-only nonce closes that. It still is not proof a human clicked, because the realtime channel authenticates with the same token. Rather than overclaim, I wrote the residual threat model down in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md . Keeping the interface domain-agnostic. It is hard not to type a domain word into a heading. What saved it was a rule on the server side. The server returns the facets present across the current result set, each with a mandatory unknown count, and the client renders whatever it gets. There is no domain branch anywhere in the front end, which is also what lets a human and an agent reason over the same vocabulary. Deployment, on the last evening. I had prepared a Coolify deployment and abandoned it at the gate. Its Traefik has documented WebSocket failures on compose stacks, and the room is a WebSocket. The January 2026 disclosure put eleven critical CVEs in a control plane that runs as root. Its baseline would have claimed a quarter of a 4 GB box before Postgres started. The existing compose file was already a correct production stack. It needed twenty lines of Caddy in front, not a PaaS. That deploy went out with nineteen minutes to spare, after a self-inflicted detour in which a redeploy overwrote the host's generated Postgres password and stranded the database behind credentials nothing had written down. Two rendering bugs that looked like design problems. Vite's dependency optimiser broke MapLibre's worker, so the basemap never drew. A CSS animation setting transform silently overwrote a positioning translate and threw pins at their anchors. Both cost hours before either was understood. Accomplishments that I'm proud of An agent that can advocate for a constraint it never discloses. The agent screens places locally and returns per-place verdicts. The council folds them into eligibility, and peers see the aggregate effect with no route back to the cause. That is the capability I most wanted WebMCP to make possible, and it works. Press and hold. Holding a need shows the map without it, live, and releasing restores it. It turns an argument about whether a need is reasonable into a number you can see, and it is the one gesture everybody understood without being told. An impasse resolver that refuses to assign blame. When nothing satisfies everyone, the room offers each person a private, quantified route out, phrased as a consequence rather than an instruction. Honest unverified state. Missing data renders as a hollow pin and a separate count. A place is never silently dropped for lacking a value, and unknown is never drawn as failure. Two independent adversarial reviews: a protocol-invariant audit and a cross-family model review of the server, then two further reviews of the rebuilt client. The privacy and agreement-integrity findings were fixed and are covered by tests. I published the deferred items instead of hiding them. What I learned An agent is not a fast user, and modelling it as one produces bugs. It participates in bursts, disappears, an
video_title: Spokes: collaborative coordination assistant · WebMCP Challenge 2026 explainer video
video_transcript_excerpt: Picking a place with friends pays for boring reason. The needs live in different heads. They arrive one at a time and one of them is something somebody will not say out loud. Spokes puts the whole group on one live map and it lets you bring your own assistant. It starts with a sentence. I tell chat GPT what the group is trying to do. Because Spokes talks to assistants directly, the assistant can work on the product on my behalf. Pick the area, set up the room, hand back the invite. Nobody learned an app, nobody filled in a form. Show the code and the others are in. Sarah would like to sit outside. She adds it. Everyone's map settles. The places that still work stay bright, the rest fade where they stand. Press and hold her need and the map shows the room without it. What a need costs becomes a number you can see instead of something to argue about. Joe has a need he would rather not explain. He marks it private. The room learns only that a private condition ruled some places out, not what it was, not whose. And now nothing works for everyone. This is where a group chat goes quiet. Spokes does not wait and it does not name who is blocking. It offers each person a private way out with a number attached. Joe sees what comes back if his need became optional. Sarah sees the same for sitting outside. I see what a wider area brings back. Each decides alone. Joe leaves his, nobody asks him why. Sarah lets hers go and the room opens up again. For some places, the information is hollow. The map does not know enough about them and it says so instead of guessing. This is where an assistant earns its place. I ask it to find out. It reads menus and websites and records what it finds in the room. Hollow pins fill in for everyone. It cannot see what Joe needs because it only knows what I know, but everything it does learn, the whole group gets. I have the assistant put forward a place it just checked. The court lands with everyone. Sarah looks and rules it out. The assistant notices the room moved, takes the veto into account, and suggests another. This time everyone is in. Only a person can settle it, and only once everyone has said so. An assistant can help you decide. It never decides for you. And then off you go. Pick how you're getting there and hand off to the map you already use. One room needs to count without being shown a way out for everyone instead of blame, and an assistant that works inside the room as you. Finds what the map cannot and keeps what you keep. Spokes.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. title: Stand: an arranging studio your agent writes in
pitch: An arranging studio your agent writes in. It writes the parts; the page refuses any note your players can't reach and says why; the agent fixes itself. You listen, choose, and print each part.
about_excerpt: An arranging studio your agent writes in. It writes the parts; the page refuses any note your players can't reach and says why; the agent fixes itself. You listen, choose, and print each part. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Published arrangements never fit a real school ensemble: six clarinets and no trombone, a first-year trumpet who tops out at written D5, a key the class can actually read. So directors rewrite by hand, part by part, checking every range and every transposition. Stand hands that work to an agent — and puts the checking in the page, at the moment the agent writes. agent → page put a D6 in the trumpet, bar 1 page → agent No. Written E6 (sounding D6) is above the elementary trumpet range F3–C5. Drop it an octave. agent → page then G4 page → agent Written. Nobody typed a note in between. The page refused, the agent read the reason, and it corrected itself. What it does Load a public-domain melody, then say who is playing: "two flutes, clarinet, alto sax, trumpet, trombone, snare — fifth grade." Your agent writes each part straight into the score through this page's tools. The page renders real notation (conductor score and transposed part views), plays it, and checks every note it is asked to write: Range — a note that player cannot reach at that level is refused , with the bar, the note in both spellings, the allowed range and the fix. Transposition — the agent never does the arithmetic. Tools take and return sounding pitch; the page derives every written part, so a clarinet reads D while the score is in C. Bar arithmetic — a bar that does not add up never lands. Taste — the one thing a model cannot judge, because it cannot hear. ask_human puts two candidate endings on screen with a ▶ on each and waits for the person to listen and choose. You drag notes by hand, lock the bars you like ( write_part skips them and says so), mute parts, and export MusicXML, one file per player, or MIDI. Nothing leaves the browser unless you export it: the Worker only serves static files. Why this needs WebMCP The page holds what the agent cannot fake. Notation, sound, per-instrument ranges at four teaching levels, transposition. That turns the tool boundary into a music guardrail — the page can say no , precisely, and the model self-corrects from the error. An agent driving a UI through screenshots gets none of that, and a backend MCP server cannot show a person the score it is changing. The agent cannot hear; the person can. ask_human is not a confirmation dialog bolted onto a chatbot. It is the one judgement a language model genuinely cannot make, handed back by design. One score, two hands. Locks, hand edits and tool calls share the same live document and the same timeline. Nobody copy-pastes MusicXML through a chat window. How I built it WebMCP : document.modelContext.registerTool with one AbortController per surface. Three phase surfaces — empty (4 tools), arranging (18), exported (3). readOnlyHint on reads, descriptions under 500 characters, bars 1-based at the API boundary and 0-based in the store, every failure written so a model can act on it, play reporting needs_gesture when the browser has not started audio yet. No tool can export, print, lock a bar, or answer for the person. Those are buttons. Music core (pure TypeScript, unit-tested): pitch and key arithmetic; a 23-instrument table with clef, transposition and a sounding range per level; the checker (bar length, unknown pitch, range, level-appropriate rhythm and key, leaps, voice crossing, parallel fifths); a rule-based harmonizer; MusicXML with correct per-part <transpose> ; MIDI; part extraction. Page : React 19 + Vite. VexFlow for the conductor score and transposed part views, with click-to-edit, lock badges and a playback cursor. Tone.js for per-section timbres and A/B variant preview. One store funnels every mutation — agent, hand, or demo — through the same validation, locks, undo and log. Tests : 104 unit tests across the music core; 8 Playwright end-to-end tests driving every tool through a faithful document.modelContext stand-in, including the refused write, the locked bar, the human's A/B choice and export-is-human-only. All pass against the deployed site. Judge mode : ?judge=1 runs the whole loop with captions and no agent. Challenges Making refusal useful instead of annoying: the error has to name the bar, both spellings of the note, the allowed range and a fix the model can act on. Transposition correctness got its own verification pass — written = sounding + transposition, but MusicXML's <transpose> is the negative of that, and six instrument ranges turned out to be entered in written pitch where sounding was required. And keeping a score readable while an agent rewrites it live. What I learned The most valuable thing a page can give an agent is not more actions. It is the ability to say no, precisely. And the most valuable thing an agent can give a musician is a first draft it knows it cannot verify alone. Try it (no login, nothing to install) Open the live URL in ChatGPT's built-in browser (model Sol or Terra). "Load Ode to Joy, set up a beginning band — two flutes, clarinet, alto sax, trumpet, trombone, snare — at elementary level, and arrange it." Watch for a refused write; the agent rewrites it an octave lower. Then "play bars 1 to 4" (the page asks for one click first — browsers only start audio on a gesture). "Give me two options for the last two bars and let me hear them." The card waits for your ear. Lock a bar with 🔒, then "rewrite the trumpet part" — the locked bar comes back untouched. "Show me the trumpet part alone" , then export Parts, MusicXML or MIDI with the buttons. No agent? Press ▶ Watch a 60-second demo on the start screen, or add ?judge=1 to the URL. What's next MusicXML import so you can bring your own tune, real instrument samples, per-player practice tracks, and a shared link so a section leader's agent can suggest changes to one part. title: VenueMind
pitch: Agent-native venue operations: design, validate, approve, run, and audit safer event layouts with humans and WebMCP agents working together.
about_excerpt: Agent-native venue operations: design, validate, approve, run, and audit safer event layouts with humans and WebMCP agents working together. Like Comment Story Updates Setup instructions, WebMCP tool references, MCP integration, and agent skills in one documentation site Review the original floor plan alongside the proposed changes and locked fixtures Inspect Plan v3.3 and the recorded approval alongside the previous version Four violet ghost changes show the proposed layout before approval Check accessible routes, capacity, circulation, and sightlines against the proposed changes Inspiration I got attached to VenueMind early. I was building solo, and I wanted to take it beyond a good-looking floor plan into a product with working validation, revision history, and tools an agent could use. Venue planning gave me a problem worth doing that for. Moving a seating block might widen an aisle but reduce capacity. Another change might improve the view of the stage while interfering with something that needs to stay fixed. A drawing can look reasonable while hiding those tradeoffs. I wanted an agent to help work through a change, with the person responsible for the room able to see exactly what it proposed before accepting it. What it does VenueMind is a venue planning and operations workspace where people and agents work on the same versioned floor plan. The demo follows one request: Keep 400 seats, widen the center aisle to six feet, improve sightlines, and preserve locked objects. The agent calls venue.inspect_layout , then venue.preview_revision . Four proposed changes appear as violet ghost shapes over the existing plan. The accepted layout stays unchanged during review. Next, venue.validate_layout checks access, capacity, circulation, locks, and sightlines. The interface shows the proposed layout alongside the measurements, so the reviewer can judge the consequences. Approval through the interface commits Plan v3.3. The agent can then inspect the activity ledger, verify replay, and export the validated plan. The wider product includes proposal branches, conflict handling, undo and redo, operational checks, and several export formats. I also built a documentation site, an SDK, agent skills, and a standalone MCP server. Why WebMCP fits A floor plan contains information an agent should not have to reconstruct from a screenshot. Objects have dimensions, stable IDs, relationships, and locks. A proposal also belongs to a particular version of that plan. WebMCP lets VenueMind expose that information as structured tools inside the page. The agent can inspect the actual layout and request validation results while the person reviews the same state visually. This avoids a frustrating handoff where an assistant describes a suggested arrangement in chat and someone has to recreate it in a separate editor. In VenueMind, the suggestion becomes a visible proposal with measurable consequences. The reviewer can inspect it where they already work. How I built it I built VenueMind with Next.js, TypeScript, and shadcn/ui. Vercel hosts the frontend. A Cloudflare Worker handles the API, with D1 for persistence. The foundation is a versioned venue model with stable object IDs. Both interface actions and WebMCP tools pass through a shared command bus, so they use the same application logic. The page registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . A shared contract registry defines their schemas and authorization requirements. Tool execution checks inputs and permissions before it reaches the underlying operations. The agent requests a proposal; application code performs the geometry checks. VenueMind does not ask a language model to decide whether an aisle meets a configured width. I deliberately left approval out of the agent tool list. The intended workflow asks a person to review the proposal through the interface before committing it. Codex helped me implement and test the application, refactor the code into TypeScript, and work through browser integration. I used HyperFrames to edit the demo and Kokoro for its narration. Challenges and lessons Getting the proposal lifecycle right took more work than drawing the preview. A proposal can look correct and still be based on an outdated plan. Validation, approval, and export need to agree about the version they refer to. That drove the work on conflict checks, command receipts, and replayable history. Browser integration also needed careful testing. Chromium 149, used for the recording, exposed native WebMCP through navigator.modelContext . The recorder aliases that native object to document.modelContext . I later verified the hosted workflow in Chrome 152 using native document.modelContext directly, without an alias or mocked registry. Hosted testing caught another issue that local testing missed. Each guest had a separate organization, but the sample projects shared one globally unique project ID. The API correctly rejected the collision, and the frontend incorrectly displayed it as a synchronization conflict. I fixed the sample identity so each organization gets its own stable project ID, then tested separate guest sessions and persistence after reload. The build made the value of a shared command bus concrete. Every separate implementation of an action creates another place for behavior to drift. Keeping UI and agent operations together made their results easier to compare and test. I also had to keep the ambition practical. I removed file storage when R2's activation requirements did not fit my available setup. What the demo proves, and what remains The 75-second demo shows the working inspection, proposal, validation, commit, history, and export loop using local guest state. Codex operates the approval button to demonstrate the reviewer interface; the recording does not demonstrate an independently authenticated human approval or multi-user cloud synchronization. Separate testing verified the full workflow on the hosted app in Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled. Native tool calls completed inspection, proposal creation, validation, ledger inspection, replay, and export, with approval through the interface. D1 retained the committed v3.3 plan after reload. A second guest received an independent sample project and could not access the first guest's project. Validation checks configured geometry and policies. It does not replace professional venue inspection or safety certification. My next priority is testing more layouts. I want to find the cases where a proposal looks convincing but fails a constraint, and make those failures easy for the reviewer to understand. title: GYST - Get Your Stuff Together
pitch: Agents are good at getting things done. GYST is for the harder part: seeing your own patterns. It reads your week and drafts the review over WebMCP — only you commit it.
about_excerpt: Agents are good at getting things done. GYST is for the harder part: seeing your own patterns. It reads your week and drafts the review over WebMCP — only you commit it. Like Comment Story Updates 1 GYST Home Page Close the day preview Weekly Review with identified context GYST in ChatGPT Desktop Inspiration I am bad at accountability. Not casually bad. I mean I have started over more times than I want to write down. This year the list was specific: clear the debt, rebuild the credit, move, get healthy, build consulting income on the side. I had tried the habit apps and the streak counters and the journal with the nice paper. Capture was never my problem. The problem was that nothing ever held me to the record. What actually worked was a ritual, not a tool. End the day by naming what moved, what got in the way, and the one commitment I am carrying into tomorrow. End the week by reading that record back and making a single decision about it. Boring, repeatable, and very hard to keep alone. So I started running the ritual with an AI assistant. And about a week in I hit the thing that turned into this project. An agent is good at exactly the parts I am bad at. It reads the week back to me. It notices I have deferred the same commitment four days running, which I would not have noticed, because I am the one deferring it. It drafts the entry while I talk. All of that is real help. But the moment it writes the record for me, the record stops being mine. And accountability you can hand off isn't accountability. It's a report. That's the whole thing. Let the agent do everything up to the decision, and nothing past it. What it does GYST — get your stuff together — is a human-owned daily and weekly ritual ledger. The entire product is one boundary, and the front page says it three ways: The ledger supplies bounded context. You and the agent prepare a visible draft. A human action commits the record. The daily ritual asks four things. What moved. What blocked you, and what kind of blocker it was — internal, external gate, capacity, clarity, dependency. How yesterday's commitment actually went. And the single commitment you're carrying into tomorrow. One. Not a list. The weekly ritual is the part I'd been missing for years. It hands you findings computed in Postgres and bounded to the current week: you've failed to complete this specific commitment three times, this blocker type keeps recurring, here's a win you wrote down and then never mentioned again, here's work you did that wasn't on any priority you named, here's a date coming at you. Not advice. Observations with the evidence attached. You supply the decision, the arrow — up, steady, down — and up to five dated priorities. Around that: reminder emails on your own schedule in your own timezone, portable JSON and Markdown exports, and account deletion that actually deletes. And a demo you can open with no account and no email, which drops you into a fictional ledger with a full committed week behind it and today left open to conduct. Why this belongs on WebMCP The ritual is a conversation. The record is a row in Postgres with an owner. Those want two different interfaces, and WebMCP is the reason I didn't have to pick one. The site declares the verbs, in its own language. A general-purpose browser agent has to drive my form by looking at it and clicking at it. Instead the page publishes gyst.record_blocker , gyst.score_previous_commitment , gyst.set_weekly_decision — the actual vocabulary of the ritual, with strict schemas and descriptions that say what I mean: Draft-only. Do not invent wording. This never commits or closes the record. Auth and isolation come along for free, and they're real. The tools run in the signed-in tab, as the person, against owner-scoped routes. There is no API key to hand an agent and no separate MCP server sitting somewhere holding privileged credentials. Row-level security on every user-owned table means an agent cannot reach another owner's ledger. Postgres enforces that. Not a system prompt asking politely. And the capability set is the argument. Fourteen ritual tools. Every one of them is read-only or draft-only. There is no commit tool, no delete tool, no export tool, no history tool, no SQL tool. Not disabled — absent. That distinction is the whole reason this belongs on WebMCP instead of in a chat window: I got to express "the agent may prepare, only the human may decide" as a real boundary instead of an instruction I hope it follows. Here's what that makes possible that I couldn't do before. I can talk through my day out loud, the way I'd talk to a person, while a structured and owned ledger fills in behind me — and then press commit myself. Before this I had to choose. A chat log gave me help with no structure and no ownership. A form gave me structure and ownership with no help, alone, at eleven at night, which is exactly when I skip it. How I built it Next.js 16.3.3 on the App Router, React 19, strict TypeScript, Tailwind 4, on Vercel. Supabase Postgres 17 is the only durable ledger. A stateless Cloudflare Worker on a */15 cron sends the reminders through Resend. Turnstile guards signup and demo entry, verified by Supabase Auth rather than by my app. AGPL-3.0, code is public. The WebMCP layer is a client component on each ritual route. It registers that ritual's seven tools through document.modelContext.registerTool with an AbortSignal , so the daily surface exists on /daily , the weekly on /weekly , and both unregister when you navigate away. Three site-level tools — status, open daily, open weekly — live on the public pages and expose no account data at all. Each draft mutation posts to an owner-scoped route handler, which validates against a strict JSON schema and writes only draft columns through a SECURITY INVOKER RPC. Every one returns uncommitted: true plus the fields it touched, and the page turns that around and shows it to you: record blocker updated blocker text; it was not committed , with the affected fields marked in the form. The ordinary form stays fully usable with no agent present. And when the tools don't register in your browser, the page says so instead of quietly doing nothing. Commit is a human-only server action with expected-version optimistic concurrency, and a committed session is immutable. I also built it the way the product behaves, which was not an accident. Four lanes — a root orchestrator, a database and security lane, an application and WebMCP lane, and an infrastructure and release lane. Agents did bounded work freely inside their lane. Every irreversible step — remote migration, secret, deployment, real email, merge — stopped at a gate and waited for me. The build process and the product are making the same argument, which is either good design or a personality trait. Challenges I ran into The judge demo almost shipped broken, and the schema is what caught it. My plan called for a shared demo account. But ritual_sessions is unique on (user_id, kind, period_start) and committed sessions are immutable, so the first judge to commit would have left every judge after them unable to do the one thing I most wanted them to do. I replaced it with a Turnstile-protected anonymous sign-in and a SECURITY INVOKER seed function that refuses permanent accounts, refuses to overwrite a ledger that already exists, closes its seeded days through the ordinary draft-to-committed path, and derives every date at call time so the demo never goes stale. Anonymous users take the same authenticated role as everyone else, so all 38 owner-only policies apply to them unchanged. Nothing was relaxed to make the demo work. Owner isolation went from something I assert to something you can watch happen. I put Turnstile in the wrong layer. I was verifying the challenge in the application before calling signup, which felt fine until I looked at it properly. It can't protect the anonymous sign-in endpoint, because that endpoint is publicly reachable with the browser's own publishable key. My check wasn't in the path. Verification moved into Supabase Auth and the secret left my app entirely. The agent was editing my draft silently. Early on it would call a tool and the page would just change. Which is the exact feeling I built this thing to prevent. (Nothing quite like watching your own product do the thing you wrote it to stop.) The field-level provenance markers and the live "recent agent draft changes" panel came out of that afternoon. And I kept wanting to add a commit tool. Three times, at least. Every one of them would have made a better ninety-second video and a worse product. Accomplishments I'm proud of Fourteen WebMCP tools with zero write authority over the ledger, and a test that proves it rather than a paragraph that claims it — a source-level contract check that fails if a commit path ever appears in the tool surface. Nine pgTAP files and 270 database assertions, including negative cross-owner tests. 92 unit tests. Six Playwright specs.

title: careercrew
pitch: CareerCrew uses AI and WebMCP to find best-fit jobs, tailor evidence-based resumes, and assist applications while candidates approve every submission and stay in control
about_excerpt: CareerCrew uses AI and WebMCP to find best-fit jobs, tailor evidence-based resumes, and assist applications while candidates approve every submission and stay in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Job searching is often repetitive, fragmented, and stressful. Candidates move between career pages, compare job descriptions, rewrite resumes, prepare for interviews, and repeatedly enter the same information. Existing automation tools may save time, but they can also recommend irrelevant roles, invent resume content, or submit applications without enough candidate oversight. We created CareerCrew to offer useful automation without taking control away from the candidate. Our goal was to build a trustworthy career assistant that uses WebMCP to connect AI agents with structured web actions while keeping every important decision transparent and candidate-approved. What it does CareerCrew supports the job-application journey from resume review to guarded application assistance. Candidates can upload a PDF, DOCX, or TXT resume. CareerCrew extracts their skills, experience, contact information, and suitable career tracks for review. It then evaluates available jobs using an explainable 0–100 fit score and recommends the strongest qualifying role from each company. For a selected role, CareerCrew prepares an application packet using only evidence-backed, candidate-approved experience. It also creates cited interview-preparation plans covering technical questions, coding, system design, and behavioral interviews. CareerCrew exposes structured WebMCP tools for working with candidate profiles, campaigns, job matches, and application questions, approvals, and interview plans. After receiving explicit approval, its Chrome companion can preview and fill verified information into supported Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby application forms. It pauses whenever a mandatory question needs candidate input and never guesses sensitive answers such as salary expectations, work authorization, relocation, or notice period. How we built it We designed CareerCrew as a modular full-stack platform: Next.js, React and TypeScript power the candidate dashboard. FastAPI, Python and Pydantic provide the backend workflows and validation. WebMCP exposes nine structured tools through the web interface. Auth.js provides configurable Google authentication. PDF and DOCX libraries process uploaded resumes. A Manifest V3 Chrome companion supports guarded ATS form assistance. One-time, origin-bound application codes connect approved CareerCrew data with the browser companion. Vitest, Testing Library and Pytest verify the frontend, extension, and API. Synthetic Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby portals allow us to demonstrate and test the workflow safely. The hackathon version uses clearly labelled demonstration jobs and ATS pages, so we do not represent demo actions as real applications. ## Challenges we ran into One major challenge was balancing automation with candidate control. Automatically filling and submitting forms sounds convenient,but sensitive questions cannot be answered safely without the candidate. We designed explicit approval boundaries and pause states instead of allowing the system to guess. Another challenge was supporting different ATS structures. Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby organise their forms differently, so the browser companion needed separate adapters and careful field detection. We also needed to keep resume tailor-trustworthy. CareerCrew links generated resume content to approved evidence so that stronger wording does not become fabricated experience. Finally, we had to design WebMCP tools that were useful to AI agents while remaining narrow, predictable, and safe for sensitive actions. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that CareerCrew is more than a static concept—it is a tested, end-to-end local vertical slice. It can process resumes, build a candidate profile, explain job-fit scores, shortlist roles, prepare evidence-based application content, generate cited interview plans, request approval, and securely hand verified information to a browser companion. We successfully integrated nine WebMCP tools and demonstrated the guarded workflow across synthetic Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby portals. Most importantly, CareerCrew does not sacrifice trust for automation. It never fabricates qualifications, treats a fit score as hiring probability, or assumes that clicking a button means an application was successfully submitted. What we learned We learned that responsible automation is not about automating every possible step. It is about knowing which actions can be automated safely and where human judgement is essential. WebMCP showed us how structured tools can make interactions between AI agents and web applications more reliable than coordinate-based browser automation. We also learned that explainability matters in career technology. Candidates should understand why a role was recommended, where resume claims came from, what information will be entered, and what action the system intends to take. Building synthetic ATS portals was another important lesson. They allowed us to test realistic workflows without risking accidental submissions or interacting with real employers. ## What's next for CareerCrew Our next step is to turn the hackathon prototype into a production-ready candidate platform. We plan to add: Live role discovery from official company career pages Job freshness and source verification Durable encrypted data storage Model-assisted resume tailoring with evidence controls Production-quality resume and cover-letter generation Additional ATS adapters Stronger audit trails and submission confirmation Cloud deployment and monitoring Candidate feedback loops for improving recommendations Calendar, email, and interview-tracking integrations Our long-term vision is for CareerCrew to become a trusted career command centre: one place where candidates can discover opportunities, prepare credible applications, practise for interviews, and move through their job search with confidence—powered by AI and WebMCP, but always controlled by the candidate.  HomeOps gives homeowners and AI agents one shared view of upcoming, overdue, and safety-critical maintenance. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent reviews household data and proposes a safe, prioritized 30-day maintenance plan for human approval. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Home maintenance often breaks down for a simple reason: people lose track of what was done, when it was done, and what needs attention next. 

 That information is often scattered across reminders, receipts, manuals, notes, and memory. Traditional maintenance apps also create another system the homeowner must constantly update. 

 HomeOps creates one shared household-maintenance workspace that both a person and an AI agent can understand. 

 HomeOps tracks recurring household responsibilities such as HVAC filter replacement, smoke-detector testing, dryer-vent cleaning, and water-heater flushing. 

 For each item, it stores: 

 
 The last service date 
 The recurring maintenance interval 
 The calculated next due date 
 Overdue status 
 Estimated completion time 
 Useful notes, such as filter sizes or service instructions 
 

 Through WebMCP, an agent can: 

 
 Read the current household-maintenance record 
 Find overdue and upcoming work 
 Look up the history of a specific item 
 Create a prioritized maintenance-session proposal 
 Wait for the homeowner to approve it or request a revision 
 Read the homeowner’s decision 
 Record completed maintenance after explicit human confirmation 
 Add a new recurring responsibility after explicit human confirmation 
 

 The homeowner sees the same shared information in the visual interface. Agent actions and human decisions are also displayed in an activity history. 

 The central HomeOps workflow is collaboration rather than uncontrolled automation. 

 A homeowner can ask: 

 
 Audit my home for the next 30 days and propose the best three-task work session. 
 

 The agent reads the maintenance record, identifies urgent work, and creates a visible proposal. 

 It then stops. 

 The homeowner can approve the proposal or request a revision, such as asking for only the two shortest tasks. The agent can read that decision through a separate WebMCP tool before continuing. 

 HomeOps also prevents an agent from recording completed service or adding a recurring maintenance item unless explicit human confirmation is included in the tool call. 

 This allows the agent to take useful initiative while keeping meaningful decisions under human control. 

 HomeOps registers seven structured tools: 

 
 homeops_get_state 
 homeops_list_due 
 homeops_lookup_item 
 homeops_propose_session 
 homeops_get_plan_status 
 homeops_log_service 
 homeops_add_item 
 

 Each tool includes: 

 
 A focused natural-language description 
 A narrow JSON input schema 
 Required fields and validation limits 
 Read-only or state-changing annotations 
 A dedicated execution handler 
 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to inspect page text, locate interface elements, and guess which sequence of clicks changes the correct record. 

 With WebMCP, the website explicitly tells the agent what capabilities are available, which inputs are valid, and which operations modify state. 

 The visual interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same household data. 

 HomeOps is a lightweight browser application built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 The application: 

 
 Registers WebMCP tools directly in the browser 
 Stores household records in browser local storage 
 Calculates overdue and upcoming maintenance dynamically 
 Displays agent proposals and human decisions in one interface 
 Uses constrained schemas for safer tool calls 
 Requires no account, external database, paid API, or API key 
 Includes a fallback demonstration using the same tool handlers when experimental WebMCP browser support is unavailable 
 

 The working application is deployed publicly, and its complete source code is available in a public MIT-licensed GitHub repository. 

 The main challenge was designing a useful human-agent workflow rather than simply exposing buttons to an agent. 

 We wanted the agent to make meaningful progress while preserving clear human control. That led to the proposal-and-approval workflow: the agent may analyze the household record and recommend a plan, but the homeowner makes the final decision. 

 Another challenge was defining tools narrowly enough for an agent to choose the correct action reliably. We used descriptive names, limited responsibilities, strict schemas, bounded values, and explicit human-confirmation requirements for durable changes. 

 Because WebMCP is experimental, we also made the core application functional in ordinary browsers while exposing its full structured tool layer in supported environments. 

 
 Seven functional WebMCP tools 
 A working public application 
 Shared state between the interface and agent tools 
 A visible human approval and revision loop 
 Explicit confirmation requirements for important changes 
 Auditable human-agent activity 
 Persistent browser-based household memory 
 Responsive desktop and mobile design 
 No paid API or account requirement 
 Public MIT-licensed source code 
 

 WebMCP is most valuable when it does more than make an existing button easier for an agent to press. 

 It allows a website to become a shared workspace where a person understands the context visually while an agent receives precise and structured capabilities. 

 We also learned that good human-agent collaboration needs explicit intermediate states. “Proposed,” “approved,” and “revision requested” give both sides a reliable understanding of what should happen next. 

 The best agent experience is not necessarily the one with the most autonomy. It is the one with useful capabilities, reliable, shared context, clear boundaries, and understandable stopping points. 

 Future versions could add: 

 
 Optional calendar and reminder handoffs 
 Shared household-member roles 
 Appliance manuals and model information 
 Maintenance receipts and service records 
 Seasonal maintenance templates 
 Parts and supply lists 
 Contractor coordination 
 Proactive maintenance briefings 
 Optional encrypted cloud synchronization 
 

 The broader vision is a household operations layer where people remain in control while agents help organize, remember, and coordinate the work required to maintain a home.

title: ShowBranch
pitch: Teach catalog rules by example with WebMCP: an agent turns human edits into isolated preview proposals, learns from corrections, and leaves final merge authority to the human.
about_excerpt: Teach catalog rules by example with WebMCP: an agent turns human edits into isolated preview proposals, learns from corrections, and leaves final merge authority to the human. Like Comment Story Updates An isolated Current vs Preview review showing 10 product proposals and 20 changed fields before a human-controlled merge. Inspiration Catalog rules are often easier to show than explain . A catalog operator may instantly recognize how a product should be classified, but turning that intuition into a complete written rule — and then applying it safely across many related products — is repetitive and error-prone. ShowBranch explores a different human-agent workflow: Teach by doing. Preview before you commit. Instead of writing a long instruction, the human makes one real edit in the product UI. An agent reads that activity through WebMCP, generalizes the demonstrated pattern, and proposes related changes inside an isolated preview branch. If the initial generalization misses a catalog-specific rule, the human can correct one proposal directly in the preview. That correction becomes new activity the agent can read and use to revise related proposals. Final merge authority remains with the human. Human demonstration → Agent preview → Human correction → Agent revision → Human-controlled merge What it does ShowBranch is a catalog-classification demo built around a ShowOnce + BranchMode interaction. A human first edits one product in the main catalog. ShowBranch records the complete before-and-after product state as human activity. The browser agent can then use WebMCP to: read products and human activity; create an isolated preview branch; propose updates to related products; read human corrections made inside that branch; revise proposals based on those corrections; and inspect the final Current vs Preview diff. Agent proposals remain isolated from main until the human reviews them. The review surface shows changed products and fields, proposal rationale, confidence, and human-facing Merge Branch and Discard Branch controls. This creates a collaboration loop where the agent can generalize and adapt without immediately committing its work to the canonical catalog. Why WebMCP The key idea is not simply giving an agent functions to call. It is letting the human UI and the browser agent collaborate over the same application state . Without WebMCP, an agent would need to scrape rendered UI text or depend on a separate API that could drift from what the human actually sees and edits. ShowBranch exposes exactly five WebMCP tools: list_products get_activity create_preview_branch apply_branch_updates get_branch_diff These tools let the agent work directly with products, human activity, preview branches, and diffs. Merge, discard, reset, main editing, and human correction are intentionally excluded from the WebMCP capability surface. Final merge is exposed through the human UI rather than as an agent tool. WebMCP therefore acts as the semantic collaboration layer between the human-facing product experience and the agent. How we built it ShowBranch is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP , and is deployed on Vercel . The UI and WebMCP tools share the same browser-side domain store for: the canonical product catalog; preview-branch patches; human and agent activity; branch lifecycle state; and main revision state. Preview branches are sparse isolated overlays rather than immediate mutations to main. The effective preview is composed from the current main state plus branch-specific patches. Human edits store complete before-and-after snapshots. A correction made inside a preview branch becomes branch-scoped human activity, so the agent can immediately read that new evidence and revise its proposal. Agent batches are applied atomically, and the application tracks branch lifecycle and main revisions so stale merges can be detected rather than silently applied. WebMCP registration is also all-or-nothing: the page reports WebMCP ready only after all five tools register successfully. The current MVP intentionally keeps state document-local, making the demo account-free, resettable, and easy for judges to reproduce. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the agent useful without giving it unnecessary authority. We wanted the agent to generalize confidently across related products, while ensuring those proposals stayed isolated from the canonical state until a human review. A second challenge was making human correction part of the collaboration loop rather than treating it as a one-off UI edit. A correction inside the branch needed to become structured evidence that the agent could reliably discover and use in its next revision. Activity ordering introduced another subtle problem. An agent reading only an older branch should not mistake that branch's latest event for the globally latest human activity. ShowBranch therefore tracks scoped and global activity information so newer demonstrations are not silently overlooked. We also had to handle atomic preview updates, stale-branch detection, registration cleanup, and exact reset behavior. Finally, the security boundary needed to be described precisely. ShowBranch removes merge from the WebMCP capability surface and exposes merge through the human UI, while broader browser-automation permissions remain the responsibility of the browser or host. Accomplishments that we're proud of We completed the full human-agent correction loop end to end: Human demonstration → isolated agent preview → human correction → agent revision → human review → merge A single human edit can lead the agent to identify multiple semantically related products rather than blindly applying the same change to every item. The human can then teach a catalog-specific rule inside the preview, and the agent can use that new evidence to revise related proposals while preserving product-specific details. We also implemented: exactly five WebMCP tools with strict capability boundaries; a shared state model used by both the UI and the agent; isolated preview branches with normalized diffs; full before-and-after human activity snapshots; rationale and confidence on agent proposals; Current vs Preview review with aggregate change counts; stale-branch protection; atomic branch updates; human-facing merge and discard controls; and a one-click reset that restores the canonical demo state. The result is a live, account-free demo that judges can reproduce directly in a WebMCP-capable browser. What we learned The biggest lesson was that proposal and commitment should be separate concepts in human-agent systems. An agent does not need unrestricted write access to be useful. It can generalize aggressively inside an isolated branch, receive human corrections as new evidence, and revise its work — while the human retains a clear review and commitment point. We also learned that human corrections become much more powerful when they are stored as structured activity rather than treated as ephemeral UI interactions. One correction can teach the agent a catalog-specific rule without requiring the human to rewrite the entire instruction. WebMCP makes this interaction natural because the agent works with the application's semantic state instead of reconstructing intent from rendered text. What's next for ShowBranch ShowBranch is intentionally a focused demonstration of this interaction pattern. Future directions include: persistent branches and activity history; state-aware WebMCP tool registration; richer approval and permission policies; multi-user review workflows; larger catalogs and persistent backends; and applying the same ShowOnce + BranchMode pattern beyond product classification. The broader idea is simple: Let agents propose and adapt quickly, while keeping consequential commitment understandable and human-controlled. title: Resident
pitch: A human-agent record store where an agent digs, plays and curates in full view—while the listener stays in control.
about_excerpt: A human-agent record store where an agent digs, plays and curates in full view—while the listener stays in control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Enabled + WebMCP Tool Plugin Sidebar Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Enabled Desktop Interface with Agent Mode Playing Music Mobile Interface with Agent Mode Enabled (Light Mode) Mobile Interface with Agent Mode Enabled (Light Mode) Inspiration Most browser-agent experiences happen behind the scenes. A user asks for something, waits, and receives a result without seeing what the agent searched, what it considered, or when control changed. Resident explores a different model: the agent joins the music interface instead of operating behind it. What we built Resident grew out of my existing 3D digital record crate at https://sephmartin.com/ . For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended that same environment rather than building a separate demo. The original experience remains at https://sephmartin.com/ , while the challenge build lives at https://demo.sephmartin.com/ . The result is a meaningful page-level WebMCP extension, not a separate wrapper. The agent can orient over the catalog, search and rank releases using conservative metadata-only Song DNA, focus and inspect records, play and navigate previews, move between tracks and releases, manage a reversible local My Crate, and prepare checkout. The interface makes the agent's work legible. Agent Mode, Thinking, Digging, Listening, Returning and Human Mode are visible states; the orb mirrors the active release and operation; and the crate, player and detail panel update together. The same page remains usable by a person through pointer, keyboard and touch input. How WebMCP is implemented The adapter feature-detects document.modelContext and keeps a compatibility fallback for navigator.modelContext. It registers narrow tools with explicit schemas and read-only or UI-mutation annotations. The tools call a small page facade exposed by the existing crate runtime rather than reaching into arbitrary DOM nodes. A local browser diagnostic log records the tool sequence, visible state and failures so the interaction can be inspected during a demo. The Song DNA layer is evidence-bound: it uses catalog fields such as tags, descriptions and track titles, labels text-derived matches, and reports unavailable audio analysis instead of inventing BPM, key or texture. Stable record IDs keep agent actions reliable across sorting and browsing. Human control and safety The human remains in the loop. A pointer, keyboard or touch gesture can reclaim the page immediately and return it to Human Mode. Crate changes are reversible. Checkout is intentionally split into review and confirmation: the on-site challenge simulator records no real payment, and the final download step ends at a copyright-safe DEMO COMPLETE boundary rather than delivering an original audio file. What I learned I don’t come from traditional software engineering; I come from music, where experience, rhythm and emotion matter as much as functionality. AI gave me a medium for turning that perspective into software. I didn’t get into AI to write code. I got into it to build experiences that didn’t exist before. I built Resident iteratively with coding agents on a standard ChatGPT Plus subscription. I brought the product vision, music knowledge and interaction design; the agents helped me test, break and refine the implementation until it matched what I had imagined. The original 3D crate was already a long-running creative project. The challenge gave me the spark to extend it into a shared human-agent space. WebMCP is valuable here beyond button automation: it lets an agent operate inside a stateful, visual application while the person can see, interrupt and review the work. The strongest interaction is not a one-shot recommendation; it is the visible loop from natural-language intent to digging, focus, playback, curation and human handoff. Try it Open the live demo in ChatGPT's in-app browser, ask the agent to start the curator session, request a late-night disco or house selection, play and inspect a result, add it to My Crate, and prepare checkout. The purchase is a no-payment demo flow. If audio does not start immediately, click or tap the page once: browser autoplay policies require a user gesture before sound can play. A human gesture during Agent Mode demonstrates immediate priority. title: Excalidraw-WebMCP
pitch: Excalidraw, made agent-native: stop drawing yourself. With WebMCP, you and AI build, edit, and shape the same live canvas together.
about_excerpt: Excalidraw, made agent-native: stop drawing yourself. With WebMCP, you and AI build, edit, and shape the same live canvas together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates testing using chatgpt's in-app browser Simple diagram generated by webmcp in excalidraw chat system diagram generated by excalidraw-webmcp and chatgpt distributed webcrawler digram made with webmcp n chatgpt Inspiration Every developer knows this pain. You finish building something cool, and then u need to document it. And somehow, even worse than writing the docs, is drawing the architecture diagram for them. Boxes. Arrows. Labels. Move the box. Fix the arrow. Realize the box is slightly misaligned. Move everything again. Architecture diagrams are incredibly useful for READMEs, system-design discussions, demos, presentations, and explaining how a project actually works, but creating them manually is still tedious. Meanwhile, AI agents have become good at understanding codebases, architectures, and technical ideas. They can explain the system perfectly, but when it comes to actually putting that understanding onto a visual canvas, the human usually ends up doing the drawing. So I built Excalidraw WebMCP . The idea is simple: What if Excalidraw wasn't just a canvas for humans, but a canvas where humans and AI agents could work on together? What it does Excalidraw WebMCP makes Excalidraw agent-native. Humans and browser agents operate on the same live canvas . An agent can understand what is currently on the canvas, reason about the diagram, make structured changes, connect elements, and export the final result. The human stays in the loop and can continue moving, editing, deleting, or adding elements normally through Excalidraw. There is no separate "AI-generated preview" that has to be copied back into the editor. There is just one canvas shared between the human and the agent. How I built it The project is built around a simple rule: There should be one source of truth for the canvas, regardless of whether a human or an agent changes it. The central canvas state and mutation boundary lives in: src/canvas/canvas-controller.ts All changes to the canvas flow through this layer. On top of that, I created a semantic operation layer which translates higher-level operations into actual Excalidraw elements in: src/canvas/semantic-operations.ts The WebMCP layer lives inside src/webmcp/ . It contains the schemas, tool registration, validation, and the execution bridge used by the exposed tools. When the browser provides document.modelContext , the application registers its WebMCP capabilities and allows compatible browser agents to interact with the current board. The canvas is stored locally in the browser using localStorage , keeping the project intentionally lightweight. Challenges I faced 1. Turning drawing actions into semantic operations Drawing applications are very coordinate-heavy. Agents, however, work much better with concepts. I didn't want the interface to expose something like: drawRectangle(x: 417, y: 263, width: 188...) as it would confuse the agent. Instead, I needed an abstraction where the agent could express meaningful operations while the application handled the Excalidraw-specific details. Finding that between agent-friendly semantics and precise canvas geometry was one of the biggest challenges. 2. Keeping connectors and elements stable A diagram is not just a collection of rectangles. Elements have relationships. Connectors need to stay attached to the right shapes, elements need stable identifiers, and updates must avoid unexpectedly breaking the rest of the canvas. 3. Letting humans and agents edit the same state I didn't want an “AI mode” and a separate “human mode.” The agent needed to modify exactly the same board the user was looking at, while keeping normal Excalidraw interaction intact. Designing a single mutation boundary helped make both interaction models coexist without creating two competing versions of the canvas. What I learned WebMCP showed me how powerful browser-native agents can be, and we are only getting started on this tech. I think it could become a major frontier for browser agents, with applications far beyond this project. What's next This project is a prototype , and there is a lot more in Excalidraw that I would love to bring into WebMCP. Right now, the agent can work with the core canvas primitives, but Excalidraw itself has a much richer set of capabilities. The next step would be to expose more of those features through WebMCP so an agent can interact with the canvas almost as completely as a human can. That could include things like image insertion, richer element controls, and Mermaid-to-Excalidraw , where Mermaid syntax can be turned directly into editable Excalidraw diagrams. I also want to make the natural-language → diagram experience much more robust. The current prototype works well for many diagrams, but there is still room to improve how agents reason about layout, spacing, connector placement, and iterative refinement instead of trying to get everything perfect in one pass. Beyond that, I would love to explore: Canvas history and revisions so agents can understand and restore previous states Better real-time human + agent collaboration on the same board Multi-agent collaboration , where multiple agents can contribute to one canvas Deeper support for Excalidraw's existing tools instead of maintaining a smaller agent-specific subset And if I get the opportunity to take this further, I would love to contribute these ideas back toward the actual open-source Excalidraw ecosystem . Excalidraw already has an MCP App Server. I think WebMCP could complement that by making the Excalidraw web app itself natively understandable and operable by browser agents, without treating the browser as just a screen to click around. The end goal is simple: Take everything humans can do inside Excalidraw and make those capabilities equally accessible to agents through WebMCP.
