title: Relay WebMCP
pitch: An AI stand-in that handles what you'd approve, refuses what you'd not, and hands off the rest while you're away.
about_excerpt: An AI stand-in that handles what you'd approve, refuses what you'd not, and hands off the rest while you're away. Like Comment Story Updates the tightened copy, heartbeat dot, RELAY label, one-line pitch Project Links Inspiration People who need to step away unexpectedly, a scheduled procedure, a custody handoff, a hospital stay with no warning, have always faced the same bad choice: hand someone full access and hope they use good judgment, or go dark and let everything queue up until they're back. Password managers solve access, not judgment. Auto-replies solve nothing, they just defer. What was missing was a way to hand off exactly the part of a decision someone is comfortable handing off, nothing more, with everything outside that boundary going to a person they trust instead of an inbox nobody's watching. WebMCP made a genuine version of that possible: a tool surface that changes based on who is looking and what state things are in, computed live in the browser rather than fixed on a server, is what lets the boundary actually get enforced instead of just described in a policy nobody reads. What it does Relay lets someone prepare a delegate agent before they become unreachable, one that keeps answering the people who depend on them, inside limits they set in advance, escalating anything outside those limits to a person they trust. The absence doesn't have to be the same shape twice. A contractor covering client work during a scheduled procedure. Two co-parents who need logistics handled without every message pulling one of them out of their day. Someone who ends up in the hospital with no warning and no time to write instructions for anyone. A support lead pulled into a family emergency mid-shift. Relay works the same way whether the absence was planned six weeks out or started an hour ago. A person prepares a delegate agent in advance: an interview-style briefing agent asks about their specific situation and drafts a full configuration for them to review, rather than making them author policy from scratch. When the person goes unreachable, the delegate starts answering the people and agents who depend on them, inside a boundary of autonomy the principal defined, escalating anything outside that boundary to a named human, and producing a complete accounting of what happened. How we built it Relay registers seven WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, but which tools are visible depends on who's looking and what state the relay is in: the principal sees five configuration tools while their relay is still in draft, a recipient sees nothing until the relay goes active and then sees exactly one tool (ask_delegate) scoped to their own access token, and everyone can request a record of what happened, filtered to what they're allowed to see. That conditional, per-visitor tool surface, not just per-server but per-session, is something a hosted MCP server can't express, and it's the core of why this is a WebMCP-native product rather than a chatbot with extra steps. Underneath that, the delegate's reasoning loop uses Claude to classify every incoming request into a tier (autonomous, flagged, refused) and propose a reply, then a deterministic check runs after the model and before any action is taken. Challenges we ran into The interesting part of building this turned out not to be the AI, it was the governance. Anyone can wire a chatbot to answer messages while someone's away. The harder problem is making sure it never quietly does more than it was authorized to do. If a request's dollar value exceeds an autonomous ceiling, it has to be forced to flagged regardless of what the model said. If nothing matches, it has to fall through to a configured default and never default to autonomous. The model proposes. The code disposes. Getting that rule to actually hold, every time, took more iteration than the AI side of the build did. The other hard challenge was the permission surface itself, described above, getting the tool set to genuinely change per visitor and per state rather than just claiming to. Late in the build, rehearsing the actual demo flow surfaced a genuine problem: the briefing interview was losing its own memory mid-conversation, because session state lived in server memory with no guarantee two requests land on the same instance. We caught it by testing the exact path a judge would take, not by reading the code, and moved session state into the database before it ever reached a recording. Accomplishments we're proud of The deterministic override actually holds under a live test, not just in theory: a request the model classified one way gets forced to a different tier the moment it crosses a rule the principal set, and the reply shown updates to match, so the tier badge and the words never contradict each other. The tool surface is genuinely live, not simulated, confirmed by calling document.modelContext.getTools() directly in an actual WebMCP-enabled browser and watching the exact same page return a different tool list depending on who's asking. And we found and fixed the session-memory bug above before it ever showed up in a recording, by actually rehearsing the demo end to end instead of assuming the happy path would hold. What we learned For a product where an agent has a multi-turn conversation, the failure modes that matter show up in an actual multi-turn conversation, not in a single request, and the only way to catch them is to actually run the conversation end to end rather than trust that a single successful test proves the whole path works. What's next There's no principal login yet, a relay's own URL currently acts as the access credential the way a recipient's token does, which is fine for a single-user demo but not for a multi-tenant product. Principal authentication is the next piece. Beyond that, more activation conditions (calendar-based, not just missed check-ins) and letting an approver resolve a flagged request directly through their own agent, not just by clicking Approve, are the two directions we'd take this next. title: Grounded - Collaborative AI Workspace for Construction
pitch: Agents excel at pulling evidence across a pile of docs. People excel at reading drawings. Grounded is built so each can stay in that lane instead of forcing one to do both.
about_excerpt: Agents excel at pulling evidence across a pile of docs. People excel at reading drawings. Grounded is built so each can stay in that lane instead of forcing one to do both. Like Comment Story Updates What I built I built Grounded because construction document review mixes work that agents handle well with judgments they should not make alone. An agent can search schedules and compare written requirements. Reading plan symbols, following linework, or counting openings on a drawing still needs a construction professional to do reliably. The tools are meant to work in a lot of review setups, but most people do not have contract drawings sitting around, so the demo ships with a fixed project. It includes an open-source Virginia Farmhouse drawing set and two example submittals. The door package is seeded with real issues for the agent to find. The window package is clean on purpose, so the review has a known pass case next to a known fail. What the agent actually gets is structured. It can search the evidence we already extracted from the PDFs, jump the workbench to a page, block, or region, and open an Assistance Request when it hits something it should not guess at. The human answers in the same workspace. The agent comes back later and finishes the disposition from that structured response. Why WebMCP fits These workflows are a mess of strengths and weak spots. Agents are good at finding textual evidence across a pile of sources and stitching it together. They still struggle at reading construction drawings the way the job requires. AEC-Bench is a useful look at how hard that still is. I treat drawings as close to a worst case for today's agents, and the cost of a miss is high. A denied submittal can add weeks. A bid off by 50% can be hundreds of thousands of dollars. So I stopped asking the model to do the part a construction professional already does well, and I stopped asking that professional to do the part the model does well: collecting and reconciling evidence across a pile of documents. WebMCP is what makes that split practical. Without it you usually get a painful loop. The agent asks for something, you open another app, mark up the drawing, export it, and paste answers back into chat. With WebMCP the agent discovers tools on the live page, works from immutable document versions, and creates a request tied to exact pages. The reviewer answers in place. After a reload the agent can recover the response without depending on conversation memory. I do not think this pattern is limited to construction. Anywhere an agent needs a durable human judgment tied to a specific artifact, the same shape applies. How I built it Grounded registers eight WebMCP tools in one all-or-nothing attempt and only reports "WebMCP ready" when the full set is up: get_grounded_help , get_project_workspace , list_project_documents , search_project_documents , inspect_document_evidence , navigate_document , create_assistance_request , get_assistance_request The document tools expose prepared artifacts. There is no runtime OCR and no external document-processing call in the demo path. Search can point at likely content, but a claim has to come from inspected evidence. Navigation moves the visible PDF workbench to a page, a semantic block, or a normalized region for visual inspection or to direct the user where they should be looking. Assistance Requests are the durable handoff. For a Point Set, the reviewer clicks locations on the PDF. Marks live in an overlay separate from the PDF.js display layer so they stay aligned through resize and zoom. Responses persist in IndexedDB under a tab-scoped Demo Session. Unfinished Zustand drafts intentionally die on reload. Committed responses do not. Contracts use TypeBox for TypeScript inference, browser registration, and runtime validation. A recording Model Context adapter exercises the same behavior under Vitest. Stack is React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Dexie, Zustand, a custom PDF.js display layer, and Cloudflare Workers with static assets via Wrangler. Challenges I ran into Getting the agent to stop inventing visual counts was the hard product problem. Early versions would "see" openings that were never marked. The fix was process, not prompting: search is a hint, inspect is required, and drawing interpretation goes to the human through a Point Set instead of a freeform chat answer. The other hard part was teaching the agent how to use the app without a skill. Normal MCP is starting to grow discoverable skills that come with the server. WebMCP has something drawn up for that, but it is early, and I did not want to hand judges a big skill install just to run the demo. So a lot of the work went into tool names, descriptions, and contracts that could carry the workflow on their own. That ended up working, but a skill would have made the same behavior clearer, and on a real project I would almost certainly put one on the agent so it knows how to work with our documents. I also wanted a much larger tool set than the eight that shipped. Context made that a bad idea. These reviews chew through a lot of the agent's window. A lot of it is cached across repeated tool calls, which can get better, but the structured evidence coming out of the document parser was still token-heavy and full of fields that did not help the decision. We had to thin that payload until the loop fit. It is in a decent spot now, but still could be better. What I learned The real benefit of WebMCP, for me, is collaboration. I went into this hoping an agent could own more of the review than it can. It cannot. Not yet. Drawing interpretation, accountable counts, and the judgment call behind a disposition still need a person who knows the work. That does not make the collaboration temporary. Even as the models get better at reading drawings, a shared workspace like this stays useful. The human still needs to stay current on what the agent found, what it skipped, and what it is asking for. WebMCP is a clean way to keep that loop in one place instead of exporting screenshots and pasting answers back into chat. I do not see WebMCP as a stopgap. Once you have a durable way for an agent and a professional to hand work back and forth against the same artifact, a lot of other workflows open up. Construction is just the one I built first. What's next Widen the Assistance response types past Point Sets, support real project imports beyond the bundled Virginia Farmhouse set, and harden the review trail so a disposition can cite every mark and every document version it used. Longer term I want this sitting inside an actual submittal workflow, not only a hackathon demo session. title: Euterpe
pitch: Euterpe is a browser music maker where a person hums or plays and their own agent becomes a teacher-producer.
about_excerpt: Euterpe is a browser music maker where a person hums or plays and their own agent becomes a teacher-producer. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a middle ground between learning a full music-production application and asking a generator to make a finished song. A beginner may already have the important part — a line they can hum or sing — but not yet know how to turn it into chords, a bass part, drums and an arrangement. The useful collaborator is not one that replaces that idea. It is one that can work on the same song, explain a choice, let the person hear it, and accept “undo” as a normal part of making music. Music also exposes why WebMCP is useful. The page owns the microphone, song document, audio clock and speakers. The person is the only one who can hear whether a change works, while the browser’s agent needs exact notes, chords, bar ranges and revision state rather than a screenshot. WebMCP gives the site a structured way to expose those actions to the agent, as described in OpenAI’s Site tools guide and Chrome’s WebMCP guide . What it does Euterpe opens as an empty eight-bar song with one melody track. A person can record a hum or sung line, import a browser-decodable voice memo, play the musical-typing keyboard, or use a MIDI input where the browser supports it. Every path produces a take with rough symbolic notes; microphone and imported takes also retain the original audio. The browser’s agent has 29 registered tools. It can read the song, notes, chords and takes; suggest or set chords; offer two or three alternatives that the person can audition before choosing; ask the person to perform a named part over particular bars; set the key and tempo; add tracks; generate deterministic chord, bass and drum parts; arrange sections; mix, play, stop, undo and redo; and start cancellable WAV, MP3 or MIDI export jobs. The five track kinds are melody, chords, bass, drums and vocal. The vocal is part of the song rather than disposable input to pitch detection. A dedicated vocal track can hold the retained recording. tune_vocal applies reversible, key-aware pitch correction, set_quantize aligns its timing with adjustable strength and optional swing, and set_mix controls level, pan, mute and solo. WAV and MP3 renders include retained voice clips. MIDI is notes-only, so Euterpe refuses MIDI export when the song contains retained audio instead of silently dropping the singer. The agent does not hear the audio and the tool boundary does not send it audio. It receives bounded JSON descriptions of musical state; the person remains the ears and makes the final choice. Every newly authored musical change carries a plain-language why , appears in the activity strip and producer notes, points back to the bars it changed, and can be undone. The agent also cannot grant microphone permission or bypass the browser’s audio rules for the person. How we built it The application is a TypeScript and React client built with Vite and hosted as a static site. There is no model or music-generation service inside the page. The browser’s agent chooses the tools; deterministic local code handles state, music theory, pitch analysis and audio. All human and agent edits go through one serialised command bus and one song reducer. A successful edit increments a monotonic revision and returns the changed fields, summary and target bars. Tools can include an expected revision, so a stale write is refused with a short account of what changed instead of overwriting newer work. Human drags on the piano roll briefly hold agent writes, and a track being recorded is locked while other tracks remain editable. Each tool has a Zod input schema exported as strict JSON Schema, a short description, annotations and an execute function. The registry installs the same 29 definitions through document.modelContext.registerTool and the compatibility navigator.modelContext path, deduplicating them when both names refer to the same context. Six tools are marked read-only. Results use one compact success-or-error envelope and stay within the application’s 1,500-character budget. The audio path uses Tone.js and smplr for scheduled instruments, with an AudioWorklet and Pitchy for live and offline pitch tracking. Tonal supplies note and chord primitives. Recorded mono PCM is stored with the take, referenced by clips on the timeline, and scheduled through the same vocal path for live playback and offline rendering. WAV is encoded as PCM; MP3 work runs in a separate worker through Mediabunny ; MIDI is written from the symbolic tracks. Recording over an arrangement uses a shared worklet clock and the scheduled count-in boundary, then combines those with the active input device’s reported latency and the audio context’s base and output latency. These are browser and device estimates under the Media Capture and Streams and Web Audio APIs, not a claim of acoustic sample-accurate alignment. If the input device does not report latency, Euterpe refuses microphone capture rather than inventing an offset. At the submission commit, the unit and integration suite passes 817 tests across 110 files. The browser harness contains 126 asserted steps across seven scenarios, covering the 29 tool behaviours, revisions, error envelopes, recording locks, retained-vocal alignment, real audio export and sample fallback. Challenges we ran into The largest mistake in the first version was architectural: a hummed take was analysed into notes and then the recording itself was thrown away. That was acceptable for a transcription demo but wrong for a music maker. Keeping the singer meant adding serialisable PCM to the take model, clip references to tracks, persistence and history support, clip copying during arrangement, a separate live-audio path for vocal tracks, and the same path again in offline WAV and MP3 rendering. Recording over music was another real boundary. The capture worklet, count-in and output device expose related but different timing information. A fixed “latency compensation” number would have looked convincing on one machine and been wrong on another. The implementation now records the worklet boundary, scheduled arrangement boundary and the browser-reported input, processing and output estimates with each microphone take. Missing or non-monotonic evidence causes a refusal, not a guessed placement. Making vocal changes reversible also took more than moving note rectangles. The original note timing has to survive quantisation, while the retained PCM needs a corresponding time map. Pitch correction has to use voiced pitch frames and the current key without changing the stored recording. Both operations therefore live as adjustable clip settings in the song history rather than destructive rewrites of the source audio. Export forced an explicit product decision. A Standard MIDI File can represent the note tracks but not the retained PCM recording. Silently exporting the instruments would produce a valid file that was not the song the person heard. The encoder and WebMCP tool both reject that case and direct the person to WAV or MP3. Finally, WebMCP’s structured boundary cannot listen for the agent. Read tools therefore return small musical facts — notes, chord symbols, bar ranges, take quality and revision — while the page makes every action visible and leaves listening to the person. That constraint shaped the product more than adding a chat panel would have. Accomplishments that we're proud of The singer survives the whole journey. A hummed or sung line is recorded, retained as audio, tuned to the key, aligned to the grid, mixed, and exported inside the finished WAV or MP3 — while the same take also drives the symbolic notes the agent reasons over. Both representations stay in one song document with one history. Euterpe refuses in three places where it would have been easier to guess. It refuses microphone capture when the input device will not report its latency, rather than applying an offset that looks right on one machine and is wrong on another. It refuses MIDI export when the song contains retained audio, rather than producing a valid file that is not the song the person heard. And it refuses a stale write when the revision has moved, rather than overwriting newer work. Each refusal says what happened and what to do instead. The agent is genuinely useful without ever hearing the music. Twenty-nine tools give it notes, chords, bar ranges, take quality and revision state as bounded JSON; it proposes, explains and edits; the person listens and decides. Every authored change carries a plain-language reason, points at the bars it touched, and can be undone. The evidence is real rather than asserted: 817 tests across 110 files, and a browser harness of 126 asserted steps in seven scenarios covering every registered tool, the revision and locking rules, retained-vocal alignment and actual audio export. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when a site has live state or local capabilities

title: ShowMeOnMap
pitch: Ask for a map. With WebMCP, the agent in your browser builds it, queries it and hands you the export — on the canvas you're watching.
about_excerpt: Ask for a map. With WebMCP, the agent in your browser builds it, queries it and hands you the export — on the canvas you're watching. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration ShowMeOnMap is a live product: you type a geographic question in plain language and get a professionally rendered map built from real, fetched data — never invented values — with a legend, a grounded caption and a shareable page. It already had a server-side MCP endpoint and a REST API for headless agents. What it did not have was any way for the agent in your browser to work with you on the page you are both looking at. That gap is sharper for a map than for almost any other kind of site. A WebGL canvas is the most illegible thing a browser agent can meet: pixels it cannot read, data it cannot touch, a camera it cannot move. Screen-reading it is hopeless; the DOM contains a <canvas> and a legend. WebMCP flips the problem: instead of the agent guessing what the page shows, the page tells the agent what it can do — and, crucially for us, what it currently shows. What it does showmeonmap.com registers 8 tools on document.modelContext . In an agent-capable browser (ChatGPT's built-in browser, or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled) you can now say: "We just moved to Vancouver — show me the elementary schools in Kerrisdale and their catchment areas. How many are actually inside Kerrisdale? Zoom to them. Export a PNG." and watch it happen on the canvas: build_map → query_features → zoom_to_layer → export_image . Then "show me the secondary schools instead" ( mutate_map ) and "undo that" ( undo ). Tool What it does Cost build_map(query) natural-language query → fetched real data → rendered map 1 free daily map (anonymous) / 1 credit mutate_map(instruction) refine the current map's data or style 1 credit, auto-refunded on failure get_map_state() read-back: layers, exact feature counts, camera, filters, analysis headline free query_features(layerId, predicate) exact answers from the rendered data via a typed predicate grammar free set_camera(center?, zoom?) move the live MapLibre camera free zoom_to_layer(layerId) fit the camera to a layer's real extent free export_image(format?) render a legend-complete PNG/JPEG/PDF and hand the human the Save button free undo() rewind the last map change free Why WebMCP fits this use case. Half of these tools write to the page; the other half read from it. The read-back channel is the part a screenshot or a DOM scrape can never give an agent: query_features answers "how many schools are inside Kerrisdale?" with the exact count from the rendered layer, not a model's guess. The map stops being a picture the agent describes and becomes a grounded data source for the agent's next sentence. What people and agents can now do together. The person keeps the canvas, the legend, the undo history and the Save button. The agent gets typed verbs and honest read-back. Neither side has to trust the other's description of the map, because both are looking at the same post-apply state. "Agents propose, people click" is literal here: browsers block downloads that a human did not initiate, so export_image renders the full-size image and puts a real Save button on the page for the person. How we built it The integration is deliberately one thin boundary, three touch points: Mount. A WebMCPBridge component (renders nothing) runs registerWebMcpTools() once on the client. For the ~99% of visitors without an agent runtime that is a single property probe ( document.modelContext , with the legacy navigator.modelContext name as fallback — the entry point has been renamed twice already). Teardown aborts the registration's AbortController . The chat bridge seam. The chat panel owns sendMessage — the same submission pipeline behind the composer (mutate-first ladder, SSE streaming, store application, billing refresh). It registers that callable with the WebMCP layer, so build_map / mutate_map are processed exactly as if the human had typed: same quota, same 1-credit billing with auto-refund, same anonymous-visitor rules (anonymous sessions get a typed sign-in prompt from mutate_map , never a silent no-op). Store reads. The free tools read and write the app's existing map store directly — no server calls. Every result is summarized from post-apply state: layer and feature counts come from what actually landed, never from "the request was sent". If nothing rendered, the result says delivered: false — do not claim a map exists . Two safety pieces sit on top: every paid tool states its cost in its description (that is what runtimes use to classify a call as consequential — a silently-costed tool is the prompt-injection amplifier), and a gesture-reset budget refuses paid calls after 8 of them with no human interaction until the person touches the page. Tests: a unit suite pinning the budget semantics, the grounding rule and the cost-honest descriptions; a Playwright spec in the main app's CI where a stubbed agent runtime drives the real page; and, in the public repo, a live-site contract test that drives showmeonmap.com's registered tools through document.modelContext with no access to app internals — npm test , about 7 seconds, all 8 tools. Stack: TypeScript, React / Next.js on Cloudflare Workers (OpenNext), MapLibre GL + deck.gl, Zustand stores, Playwright. The tool schemas are plain JSON Schema. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. window.agent → navigator.modelContext → document.modelContext , and Chrome's docs show execute returning a string while ChatGPT's show an object. We probe both entry points and return JSON text, which both runtimes accept. A tool that says "ok" while the canvas didn't change is lying. Our first camera tool wrote to a legacy config channel the renderer ignores while a plan is active — it reported success and nothing moved. Caught in the first live ChatGPT-browser test, fixed by driving the live MapLibre instance and reading the camera back through get_map_state . Downloads. Agent-initiated tool calls carry no user activation, so export_image cannot save a file. It renders the image and hands the human a real Save button instead. Reading a map back honestly at neighbourhood scale. "Schools in Kerrisdale" means the area people call Kerrisdale, not the cadastral polygon; strict containment cut schools a block outside the line. Solid dots are inside, faded ones sit within 800 m outside, and the read-back says which is which. Cost. An agent in a loop can spend a person's credits. Cost in the description plus the gesture-reset budget is the answer we shipped; it is also why paid tools go through the same billing path as the composer, with auto-refund. title: Torque Run
pitch: A browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover through WebMCP tools on one identical live track, scored on time, energy and integrity.
about_excerpt: A browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover through WebMCP tools on one identical live track, scored on time, energy and integrity. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every WebMCP demo we saw was a form filler. We wanted a benchmark instead: put different models, prompts and agent harnesses on one identical live challenge and let the track decide. Torque Run turns WebMCP into agentic esports. What it does Torque Run is a browser-native 3D proving ground where AI agents race a rover on time, energy and chassis integrity. Each pilot launches from a guarded arena, crosses a 216 m course of asphalt, gravel, sand and ice with banked turns, potholes, bowling pins, rocks and a brick wall, and must reach the finish checkpoint before a fixed 150 EU battery runs out. Picking up the cargo cell with the rear-mounted arm is optional and worth a 1000-point bonus. Every completed run scores speed, energy efficiency and integrity, and lands on a persistent leaderboard that keeps vendor, model and prompt identity. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The page is the referee. All gameplay is exposed as WebMCP tools registered by the site itself, so any agent, from any vendor, with any harness, gets exactly the same interface and the same seeded physics. There is no parallel simulation and no screen scraping: the tools are the only way an agent can drive. That makes results comparable, repeatable and inspectable, which is what a benchmark needs. How it creates a better user experience Humans watch a real 3D race with sound, telemetry, damage and a score breakdown instead of reading a log. Every tool call appears live in an in-world call log, so a spectator can see what the agent decided and when. The leaderboard lets you switch the model, the prompt or the whole harness, rerun the identical seed and compare. What people and agents can do together A developer writes a strategy prompt, an agent races it, and the human reads the outcome on the same track a human can also drive with the keyboard. Before WebMCP this needed a custom API and a custom client per model; now the browser tab is the shared arena for humans, agents and judges. How we built it Next.js on Vinext, React Three Fiber and Three.js for the scene, a deterministic fixed-step physics engine in TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers with D1 and Drizzle for the leaderboard, Playwright for tests. Procedural Web Audio, instanced geometry and a 60 Hz state cap keep it smooth in the browser. How we implemented WebMCP Before a race only read_game_manual is registered via document.modelContext.registerTool . A valid call must declare pilot name, vendor, model and prompt name; it starts the official timer, returns the rules and unlocks observe , get_telemetry , drive , execute_motion_plan , set_gripper and finish_run . Every tool drives the same simulation as the manual controls, and entering the checkpoint stops the timer automatically. Test in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing or in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Challenges we ran into Keeping physics deterministic across agents while rendering at variable frame rates, making collisions punishing but recoverable, and tuning scoring so that skipping cargo is a real strategic choice rather than a mistake. What's next Server-side validation of runs, more tracks and seeds, team relays, and a public API for harness authors. title: Branchiverse
pitch: Build alternate futures with AI on a shared WebMCP-powered canvas.
about_excerpt:
Build alternate futures with AI on a shared WebMCP-powered canvas.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI decision tools end with an answer. Real futures are not answers: they are living systems of choices, assumptions, turning points, and consequences. We wanted a shared space where a person could bring their values and lived context while an agent contributed imagination, structure, and overlooked possibilities. 

 What it does 

 Branchiverse turns an open-ended scenario into an interactive branching universe. A person manipulates branches and events directly on the canvas while an external AI agent inspects the same state and uses structured WebMCP tools to add branches, edit events, explore what-ifs, duplicate paths, collapse branches, and compare outcomes.
The demo follows a personal future: moving to Lisbon or staying in Montréal. After inspecting both paths, the agent discovers a third option—a seasonal, transatlantic life—and adds connected events that make the original decision reversible.
The final artifact is not an AI answer. It is a future model that neither participant would have created alone. 

 How we built it 

 Branchiverse is a responsive React application built with Vinext, TypeScript, and CSS. Its shared universe is structured branch and event data. The page registers eleven tools through document.modelContext, allowing compatible external agents to act on that state while React immediately reflects changes on the visual canvas.
The WebMCP tools are create_universe, add_branch, add_event, edit_event, remove_event, branch_from_event, explore_what_if, compare_branches, duplicate_branch, collapse_branch, and get_universe_state.
WebMCP is a progressive enhancement: the canvas remains usable when no agent is connected. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 Without WebMCP, the agent could only describe suggested changes in chat and ask the human to reproduce them. With WebMCP, the agent participates in the same creative surface. The canvas—not the chat transcript—becomes the shared artifact. 

 Challenges 

 The central design challenge was keeping collaboration legible. Agent actions needed to feel immediate without obscuring human authorship. We addressed this with provenance labels, live activity, distinct branch colors, tool-use summaries, and a focused action surface. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 A complete eleven-tool WebMCP surface 
 Real-time agent mutations reflected on the canvas 
 A polished, responsive scenario that communicates the concept immediately 
 Graceful behavior with and without WebMCP support 
 A focused demo flow under three minutes 
 

 What we learned 

 The most compelling agent experiences are not necessarily autonomous. Branchiverse works because human intention and agent exploration remain visible at the same time. Structured browser tools let the agent become a collaborator inside an existing interface rather than replacing that interface with chat. 

 What's next 

 Future versions could add persistent universes, multiplayer sessions, uncertainty ranges, evidence attached to assumptions, replayable history, and templates for business futures, alternate history, fictional worlds, and civic planning.

title: elcaro
pitch: Elcaro: a prompt-injection firewall where the human and the agent review the same near-miss together, live on the page.
about_excerpt: Elcaro: a prompt-injection firewall where the human and the agent review the same near-miss together, live on the page. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Prompt injection is now one of the dominant attacks against agent pipelines, yet most defenses run silently on the server. The human is cut out of the loop. We wanted to make the near-miss visible: the moment an agent is about to follow a hidden instruction is the most important moment to show the user. WebMCP lets that happen directly inside a web page instead of disappearing into a hidden log. What it does Elcaro is a prompt-injection scanner that treats the web page as shared ground truth. A human can paste an email, search result, document, or code snippet and immediately see a risk score and quarantine verdict. With WebMCP enabled, an agent can do the same thing on the same page: load a specimen, scan it, explain the verdict, and then declare what it was about to do. The key interaction is that the page shows the agent's intended action next to the hidden instruction it found. This lets the human see the near-miss and understand exactly what the agent was about to do. How we built it The site is a Next.js frontend deployed on Netlify with a Python miner. On /scan , we feature-detect document.modelContext and register five tools via registerTool : scan_content load_specimen list_specimens explain_verdict contrast_intent Each tool mutates the React form state and calls the same /api/scan endpoint that a human would use. This means the human and the agent are always looking at the same underlying results. The contrast_intent tool computes a three-way contrast between the agent's intended action, the hidden instruction, and the safe remediation. Verdicts can also be Ed25519-signed for non-repudiation, and the repo already exposes a stdio MCP server for IDE-based workflows. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is a pre-standards draft, so the surface has shifted during development. The registration API moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext , and ChatGPT's in-app browser behaves slightly differently from Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . We also had to separate in-page discovery from the actual tool surface. The home page advertises the site's WebMCP support through /.well-known/webmcp.json , but the tools only register on /scan , because that is where the shared UI lives. The biggest design tension was keeping the page human-readable while making the tool schemas explicit enough for an agent to use reliably. Accomplishments that we're proud of The contrast_intent tool is the core win. Having an agent declare what it was about to do and showing that declaration next to the quarantined content creates a genuinely new human-agent interaction. We're also proud that the WebMCP implementation is not a fake API. The same tools update the same React state that the human sees, and the same scanner endpoint backs both the form and the tools. The signed verdicts, llms.txt agent instructions, and overall "agents as first-class users" design all reinforce the same idea: agent activity should be visible, understandable, and accountable. What we learned WebMCP is not just a way to expose actions; it is a way to make an agent's behavior legible to the human. If a tool does not update the page visibly, the human has no reason to trust it. We also learned that tool descriptions are load-bearing: an agent needs to know when to call each tool, not just what the tool does. We also confirmed that a /.well-known/webmcp.json manifest plus <meta name="webmcp"> helps agentic browsers and challenge evaluators discover the site before navigating to the tool page. What's next for elcaro Next, we want to expand WebMCP to the home page with a lightweight wayfinding tool, add a review_history tool, and ship a browser extension that automatically scans content retrieved by an agent and calls the WebMCP tools on the user's behalf. We also want to expose an organization dashboard for audit trails of agent-declared intent and integrate Elcaro with agent platforms beyond ChatGPT and Chrome. title: Sprintfy
pitch: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan.
about_excerpt: Agent-native sprint planning where the agent proposes and the human approves. No WebMCP tool ever writes to your plan. Like Comment Story Updates Landing Page Live: https://sprintfy.vercel.app — no account needed to see the whole idea. Open it in the ChatGPT desktop app, in ChatGPT mode : its built-in browser exposes WebMCP on its own, so the tools register with no flag and no extension. Desktop Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing works too, as does Chrome with the ChatGPT extension. One caveat: Codex mode in that same desktop app does not expose WebMCP , so the tools stay dormant there and the page will honestly say so — same app, two modes, two answers. Ask your agent for start_guided_demo , or press "Show me a demo", and you land in a real workspace with a proposal already waiting in the review panel and six tools live. Inspiration Every "agent-ready" app I looked at exposed the same shape of tool: create_task , update_task , delete_task . The model writes straight to the database. That is fine until the model is confidently wrong about your sprint plan, and then you are doing archaeology on a project board, trying to work out what it touched and in what order. Project planning is exactly the wrong domain for blind writes. A plan is an argument about sequencing and effort — it is the thing a lead is paid to have an opinion about. Handing that to an agent as unsupervised INSERTs gets you a plan nobody trusts and everybody re-checks, which is more work than writing it by hand. So I wanted to find out whether WebMCP could carry something other than commands. Can a tool call ask a question and wait for a human's answer? If it can, the agent stops being a thing you supervise and becomes a thing you argue with. What it does Sprintfy is a sprint planner — requirements, sprints, tasks, hour estimates — that exposes its workspace to agents over WebMCP. No agent tool writes to the plan. The loop has three moves: 1. The agent reads the room. get_project_context returns the plan and what the human is currently looking at: active view, selected sprint, status filter, which proposal is open. The agent plans into a context, not a vacuum. 2. The agent proposes a diff. Every write tool authors a change set — an ordered list of operations stored as JSON, rendered in the review panel as a real diff: additions in green, field-level changes as before → after, removals struck through. Nothing has touched the domain tables. An agent can propose a sprint and the twelve tasks inside it as one unit, using local ref ids that resolve to real primary keys only at apply time. 3. The human decides, and the agent hears the answer. apply_pending_changes opens the diff and blocks — the tool call's promise stays open while the person reads it. Approve applies the whole change set in a single Postgres transaction and the tool resolves with what landed. Reject resolves with the reason they typed, delivered back to the agent as the tool result. You do not start from an empty board either. You hand Sprintfy the thing you already have — a backlog note, a PRD as .md , .txt , .pdf or .docx , or a few paragraphs typed in — and it returns a plan sequenced by risk rather than by comfort. A real Turkish brief produced 8 requirements, 4 sprints and 38 tasks in 56 seconds, in Turkish, with the database migration ranked critical and placed first. Sprintfy's own planner is held to the same rule. It does not write the plan either: it authors a change set marked source: "planner" that lands in the same review panel, behind the same gate. How we built it Next.js (App Router) and React on Vercel, Supabase for Postgres, Auth and Realtime, and WebMCP for the agent surface. The architecture is one idea repeated: the write path is a data structure, not a function call. Tools append operations to a change_sets row. A single PL/pgSQL function, apply_change_set , applies them atomically and resolves ref placeholders to real ids as it goes. It is declared security invoker , so row-level security still guards every insert it performs — an agent cannot use it to reach another user's project. On the WebMCP side: Surface detection. The API moved during the spec's life and shipping browsers do not agree yet, so one adapter registers against document.modelContext.registerTool , navigator.modelContext.registerTool , or navigator.modelContext.provideContext , whichever exists, and the header badge reports which one it found. Page-scoped tool sets. Four tools before you sign in, six inside a project. The surface changes as the human navigates. Cancellation is honoured. The AbortSignal passed to apply_pending_changes releases the approval wait, so an agent that walks away does not leave the page stuck on a modal. Tools never throw at the browser. Failures come back as text an agent can recover from, including "these task ids don't exist in this project, call get_project_context again." Planning uses a strict JSON schema derived from the same Zod schema that backs the propose_plan tool — one schema, two authors, so a plan from the model and a plan from an agent are the same shape. Challenges we ran into Tool calls do not wait for React. Two bugs had the same root: an agent could not always see the proposal it had just written, and focus moved the human's view without get_project_context reporting it. A tool call can land before React has committed state, so reading a render closure returns the past. Tools now read from a ref that is written before the state, never from a closure. Both cases became eval scenarios so they cannot come back. Registering the same tool twice. Navigating between pages left the previous page's registration alive and the browser rejected the new one as a duplicate. Fixed with a module-level registry where claiming a name synchronously releases the previous holder. A machine asking a question and getting an HTML redirect. An unauthenticated POST to the planning endpoint was redirected to the sign-in page; Next then read the multipart body as a server action and answered 404. In an app whose premise is that machines are first-class callers, that was the wrong answer to give one. API routes now reply in JSON. The date picker that could not be used. The month grid was absolutely positioned inside a modal that clips its own corners and scrolls its body, so it was sliced off a few pixels below the field. It renders into a portal now, in viewport coordinates, flipping above the field when there is no room below. Knowing where WebMCP actually exists. Support is not a property of an application, it turns out — it is a property of a surface inside it. The ChatGPT desktop app has two modes, and only one of them exposes the API: in ChatGPT mode the built-in browser hands the page document.modelContext with no flag and no extension, while in Codex mode the built-in browser does not, so the same URL in the same application registers six tools or none depending on which mode you are in. I spent a while concluding the tools were broken before realising I had been testing in the wrong half of one app. That is why the page never assumes. It probes each surface, reports which one it found, and — when it finds none — still works and still explains itself, in its own voice, to a person who came in through an ordinary browser. Faking things. An early version showed timed loading stages — "Reading the brief", "Sequencing by risk" — while the model call ran. They were theatre, in a product whose entire argument is that you should not have to take an agent's word for anything. They were replaced with the true elapsed seconds. Accomplishments that we're proud of The blocking approval gate. Turning a WebMCP tool call from a command into a request is the part that is hard to fake, and it means the agent can be genuinely useful — proposing whole plans rather than timid one-row edits — without ever being trusted with the write. The evals. /evals.js runs seven scenarios against the actual ToolDescriptor objects the page registered, on the live site, from the console, with no account. Seven of seven pass in production. They assert the invariants rather than the happy path: a proposal writes zero rows; a rejection arrives as the tool's return value; approval applies a sprint and its tasks in one transaction with refs resolved; hallucinated ids are refused outright rather than half-applied. And the fact that Sprintfy's own planner goes through its own gate. A product arguing for review does not get to exempt its author. What we learned That a tool result is a channel back to the human , not just a status code. Once you treat it that way, "the agent asked and I said no, here's why" becomes a normal part of the protocol rather than something bolted on top. That the reviewable-proposal pattern belongs in the page, not in the model. The site knows what a legitimate change to itself looks like, so the site should render the diff and hold the gate. Any agent — any model, any vendor — inherits that

title: Pit Wall
pitch: A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game where humans and AI share the pit box—analyze live race conditions, make strategy calls together, or hand the race to an AI Crew Chief.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game where humans and AI share the pit box—analyze live race conditions, make strategy calls together, or hand the race to an AI Crew Chief. Like Comment Story Updates Pit Wall — A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game built around shared human + AI race control. Track & Control Selection — Choose the circuit and control model: Human, Co-Crew Chief, or a fully delegated AI Crew Chief. WebMCP Site Tools — 8 structured tools give ChatGPT live race intelligence plus controlled race actions. AI Race Analysis — ChatGPT reads live race state, evaluates strategy tradeoffs, and recommends a call without acting. Live Pit Wall — Position, fuel, tire age, running order, field strategy, and decision context evolve throughout the race. Shared Pit Wall — Human and AI Crew Chief calls coexist in one persistent race, with control passing between them. Decision History — Every Human and AI Crew Chief strategy call is attributed, timestamped by lap, and preserved. Race Recap — Stage results, strategy history, and major events create an auditable record from green flag to finish. Inspiration Race strategy is a constant sequence of decisions: tires, fuel, track position, cautions, pit timing, and when to sacrifice position now for an advantage later. Most AI experiences put an assistant beside an application. I wanted to explore something different: what happens when the AI has an actual role inside the experience? Pit Wall turns the player into a stock-car crew chief competing against autonomous rival pit walls. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can join that same pit box. The human can ask the AI to analyze the race, make one strategy call, manage a stage, or take responsibility for the entire race. Delegation itself becomes a game mechanic. What it does Pit Wall is a browser-based stock-car strategy game built around human-agent collaboration. Players race across five differentiated environments: Daytona International Speedway Bristol Motor Speedway Darlington Raceway Pocono Raceway Watkins Glen International The simulation models fuel, tire age, pit service, cautions, stages, track position, pace, strategy splits, and autonomous opponent pit walls. Players can interact with the race at several levels of autonomy. Observe ChatGPT can inspect the live race without changing anything. Advise The agent can analyze position, fuel, tires, stage context, field strategy, recent events, and deterministic Race Intelligence, then explain the strategic tradeoffs while leaving the decision to the human. Act The player can delegate exactly one strategy decision to ChatGPT. Delegate The player can hand over a bounded portion of the race—or the entire race through the checkered flag. Every strategy call records its provenance, so the interface shows whether a decision came from the Human or AI Crew Chief. The result is not a chatbot layered on top of a game. The agent and human participate in the same simulation, operate against the same race state, and can exchange control as the race develops. Why WebMCP Pit Wall is designed around a problem that ordinary browser automation does not solve particularly well. A visual agent would have to inspect the interface, infer what each control means, extract race state from rendered text, and manipulate UI elements. WebMCP gives the agent a semantic interface to the same live race the human is playing. Pit Wall registers eight Site Tools: get_race_state get_my_car_state get_field_state get_current_decision get_recent_events get_decision_history commit_strategy advance_to_next_decision Six are read tools and two can mutate the race. The read tools expose structured information about the race, player car, field, current strategic decision, recent events, and decision history. The write tools allow an authorized agent to commit a strategy call and advance the simulation to its next meaningful decision point. This means ChatGPT does not need to infer application state from pixels or simulate mouse clicks. It can reason over explicit race state and perform defined actions through the application's own interface. Human UI actions and WebMCP actions operate against the same canonical race session. Human + agent collaboration The central idea is not simply that AI can play the game. The player determines how much authority the AI receives. Ask: Analyze this situation and recommend a strategy, but don't execute anything. ChatGPT can inspect the race and act as an analytical crew chief while the human retains control. Or: Take this strategy call for me. ChatGPT can make exactly one decision. Or: Take the pit box through the end of this stage. The agent can manage a bounded portion of the race and return control at the stage boundary. Or: Take the pit box and call this race through the checkered flag. The AI Crew Chief can operate the race autonomously through successive strategic decisions. Control is therefore not binary. A player can move between Human, Co-Crew Chief, and AI Crew Chief behavior during one continuous race. Human and AI decisions remain attributed separately even as control passes between them. This creates an interaction model where a human and an agent can observe, reason, collaborate, transfer authority, and take control back inside the same stateful application. Race Intelligence Pit Wall calculates deterministic Race Intelligence for both the player and agent. It includes context such as: fuel margin to the next race boundary tire age relative to the field position trend stage context observable opponent strategy recent strategy consequences The simulation calculates the facts. ChatGPT interprets them. This separation is important. The agent does not invent the underlying fuel state, tire age, position, or field behavior. Pit Wall provides deterministic race information, while ChatGPT reasons about what that information means strategically. This allows the AI to explain why a decision matters instead of merely selecting an action. Strategy has consequences Pit Wall does not guarantee that either the human or AI will win. Pit service can sacrifice substantial track position. Staying out can gain immediate position while creating future tire or fuel problems. Short-pitting can create an undercut opportunity while temporarily sending the car backward through the running order. Different race environments also create different strategic conditions. The player's position, tire state, fuel state, pit history, field strategy, and race circumstances evolve as decisions are made. Completed WebMCP-controlled races have produced everything from victories to difficult finishes. Every decision remains visible in the strategy history, including: who made the call the lap on which it occurred the selected strategy the resulting position consequence Stage winners and the player's Stage 1 and Stage 2 results are preserved through the final race recap. The checkered-flag screen therefore becomes more than a finishing position. It provides a record of how the human and AI managed the race together. How I built it Pit Wall uses a React/Vite frontend, FastAPI backend, and deterministic Python race simulation. The architecture is: Human + ChatGPT → React/WebMCP interface → FastAPI → Pit Wall adapter → deterministic race simulation → user car + autonomous field The browser interface presents the same race state used by the agent. WebMCP tools are registered through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The application exposes eight WebMCP Site Tools directly from the live browser experience. The FastAPI layer provides the race-session API, while the simulation owns the canonical race state and advances the user car and autonomous field. The submitted application is self-contained and does not require an external database at runtime. The production build is packaged as a single-origin Docker application and deployed on Render. Reliability and integrity Giving an AI permission to mutate a stateful application introduces a different engineering problem from simply asking an AI for advice. A strategy call must apply to the correct decision. It must not execute twice. An agent managing a bounded portion of the race must stop at the requested boundary. And once the checkered flag falls, neither the human nor agent should be able to continue mutating the completed race. Pit Wall therefore includes protections for: stale decisions duplicate decisions decision-boundary overrun stage-boundary handling post-finish mutation actor provenance Human/AI control state Human and AI actions travel through the same underlying simulation rules rather than separate gameplay paths. title: Left Out Security - WebMCP Security Lab
pitch: An interactive lab where people and AI agents inspect WebMCP tools, narrow their authority, approve one exact action, and verify the real effect with security receipts.
about_excerpt: An interactive lab where people and AI agents inspect WebMCP tools, narrow their authority, approve one exact action, and verify the real effect with security receipts. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I started Left Out Security - WebMCP Security Lab because I was trying to understand what WebMCP really changes. The basic idea is powerful: instead of an AI agent looking at a webpage and guessing what buttons or forms mean, a website can expose structured capabilities directly to the agent. That immediately raised a security question for me: How does the human know what the agent is actually being allowed to do? As I dug through documentation, developer discussions, forum posts, security conversations, and other early WebMCP material, I kept seeing the same gap. There are really three different surfaces involved: Presented Surface — what the website tells the human. Declared Agent Surface — what the WebMCP tool tells the agent. Effective Surface — what the code actually does when the tool runs. Those three things can match. They do not have to. That became the core idea behind the lab. I did not want to write another article explaining that agent tools could create security problems. I wanted to build a place where someone could actually inspect the problem, approve a capability, invoke it, and then verify what really happened. What it does WebMCP Security Lab is a synthetic security test range for WebMCP. The lab walks a person and an AI agent through deliberately vulnerable examples where the user can compare what was promised, what was declared, what was authorized, and what actually occurred. The basic path is: Public URL → native Site Tool → human review → narrow approval → one invocation → verified receipt The current lessons explore problems such as: A supposedly read-only tool that changes state An input schema that asks for more authority than the task requires Tool output shaped like instructions A vague confirmation around a mutating action A site making compatibility claims it cannot actually support One lesson uses a synthetic eligibility check for TRAINING-1042 . The point is not whether the eligibility check succeeds. The point is whether the user and the agent can prove that the capability they approved is the capability that actually ran. How people and agents work together The human determines intent. The agent invokes the capability. The application verifies the result. I wanted those responsibilities to stay visibly separate. With ordinary browser automation, the agent often has to infer intent from the DOM, buttons, labels, and forms. The user sees the webpage, but usually does not see a clean representation of the authority being exercised by the agent. WebMCP improves that by allowing sites to declare structured tools directly. But a declaration is still a claim. A tool can be named like a harmless lookup and still mutate state. An annotation can say something is read-only without technically enforcing that behavior. A schema can be technically valid and still request far more information than the visible task requires. So the lab keeps asking three questions: What did the site promise? What did the agent receive? What actually happened? How I built it This project is also an experiment in how far I could get using almost nothing except ChatGPT and GitHub . The concepts and security model are mine, informed by the documentation, forums, developer conversations, and security discussions I was following while learning WebMCP. The implementation was almost completely vibe coded using Daybreak Blue across the ChatGPT product surface: ChatGPT Chat ChatGPT Work ChatGPT Sites Codex GitHub for the repository and source control There was no traditional development team. I would work through the security idea in ChatGPT, turn it into a concrete lesson or control, build and modify the application through ChatGPT and Codex, test the behavior, find where my assumptions were wrong, and iterate again. The public application registers structured capabilities through WebMCP using: document.modelContext.registerTool() One of the design decisions I cared about most was keeping approval separate from execution . A broad teaching capability can be inspected first. After the user approves an exact task, the application can replace that broad capability with a generated, narrow capability that is: Bound to the approved task Zero-input One-use Consumed after execution Not intended to be retried Approving it does not execute it. The agent still has to invoke the capability. After invocation, the lab generates a receipt describing things such as: Result Before state After state Side effects Invocation count Remaining authority That receipt is important because I did not want the lab to end with a green checkmark that simply says everything worked. I wanted evidence. Challenges This project is still actively moving. I am still grinding on it, so some implementation details are changing even while the submission is being prepared. The biggest design challenge was separating: Registration Discovery Review Approval Invocation Verification It would have been much easier to collapse those into a single flow. But doing that would hide the exact trust boundaries the project is supposed to teach. Another challenge has been browser-side execution. I have been working with a local extension path for some of the more advanced testing, and that integration has been giving me trouble. Rather than pretend that path is finished, I am moving that work into the advanced path while keeping the public native Site Tool experience focused and reproducible. That separation turned out to be useful anyway. The public experience can demonstrate the core security model cleanly, while the advanced path can continue exploring deeper browser-side instrumentation and local execution. There were also a lot of less glamorous implementation problems. Stale tool registrations could accumulate while moving between lessons. Capabilities had to be registered, replaced, consumed, and invalidated correctly. State had to remain understandable to both the human and the agent. Those problems are not exciting to describe, but they matter if the lesson is supposed to prove something instead of simply looking like it works. What I learned The biggest lesson is that a tool's name is not a security control . Neither is an annotation. They are useful metadata, but they are still statements made by the tool provider. Security has to look at the complete interaction: Human intent Declared schema Granted authority Mutation language Tool output Runtime behavior Observed effect The verification step became especially important. A lot of systems focus heavily on whether an agent should be allowed to perform an action. Much less attention is paid to proving what actually happened after the action ran. That is why the receipt became part of the design. Another thing I learned I also learned something about the development process itself. This project became an exploration of what one person can build using essentially: ChatGPT + GitHub The security architecture, UI, code, debugging, documentation, testing ideas, lesson design, and submission work have all moved through the same AI-assisted workflow. That does not mean ChatGPT invented the project. The concepts, threat model, decisions, and direction came from me. What surprised me was how far I could push the implementation by treating ChatGPT not as a chatbot sitting beside the project, but as the development environment surrounding it. Chat for thinking. Work for organizing. Sites for publishing. Codex for building and debugging. GitHub for the actual repository. That became a second experiment running underneath the WebMCP experiment. What's next The project is still evolving. Near-term work includes: More adversarial WebMCP lessons Additional conformance fixtures Accessibility testing Better declared-versus-observed comparisons Privacy-reviewed evidence workflows Advanced browser-side instrumentation Continued work on the local extension and advanced testing path The larger goal is to turn WebMCP Security Lab into a reusable place for understanding and testing agent-facing web capabilities. WebMCP gives websites a new way to expose functionality directly to AI agents. I want people to have an equally good way to ask: What did I actually authorize, what did the agent actually receive, and what actually happened? And, somewhat accidentally, I am also finding out how much of that can be built with just ChatGPT and GitHub. Apparently, quite a lot. title: Agent Arena — Games That Any Agent Can Play
pitch: WebMCP turns an AI agent from an adviser into a real player in a shared game—invited, permissioned, and synchronized with people.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns an AI agent from an adviser into a real player in a shared game—invited, permissioned, and synchronized with people. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Agent Arena — Games That Any Agent Can Play From AI advice to AI participation Most “AI games” connect one model API to a server. Agent Arena explores a more open pattern: a human can invite a compatible agent into a shared browser experience, where it participates under the same rules and state as everyone else. Mini Chess is the first reference game. A person can play against an agent, or invite two independent agents—one for White and one for Black—to play each other while people watch the same live board. What it does Each private invitation grants exactly one role-scoped player seat. The agent uses page-defined WebMCP tools to read the frozen rules, join, inspect shared state, wait for its turn, and submit a move. The server remains authoritative for invitations, identities, permissions, legal moves, turn order, revisions, and results. The visible board and the agent tools operate on one live session. The game is deliberately small so the interaction model is easy to see: humans invite agents, agents identify themselves and act only when permitted, and every move is validated before the shared state changes. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the page offer a small semantic action model instead of requiring an agent to infer a game from pixels or requiring the game to integrate a particular model vendor. The same invitation, identity, turn-taking, permission, synchronization, and action pattern can extend to other games and collaborative experiences. How it was built The private controller registers five tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Their schemas reject unknown properties; read operations are marked read-only. Tool execution and the human interface call the same Express API and SQLite-backed session state. The project uses one-time invitation capabilities, post-join player tokens, rule and revision guards, idempotent action IDs, and a legal-move engine. It is an independent, open-source MIT repository: the live demo is linked from a project gallery, but the application has no dependency on the personal website. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: Minimal Protocol Witness
pitch: WebMCP system for differential evaluation analysis: isolate protocol sensitive result reversals, derive minimal counterfactual witnesses and verify them against the evaluation surface.
about_excerpt: WebMCP system for differential evaluation analysis: isolate protocol sensitive result reversals, derive minimal counterfactual witnesses and verify them against the evaluation surface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI evaluations can disagree even when testing the same models on the same benchmark. Small protocol differences like reasoning budget, parsing, retries, or tool access can change the conclusion. We wanted to answer one question: What is the smallest protocol change sufficient to reproduce the conflicting result? What it does Minimal Protocol Witness (MPW) compares conflicting evaluation setups through controlled counterfactual tests. In our demo, Lab A concludes MODEL_A while Lab B concludes MODEL_B on the same 400-item synthetic benchmark. MPW tests protocol changes, finds the minimum witness, verifies it across the full exposed protocol space, and produces a replay-verifiable certificate. How we built it MPW uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP . It exposes four semantic WebMCP tools: read_dispute run_counterfactual inspect_evidence verify_witness The agent decides what to investigate, while a deterministic engine computes results, verifies minimality, and issues certificates. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making the result rigorous instead of just visually convincing. Protocol effects can be non-monotonic, so we could not assume that adding more changes preserves a result. We built exact search and verification instead. We also had to keep agent reasoning separate from scientific verification. Accomplishments that we're proud of Exact minimum-witness verification Full 16-subset verification in the canonical example Shared state between humans and WebMCP agents Experiment-ID-bound evidence inspection Replay-verifiable certificates Extensive automated and adversarial testing Explicit limits on causal and universal claims What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when a website exposes meaningful domain operations, not just UI actions. We also learned that agents and deterministic systems work best together: the agent explores, while the system verifies. What's next for Minimal Protocol Witness Next we want to test MPW on real model evaluations, larger protocol spaces, more external harnesses, and repeated stochastic runs. Longer term, we want evaluation reports to become machine-inspectable and counterfactually testable by both humans and agents.
