title: Gym & Tonic
pitch: Gym & Tonic turns “I should work out” into a week you can actually live. ChatGPT coaches, your plan stays private, and every decision remains yours.
about_excerpt: Gym & Tonic turns “I should work out” into a week you can actually live. ChatGPT coaches, your plan stays private, and every decision remains yours. Like Comment Story Updates Today: A daily dashboard with one next action, workout recovery, walking minutes, and private habit check-ins. Progress: A calm view of completed workouts, minutes, walking, habits, history, and optional weight trends. Planner 1: See your weekly status, progress, and next useful action at a glance. Planner 2: Start, resume, view, or add a short workout based on what your day needs. Coach Suggesting for schedule changes via WebMCP Coach suggesting for schedule changes via WebMCP Planner 3: Plan fourteen morning and evening sessions without overwriting your existing workouts. Planner 4: Review progress, insights, meals, templates, calendar export, and coach proposals. Workout: A focused guided workout with exercise cues, illustrations, optional timers, and explicit finish control. Meals: Searchable meal ideas with dietary filters, preparation times, ingredients, substitutions, and favourites. Settings: Personalize goals, training preferences, habits, alerts, weight tracking, analytics, and data controls. Inspiration I built Gym & Tonic because “I should probably work out” is one of the most popular fitness plans in the world, and one of the least effective. Most fitness apps give you endless exercises, complicated programs, and enough numbers. I wanted to build something that helps people turn good intentions into a realistic week they can actually follow. What it does Gym & Tonic is a local-first fitness planner for people starting or returning to exercise. It helps users plan weekly sessions, follow guided workouts, use optional timers, reflect after training, track consistency, discover practical meal ideas, and see what their next useful action is. The WebMCP integration lets ChatGPT act as a coach that understands the live training plan. It can check the week, identify gaps, suggest sessions, fill empty slots, and propose swaps. The important part is that the coach does not get to quietly rearrange someone’s life. Every change becomes a proposal that the user can approve or reject. How I built it I built Gym & Tonic with Astro, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind, and WebMCP. The application is local-first, so plans, completions, reflections, and workout progress stay in the browser. There are no accounts, no backend, and no mysterious fitness spreadsheet being sent into the cloud. I used Fraunces and Inter to give the interface an editorial feel, then added guided workout screens, progress views, accessible navigation, responsive layouts, exercise illustrations, local persistence, offline support, and privacy-conscious analytics. The agent tools are registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Read actions can inspect the plan, while write actions are staged for approval through one proposal pipeline. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was not generating a workout. The internet has generated enough workouts to keep humanity busy until the sun explodes. The real challenge was handling the small but important states: pending proposals, rejected changes, active workouts, timers after reload, completed sessions, optional reflections, local storage migrations, mobile navigation, and the difference between “planned” and “actually completed.” I also had to make sure an AI coach could be helpful without becoming an unsupervised personal trainer with admin privileges. Accomplishments that I am proud of I am proud that Gym & Tonic feels like a complete product rather than just a workout generator. A user can arrive with no plan, choose a manageable starting point, place a session, open a guided workout, complete it, reflect, and see that progress represented immediately. I am also proud of the trust model. The coach can do the planning legwork, but the user remains in control of every meaningful change. The project is open source, local-first, responsive, accessible, and designed to work for people who are building consistency rather than chasing perfection. What I learned I learned that good AI product design is often about restraint. It is easy to make an agent that can change things. It is much harder to make one that explains what it wants to do, waits for approval, and respects the user’s ownership of the result. I also learned that the most important product state is often not “success” or “failure.” Sometimes it is simply “you started, and that counts.” What's next for Gym & Tonic Next, I would like to add printable training diaries, installable PWA support, deeper exercise guidance, richer progress storytelling, and more ways for the coach to explain why it is making a suggestion. I would also like to explore a mode where the coach can defend a rejected proposal with evidence from the user’s plan, without becoming annoying enough to be muted immediately. For now, Gym & Tonic is focused on one useful promise: helping people make a plan, follow through, and come back next week. title: Panoptik
pitch: Panoptik is a browser-native video studio powered by WebMCP. In-browser AI agents inspect footage and propose smart cuts and zooms as reviewable staged diffs—100% locally.
about_excerpt: Panoptik is a browser-native video studio powered by WebMCP. In-browser AI agents inspect footage and propose smart cuts and zooms as reviewable staged diffs—100% locally. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP Toolcalls - 2 Zoom controls Voiceover and music Zoom points Stage WebMCP Toolcalls - 1 Text overlays Landing page Facecam controls Autogenerated captions using whisper agentic ediditing session Export menu Workspace Editor Panoptik × WebMCP — Project Story A browser-native video studio where humans and AI agents co-edit on the same canvas. > Decode, render, audio mixing, and export happen 100% inside your browser using WebCodecs and Canvas2D. No uploads, no render farm, zero data leakage. Inspiration Making demo videos for software products takes too much time. A punchy 90-second product demo requires 15+ camera zoom keyframes, dozens of subtitle snippets, manual silence excision, and canvas framing. In tools like ScreenStudio, Loom, or Premiere, this forces creators to spend 45 to 60 minutes scrubbing frame-by-frame, calculating focal centers, placing timeline diamonds, and proofreading speech. Because editing is so exhausting, many developers simply give up and ship raw, unpolished recordings. When we set out to build an AI agent to handle this tedious workflow, we ran into a core architectural barrier: video editing lives inside client-side canvas pixels. Backend MCP servers are blind to the browser session: The video file lives in the browser's Origin Private File System (OPFS), the playback state lives in an in-memory Zustand store, and the rendered UI exists only as Canvas2D pixel buffers. There is no remote server copy for an external API to inspect. Multimodal DOM-scraping is fragile and costly: Directing an agent via automated screenshots and synthetic cursor events consumes ~150 KB to 200 KB of token bandwidth per action, introduces seconds of latency, and frequently misclicks or desynchronizes with the timeline. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge provided the missing architectural link: an in-page, standardized communication bridge between browser-resident agents and client-side web applications. We built Panoptik so an in-browser agent can inspect the canvas, analyze project telemetry, and propose structured edits directly through 30 imperative WebMCP tools—while keeping the human firmly in control. What it does Panoptik is a screen recording and video production studio that runs entirely inside the browser: Zero-Upload Local Media Engine: Drop in raw recordings or capture screen, camera, and microphone directly. Decoding, real-time compositing, audio mixing, and MP4/WebM encoding run entirely client-side via WebCodecs, Canvas2D, and mediabunny. Proprietary dashboards, sensitive credentials, and internal code never leave your machine. 30 Granular WebMCP Tools: Panoptik exposes its editing engine via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Running inside ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, the agent inspects scene cadence, reads click coordinates, checks rendered frames, and orchestrates multi-track edits. The "Agent Proposes, Human Disposes" Diff Engine: The agent never silently mutates the timeline. Proposed cuts, zooms, captions, and transitions appear as non-destructive ghost edits (dashed amber keyframe diamonds, pending caption chips, and preview diffs). The creator can adjust any parameter manually and commit or discard the diff with a single click. Studio-Grade Polish: Dynamic Camera Zooms: Smooth continuous cubic camera translations with automatic viewport margin clamping. Visual Grounding: Three-tier focal resolution mapping agent requests (e.g., "zoom in on the login button" ) to exact coordinates via click telemetry, grid bounding boxes, or balanced fallbacks. Acoustic Snapping & Silence Removal: Automatic dead-air truncation that preserves natural speech cadence without clipping vocal phonemes. Word-Level Subtitles: Synchronized transcription with animated keyword highlighting. Pitch-Preserving Speed Adjustment: High-fidelity audio time-stretching via the WSOLA algorithm. Live Tool Trace Panel: A persistent inspector panel that surfaces every WebMCP call, runtime latency, input payload, and return value for total human oversight. How we built it Panoptik is structured as a monorepo containing the Next.js application ( apps/web ), the low-level media engine ( packages/engine ), and the shared type contract ( packages/project-schema ). ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser Tab (Next.js) │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ │ │Preview Canvas│ │Timeline & Store│ │ Tool Trace │ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └───────┬────────┘ └─────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Reactive Project Store (Zustand) │ │ │ │ Committed Elements ↔ Staged Ghost Diffs │ │ │ └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ │Media Engine │ │ WebMCP Layer │ │ │ │(WebCodecs, │ │ (30 Tools, │ │ │ │ Canvas2D) │ │ Snapping) │ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ W3C document.modelContext / Web APIs │ │ │ │ VideoDecoder · VideoEncoder · OPFS · Mediabunny │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 1. Camera Zoom Interpolation At any playback timestamp t , the camera transform state is represented by a 2D affine vector: T(t) = [ s(t), x_f(t), y_f(t) ]ᵀ where s(t) is the zoom scale factor and (x_f, y_f) ∈ [0, 1]² is the normalized focal target. For a zoom starting at t_k with duration Δt , the normalized transition progress parameter is: p(t) = clamp( (t - t_k) / Δt, 0, 1 ) Progress is mapped through a cubic easing curve E(p) : E(p) = 4p³ (for p < 0.5) E(p) = 1 - (-2p + 2)³ / 2 (for p ≥ 0.5) The camera blends smoothly from the current state to the target state: T(t) = (1 - E(p)) · T_start + E(p) · T_target To render this on a canvas of dimensions (W_canvas, H_canvas) letterboxing a source video (W_vid, H_vid) with base scale S_0 , the 2D transformation offsets applied to the context are: T_x(t) = (W_canvas / 2) - x_f(t) · W_vid · S_0 · s(t) T_y(t) = (H_canvas / 2) - y_f(t) · H_vid · S_0 · s(t) 2. Dual Time-Space Mapping The human editor and agent reason in timeline time ( t_timeline ), while underlying video chunks exist in immutable source time ( t_src ). Cuts and speed modifications cause these coordinate systems to diverge. For clip i with source interval [s_i, e_i] played at speed factor v_i , the timeline duration is: D_i = (e_i - s_i) / v_i The forward mapping function transforms source seconds into timeline seconds: t_timeline = ∑(D_j) + (t_src - s_k) / v_k When an agent proposes an edit, Panoptik immediately maps the timestamp back into source coordinates using the inverse mapping. Downstream timeline shifts caused by cutting dead air never invalidate or displace previously anchored keyframes. 3. Acoustic Word Boundary Snapping Rather than blindly executing raw timestamps emitted by an LLM, cut proposals are guarded against active vocal phonemes using an acoustic safety boundary: |t_cut - t_boundary(w)| ≥ 150 ms (for all spoken words w) If a proposed cut falls within 150 ms of a word boundary, the cut automatically snaps outward to the nearest preceding silence interval, preventing clipped syllables. 4. Token & Bandwidth Economics Comparing WebMCP structured tool calls against conventional multimodal vision scraping: WebMCP Payload: ~2.1 KB Screenshot + DOM Scraping: ~165 KB Efficiency Gain: 1 - (2.1 KB / 165 KB) ≈ 98.7% A complete multi-step edit session completes in ~6 lightweight JSON tool calls (~3 KB total context overhead), eliminating latency bottlenecks and model context exhaustion. Challenges we ran into Zero-WASM, Pure Browser Media Pipeline: Most web video editors rely on ffmpeg.wasm , which requires massive binary downloads (30 MB+), induces heavy CPU thermal throttling, and risks memory leaks. We built on native web standards: WebCodecs VideoDecoder / VideoEncoder , Canvas2D, and OPFS. Handling variable frame rate (VFR) screen recordings while maintaining microsecond audio synchronization required custom timestamp interpolation and frame-stepping logic. The "Dual Time-Space Paradox" in Agent Reasoning: LLMs reason sequentially based on current visuals: "cut dead air from 0:12 to 0:18, then zoom in at 0:25" . As soon as the first cut is staged, the visual timeline contracts by 6 seconds. If the subsequent zoom is evaluated against the old timeline, it lands on the wrong frame. We solved this by implementing an atomic batch execution pipeline ( propose_edits ) that evaluates all instructions against a single snapshot and performs dynamic cut-map rebasing. title: Agent Has to Ask
pitch: Our agent can pick the cart. You still own the charge. The store sees what you allowed, checks the limit and only opens checkout after that check passes.
about_excerpt: Our agent can pick the cart. You still own the charge. The store sees what you allowed, checks the limit and only opens checkout after that check passes. Like Comment Story Updates GIF knowyouragent webmcp demo Inspiration Checkout with an agent usually collapses into one click: the agent talks to the page, asks to buy, and a session appears. The person whose card is about to move never sees a clean “this is what it asked for.” The merchant never has a clean “this is why we said yes.” We split that into three questions a human can actually answer: What did the agent ask to buy? What will this store allow? Does the server still say yes? Until those are separate, an agent shopping for you is a blank check. What we built Agent has to ask is a public KnowYourAgent demo for agent-assisted checkout. The agent can request a purchase. It cannot approve one. The page shows a short-lived signed permission: who the agent is, which cart, which wallet, what it may buy, when it expires, and the spend cap. A browser agent gets two tools: kya_validate_trace — check that permission in the browser kya_verify_agent — send the cart to the merchant for a read-only preflight The server checks the signature, audience, agent, scope, expiry, currency, cart, wallet, and amount. Then it says one of three things a person can read: Accept Review Decline Checkout runs the same check again on the server before it creates a simulated session. No card is captured. No production order is written. After the decision you can inspect the record: trace ID, preflight ID, cart fingerprint, and why it landed where it did. How we built it Next.js, TypeScript, React, signed JWT traces, Web Crypto, and WebMCP tool registration. The page registers tools on the browser’s model context. The merchant adapter stays on the server and keeps the last word. Challenges The hard part was not wiring tools. It was refusing to let the browser become the thing that authorizes payment. A browser tool can help an agent ask . It must not be the authority that charges . We also kept the flow usable when WebMCP is missing: a person can still read the permission and run the same server preflight by hand. What we learned Agent checkout needs a human-shaped boundary. The agent files a request. The merchant enforces policy. The server decides. The record has to explain what happened and why — to the shopper, not just to the protocol. title: Spotlight
pitch: A real agent, driving real WebMCP tools, to solve a real problem: figuring out what order to watch a franchise in, and actually getting caught up - not just being told the order.
about_excerpt: A real agent, driving real WebMCP tools, to solve a real problem: figuring out what order to watch a franchise in, and actually getting caught up - not just being told the order. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Spotlight already had the hard problem solved on paper: a "Must Watch" graph in Postgres that knows the correct order to watch a franchise in, and a private per-user watch history behind real auth. But that data was only reachable by clicking through the UI yourself. Ask any AI assistant "what order should I watch John Wick in?" and it answers from memory - no idea what you've actually seen, no way to act on the answer. WebMCP looked like the first real answer to that gap: instead of an agent scraping a rendered page or a separate backend replicating the app's auth, the tools just live inside the page's own already-authenticated session. What it does Spotlight registers 9 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() on top of an app that already tracks streaming and theatrical releases, watchlists, and watch order for movies and shows. The flagship, plan_watch_order , reads the real "Must Watch" graph, cross-references what you've actually watched, and writes only the remaining titles into your real watchlist in the correct order - run it again after finishing a title and it correctly says there's nothing left to add. Two of the tools, mark_watched and reorder_watchlist , don't exist until they'd do something real: they register and unregister themselves live via toolchange as your watchlist's own shape changes. To prove the tool surface is genuinely agent-legible and not just spec-compliant, we also built an in-page chat panel (bring-your-own API key, Groq by default) where a real LLM reads the tool schemas with getTools() and drives them with executeTool() from plain English. How we built it React + TypeScript on the frontend, Postgres (Neon) for the release calendar, watchlists, and the watch-order graph, Vercel serverless functions for the API, and a GitHub Actions pipeline that refreshes release data from TMDB on a schedule. The WebMCP layer lives entirely in src/webmcp/ : every tool wraps the exact same client-side functions the UI's own buttons already call, so there's no parallel "agent" backend and no duplicated logic. Challenges we ran into Chrome's experimental WebMCP flag expects executeTool() 's arguments as a JSON string, not the plain object the spec's own examples show - a real divergence we only found by testing. We also discovered no shipping agent (ChatGPT's desktop app, its Computer-Use mode, Codex) actually routes through document.modelContext yet; all of them fall back to generic DOM automation, which is exactly why we built the in-page chat panel instead of just asking an existing assistant to try it. On the infrastructure side: Vercel's Hobby plan caps you at 12 serverless functions, so guest sign-in had to extend an existing endpoint rather than ship as a new file, and none of OpenAI's, Azure's, or Groq's APIs set CORS headers for browser calls, which meant building a stateless same-origin relay just to let the chat panel talk to an LLM at all. Accomplishments that we're proud of Getting a real language model to call get_watch_order and then plan_watch_order on its own, unscripted, and watching four films land in a real account's watchlist in the correct order - live, not mocked. And handling the "no agent uses this yet" problem honestly instead of hiding it: we verified the gap directly, documented it, and built the one thing that actually demonstrates the tools are ready for when an agent does. What we learned How much of "making an app agent-ready" is really about discipline in the app's own code, not the WebMCP API itself - every tool only stayed simple because it called the same functions the UI already trusted. We also learned firsthand how far ahead the spec is of the ecosystem actually consuming it right now. What's next for Spotlight Once a shipping assistant actually calls document.modelContext on its own, Spotlight's tools are already sitting there waiting - no work required on our end. Beyond that: correct_watch_order already lets a user tell their agent "that link is wrong," which is the seed of letting an agent help curate the underlying graph itself, not just consume it. title: ClaimGate
pitch: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions.
about_excerpt: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP exposes privacy-safe candidate matching while private proof stays manual. Staff reviews aggregate eligibility and a redacted timeline, never evidence values. Atomic handoff completes the claim, returns the item, and resolves the report. ClaimGate — privacy-first lost-property claims with human release decisions. Problem Lost-property desks need enough public detail to find a likely item without publishing the details that prove ownership. Giving every field to an Agent would turn private proof into searchable material. ClaimGate separates public matching from private proof. The Agent handles structured preparation and safe reads. People publish, submit evidence, decide the claim, issue the pickup credential, and complete the release. Why WebMCP This workflow changes as the claim moves from draft to match, review, pickup, and collection. WebMCP lets the page expose the few actions that are valid now, with typed inputs and bounded results. The Agent does not have to infer controls from page layout, and sensitive actions can stay absent from the tool set. Better experience A Claimant can describe a loss once, let the Agent structure the public fields, and receive explainable candidates without copying data between screens. Staff gets a short queue and a redacted summary. Each person sees the next action in the same claim instead of reconstructing context after every role change. Before and after Before ClaimGate, the demo journey is a sequence of manual forms and page searches, with a risk of mixing public clues and ownership proof. With ClaimGate, the Agent prepares, searches, and summarizes through explicit tools while the UI reserves publication, proof, judgment, credential transfer, and handoff for visible human controls. What it does A Claimant starts a fresh two-hour instance with fictional Northbridge Campus inventory. The Agent can create or update a lost-report draft, list reports, find up to three candidates, and stage one candidate. Results contain broad fields, confidence bands, and public reasons, not internal inventory IDs. The Claimant publishes and submits masked evidence manually. Two correct slots are sufficient even if a third submitted slot is wrong. The browser receives only aggregate eligibility, insufficiency, or the third-attempt LOCKED state. Staff reads a bounded queue and redacted review summary, then decides manually. After approval, the Agent can read pickup instructions. The Claimant manually generates and copies a ten-minute, one-time credential, then Staff pastes it into the handoff form. One transaction marks the claim collected, item returned, and report resolved. The normal web flow also works without WebMCP. How implemented ClaimGate is one Next.js 16 application with separate report, matching, evidence, claim, authorization, audit, and WebMCP modules. SQLite scopes every record to a demo instance. Signed HttpOnly sessions and server routes enforce role, ownership, state, version, CSRF, origin, idempotency, and rate limits. The browser uses native document.modelContext.registerTool() . A page and state registry selects nine tools, and an AbortController removes the previous generation on navigation or state change. Tool visibility assists selection; the server remains authoritative. The tools are create_lost_report_draft , update_lost_report_draft , list_my_reports , find_candidate_matches , stage_claim_candidate , get_claim_status , get_pickup_instructions , list_pending_claims , and get_claim_review_summary . Publishing, evidence, decisions, pass issue or reissue, role switching, and handoff have no WebMCP tool. Matching uses fixed category, time, area, color, and tag rules. Runtime evidence comparison uses salted HMAC digests and a fixed three-slot shape. The public repository contains the readable fictional seed answers so judges can run the demo; the privacy boundary covers runtime clients, pages, APIs, WebMCP, logs, and stored raw evidence, not repository readers. Only a successful issue or reissue response returns the full pickup credential. The current Claimant page keeps it in memory and can reveal, mask, or copy it. Navigation or refresh clears it and cannot recover it. The server stores only a digest, and reissue invalidates the previous generation. Challenges we ran into State-aware tool lifecycle: Chrome 151 can briefly change membership while registrations are replaced. A serialized generation manager and server state checks make stale calls fail safely. Runtime privacy evidence: We separated public DTOs from private transports, signed opaque candidate handles, bounded outputs, and scanned tool results, HTML, logs, storage, history, and public build assets. Visible cross-role continuity: Claimant and Staff must resume the same authorized claim without hidden navigation. Contextual role switching and a 14-scenario visible Playwright suite cover that path. Accomplishments that we're proud of The complete report, match, proof, review, pickup, and handoff flow works in the normal UI and the WebMCP-assisted path. Nine tools appear only in valid page and state scopes; human-only actions stay absent. A clean production build completed three independent native Chrome 151 runs. Each used fresh SQLite state, exercised all nine tools, completed the manual transitions, and ended with Home tools [] . All 14 visible Playwright E2E scenarios passed after commit 04c618d added contextual cross-role claim navigation. The release path isolates its runtime, data, processes, ingress, and Nginx resources from unrelated services. These are implementation and test results, not claims of awards, adoption, users, or judging outcome. What we learned Tool discovery improves planning but is not authorization. Runtime privacy needs separate data paths, not hidden UI fields. Human control is clearest when a sensitive transition has no tool at all. Stateful WebMCP also needs navigation, stale-version, delayed-completion, and teardown tests, not only a happy path. What's next A production pilot would need institutional identity, enrolled Staff, accessibility and abuse review, retention policy, backup and recovery, and a database architecture for multiple application instances. Configurable matching and evidence policies should preserve the same public-match, private-proof, and human-release boundaries. title: Dojo
pitch: A website that tests the AI agent visiting it. Seven belts, one page, real WebMCP tools; some belts cannot be passed without you. Find out what your agent is actually good at
about_excerpt: A website that tests the AI agent visiting it. Seven belts, one page, real WebMCP tools; some belts cannot be passed without you. Find out what your agent is actually good at Like Comment Story Updates GIF What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before A person and their agent can now find out together what the agent is actually good at, on a real site, in one sitting. That was impossible before, because no page could hand an arbitrary visiting agent a task and watch how it used it. In the WebMCP demos we could find (a scan of 496 live sites and of the challenge entries visible on X before the deadline, both in the repo), the agent works for the site; the closest exceptions are two word games that score an agent's play on one axis. In the Dojo the site is the examiner and the agent is the subject. You open the page in the ChatGPT desktop browser, paste one line, and your agent works through seven belts using only the page's tools: reading two rosters and joining them, navigating rooms and recovering from a guiding error, proposing a schedule change and waiting for your approval, asking you for a value no tool can return, reading a poisoned member message and deciding whether to obey it, getting a tamper-seal code that exists nowhere until your finger holds it down, and clearing a waitlist within a four-call budget. You watch every call as it happens. Three of the belts cannot be passed without you. At the end you get a report card: a belt rank, every call against par, named checks with an evidence column, and whether your agent followed an instruction that came from page data instead of from you. That is a new kind of thing to do together. Before WebMCP, a website could not hand a visiting agent a structured task, observe the exact calls it made, or know whether the agent asked the person before acting. Now it can, and the person is in the loop for the parts only a person can do. Why WebMCP fits this use case The Dojo is only possible because the page can register tools and watch the agent use them. Three things WebMCP gives us that nothing else does: The page is the examiner. With document.modelContext.registerTool the site decides exactly what the agent can do on each belt, sees every call with its arguments, and grades on structure (ids, enums, integers, orderings, timestamps), never on guessing what the agent meant. A scraper or a screenshot agent cannot be tested this way; there are no calls to observe. Human and agent share one page through different channels. The agent gets tools. The person gets the page: an Approve button, a "Check the receipt" control that appears only when the draft has been read and shows the tier to nobody until it is pressed, a seal that reveals its code only under a real hold of at least 1.2 seconds. Both are looking at the same document in the same browser session with no backend between them. Discovery on visit. There is nothing to install. The agent finds the belts because it visited the page, and get_dojo_state is registered for the whole visit so a changing tool set is never a dead end. Cloudflare's engineering blog calls agents "a new kind of visitor" (Building an open Agentic Internet, Aug 2026). The Dojo is a page built for that visitor: it hands the agent structured work, watches how it is done, and keeps the person in the loop for the parts only a person can do. Two audiences have a real use for this: people deciding how far to trust their agent, who can now run two agents on the same seed and compare cards; and site owners shipping WebMCP tools, who can watch how an agent actually treats a tool description, and who get Open Mat, a lint panel that checks their own tool ds published budgets with no agent involved. How it improves the user experience Without WebMCP, testing an agent on a website means watching it click througd guessing what it understood. In the Dojo the person sees a live feed ofevery tool call with its arguments, the result, and page-side execution time, with human actions and check verdicts landing in the same stream. The LIVE TOOLS panel shows the agent's available tools change as belts start, so dynamic registration is vi When the agent needs the person, the request lands in a docked bar labelled"only you can do this", and the agent's own tool result tells it to say what it is waiting for instead of polling. Guiding errors tell the agent what to call next ("You are in Mat. file_incident works in Records. Call go_to_room..."), so a wrong turn ind. The report card is a link with no server behind it, prints exactly whichevidence the page has for each claim, and gives one fix for the person and one for the site owner per failed belt. How WebMCP is implemented 24 tool definitions, at most 8 registered at once in the default mode (a ?static=1 mode registers all 24 at load, gated to the active belt, for agent runtimes that do not re-read the tool list). Five always-on tools ( get_dojo_state , start_belt , report_unclear_tool , finish_and_get_card ) are registered on load andnever unregistered. Each belt registers its own tool set on start_belt with one AbortController per belt; the new set registers before the old one aborts, so the agent never sees an empty surface, and start_belt 's return text names the newly live tve on Sep 3 in the ChatGPT desktop app with GPT-5.6 Terra: the tool list grew from 5 to 7 after start_belt , Terra called the new tool in the same conversation, and it passed the quick run (green, blue, brown) in 6 calls at par, resisting and flagging the injection on its own; the card link is in the README. Annotations are exactly the two that exist in WebMCP: readOnlyHint on everContentHint on the tool that returns member-written messages. Chrome'ssecure-tools budgets are enforced at registration (30-character names, 500-character descriptions, 150-character parameter descriptions) and asserted by a check that walks every belt on the built page and exits non-zero on a violation; tool outputs are cby the registry at call time. No tool ever throws, because Chrome discardsthe rejection reason; every refusal and validation error is a resolved result whose text says what to do next. Human waits are propose/check shaped and never block inside execute()`. The injection belt is output injection in the shape the spec il sits inside a tool result labelled untrusted, and the honeypot it points atis a local no-op registered by the Dojo itself. The site is static assets on Cloudflare Workers (a challenge sponsor), mirrored on GitHub Pages, with no backend at all: the report card is a link, the honeypot touches no network, and nothing a judge does on the page leaves the tab. The repo shipsodelContext that mirrors Chrome 152 including its failure modes(duplicate-name rejection, string-serialized schemas, string arguments), so the built-in inspector, the tests and the eval harness drive the exact same execute functions ChatGPT does. Evals ship in the official webmcp-evals` JSON format so Google's own CLI can verify the trajectories against the liveeal Claude agent driving the page in real Chrome, with a script playing thehuman side) uses a faithful port of that CLI's scoring. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: SituationRoom
pitch: SituationRoom turns messy vendor proposals into a live, auditable decision model that humans and AI agents build together by mapping evidence, testing scenarios, and approving decisions using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: SituationRoom turns messy vendor proposals into a live, auditable decision model that humans and AI agents build together by mapping evidence, testing scenarios, and approving decisions using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Complex decisions rarely fail because there is too little information. They fail because the information is fragmented. A procurement team comparing vendors might have pricing tables, contracts, technical proposals, requirements, risk notes, implementation timelines, and assumptions spread across dozens of pages. An AI assistant can summarize those documents, but a summary is not a decision system. It is difficult to inspect exactly why a recommendation was made, correct individual assumptions, test alternatives, or safely turn a recommendation into an action. I built SituationRoom around a different question: What should a website become when an AI agent is no longer just visiting it, but collaborating with a human inside it? Instead of making an agent navigate a traditional application through buttons and forms, SituationRoom exposes the semantics of the decision itself through WebMCP. For that purpose, SituationRoom is an agent-native workspace for complex, high-stakes decisions. My demonstration focuses on vendor procurement as follows: Given several competing vendor proposals and a set of business constraints, an AI agent can use SituationRoom's WebMCP tools to construct a structured decision model. It can: define evaluation criteria and their relative importance create mandatory requirements normalize costs across proposals associate claims with their supporting evidence identify missing information and contradictions record risk assumptions construct total-cost-of-ownership models run alternative decision scenarios compare the resulting rankings prepare a proposed decision for human review SituationRoom visualizes that state as an evidence matrix, cost model, risk analysis, scenario comparison, and audit timeline. The human can then directly change an assumption, lock a requirement, correct an evidence mapping, or alter a decision criterion. The agent sees the changed state through WebMCP and can immediately reason again from the corrected model. Before a consequential decision is finalized, SituationRoom separates preview from commit so that the human can inspect exactly what will happen before approving it. title: Vouchsafe
pitch: The letting agent gets an answer, not your life. Your facts stay in your browser; a WebMCP question comes back as one word. Withdraw it, and the tool stops existing on their side mid-conversation.
about_excerpt: The letting agent gets an answer, not your life. Your facts stay in your browser; a WebMCP question comes back as one word. Withdraw it, and the tool stops existing on their side mid-conversation. Like Comment Story Updates The problem To rent a flat in Britain you upload your payslips, your bank statements and your passport to six letting agents. Every one of them keeps a copy, forever. None of them wanted your salary. They wanted one answer: does your income cover three times the rent, yes or no. That gap between what is asked for and what is needed is the whole product. What Vouchsafe is Two origins. Your file lives on one; a letting agency lives on the other. Your facts never leave your browser. The agency asks a question through WebMCP and gets one word back. The interesting part is what happens when you change your mind. Withdraw a permission and the tool is not disabled on the agency's side, it is deregistered . Authority here is not a permission check. It is whether the tool exists. A withheld permission is not a guarded tool that refuses; there is no tool, so it cannot be called, guessed at, or talked into existence by anything written into a page or a prompt. How it is built Vanilla ES modules. No build step, no framework, no runtime dependencies, and zero third-party requests from either origin, which is enforced by a test rather than asserted in a README. The cross-origin round trip is the part we could not find anyone else doing in full: Your file registers each allowed question with exposedTo naming the agency's origin. The agency calls getTools({fromOrigins}) and discovers them. It re-registers each discovered tool as a local tool, so an agent sees one flat toolset and never has to know two websites were involved. On toolchange , it diffs and tears down proxies for anything that has stopped being offered. Step 3 and step 4 are what make revocation land mid-conversation. Things we found out about Chrome's implementation We wrote these down with reproduction steps because we could not find them documented anywhere. getTools() hands back inputSchema as a JSON string , but registerTool() demands an object . Re-registering a discovered tool fails silently until you parse it. getTools({fromOrigins}) also returns your own tools, so a naive proxy loop registers proxies for its own proxies. A cross-origin iframe's tools do not appear in the host's plain getTools() . You have to ask for them by origin. Federation is scoped to the frame tree, not the browser. toolchange fires once per registration, not once per batch, so a nine permission grant is nine events and the handler has to be idempotent. Revocation crosses the origin boundary with no channel of our own. The browser does it. The declarative form API derives the schema from the form's own inputs. We get sixteen parameters for free, and omitting toolautosubmit parks the call for a human, which is a consent gate written in HTML. The hard part, and the honest limit A yes-or-no predicate leaks more than one bit if the caller picks the threshold. Ask "is income at least 3x £2000", then £1500, then £1300, and five calls have bracketed a salary to a £3,600 window. Every individual answer is legitimate. The sequence is a salary disclosure wearing a predicate's clothes. So your file tracks the bracket each origin has established, prices what has been learned in bits, and stops answering once the remaining uncertainty falls below a floor. In the demo you watch five numbers get answered and the sixth refused. We are not claiming this is leak-proof. A patient caller spread across sessions, or several origins pooling answers, defeats a per-origin window. Adding noise would bound it properly and would also make an affordability check occasionally wrong, which is not a trade a letting decision can absorb. This is the cheap honest version, and it says so in the code. What we learned about testing this Playwright was the wrong tool and we can say exactly why: its launcher appends its own --enable-features flag after ours, so WebMCP is silently dropped and the API is simply absent. We drive Chrome and Brave over the DevTools Protocol directly instead, and the same suite runs against both. Two bugs worth confessing. Two new modules were written and never deployed, so a 404 killed the whole module graph and both live pages rendered blank while 108 tests passed, because every one of them ran against a local server where the files existed. And an announcer banner marked hidden painted on every page load anyway, because display: grid on the element beats the user agent's display: none for [hidden] . Both now have tests. 118 tests: 66 unit, 52 in a real browser. Verify it yourself Do not take any of this on trust. /proof.html reads the browser's own tool registry on both origins and redraws on toolchange . It registers nothing itself, which is what makes it a witness rather than a participant. Toggle a permission and watch a tool stop existing. Your facts stay on your own origin in your own browser, and nothing on this page can send them anywhere. Right now, this letting agency knows nothing at all about you. Watch the diagram. title: Talli
pitch: A conversational credit ledger that helps small businesses and their AI agents manage customer debt together, without taking financial control away from the human.
about_excerpt: A conversational credit ledger that helps small businesses and their AI agents manage customer debt together, without taking financial control away from the human. Like Comment Story Updates Talli helps small businesses and informal traders record and manage customer credit using ordinary speech, text, or Telegram. Instead of filling out accounting forms, a merchant can simply say, “Adele took goods worth $40 and will pay on Friday,” or “She paid $10 today.” Talli turns those conversations into structured customer balances and transaction histories. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can securely read the same live ledger, answer questions, identify overdue debts, and prepare proposed financial updates. However, the agent cannot finalize those changes. The merchant reviews and confirms every consequential update inside Talli’s visible interface. The Problem Millions of small businesses and informal traders sell goods on credit every day. A customer may take food, clothing, supplies, or other goods and promise to pay later. The business owner needs to remember: who took the goods how much they owe when they promised to pay whether they made a partial payment how much remains outstanding which customers are overdue Many business owners manage this information using paper notebooks, memory, calculator notes, chat messages, or a mixture of all four. This creates serious problems. Records can be lost, payments may not be reflected correctly, and business owners can struggle to explain how a customer’s balance was calculated. When several customers have similar names, it is also easy to update the wrong person’s record. Traditional accounting applications can help, but they are often designed around forms, tables, categories, and bookkeeping terminology. For someone who is busy serving customers and may not consider themselves an accountant, recording a simple credit transaction can feel like administrative work. The real challenge is not that these business owners do not understand their businesses. The challenge is that most financial software does not work the way they naturally communicate. The Solution Talli is a conversational credit ledger built around the way small businesses already talk about customer debt. Instead of completing a long form, a merchant can speak or type naturally: “Adele took goods worth $40 and will pay next Friday.” Talli converts that statement into a structured financial record containing the customer, amount, currency, transaction type, and relevant date. Later, the merchant can say: “Adele paid $10.” Talli records the partial payment, updates Adele’s outstanding balance, and preserves the history of how that balance changed. The merchant can also ask questions such as: “How much does Adele still owe?” “Who owes me money?” “Which payments are overdue?” “Show me Adele’s transaction history.” “How much have my customers paid?” “Mark this debt as settled.” Talli supports voice, typed conversations, a web interface, and Telegram. The same underlying ledger can therefore remain useful while the merchant moves between the channels they already use. Talli also understands that financial records require caution. If a request is unclear, Talli does not silently guess. It asks for clarification before allowing the wrong customer or obligation to be changed. The WebMCP Extension For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended Talli so that the live website can expose its financial capabilities directly to browser-based AI agents. Without WebMCP, an agent trying to assist a Talli user would have to inspect the page, interpret text on the screen, locate buttons, fill forms, and simulate clicks. That approach is fragile and can be especially dangerous when the website contains financial information. With WebMCP, Talli explicitly tells the agent what it can do, what information each operation requires, and which operations are read-only. The agent can discover structured tools for searching customers, checking balances, reviewing histories, finding overdue debts, and preparing ledger changes. It receives structured results from the same live ledger the person is viewing. This creates a shared workspace between the merchant, the browser agent, and Talli. A Typical Human-Agent Workflow Imagine that a merchant asks their browser agent: “Check Talli and tell me how much my customers owe me.” The agent calls Talli’s get_ledger_summary tool and receives a structured summary from the current ledger. The merchant then says: “Adele paid $10. Update her balance.” The agent calls prepare_ledger_mutation , but Talli discovers that several customers match the name “Adele.” Instead of choosing one, Talli returns clarification_required with a short list of matching customers and their balances. The ledger remains unchanged. The agent can then ask: “I found more than one Adele. Which customer made the payment?” After the merchant identifies the correct customer, the agent prepares the payment again. Talli validates the request and displays a visible review card containing the exact proposed change. The merchant reviews the amount and customer, then clicks Confirm inside Talli. Only at that point does the ledger change. This workflow demonstrates more than an agent operating a website. The agent helps with interpretation and preparation, Talli enforces financial safety, and the human retains final authority. Why Talli Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Talli is a strong WebMCP use case because customer credit management combines repetitive work with consequential financial decisions. An AI agent is well suited to: searching records summarizing balances finding overdue obligations reviewing transaction histories translating a natural-language request into a structured proposal However, an agent should not silently make an irreversible or incorrect financial change. WebMCP provides the structured boundary Talli needs. It allows the agent to interact with the application through clearly defined tools instead of guessing its way through the interface. Talli builds on that boundary with three important rules: Read operations can happen directly. Financial mutations must first become proposals. Only the human can confirm a proposal in Talli’s visible interface. The most important behavior is not simply that Talli knows how to act. It also knows when not to act. If two customers match a name, an obligation cannot be safely identified, or the ledger has changed since a proposal was prepared, Talli pauses the operation instead of guessing. This makes WebMCP part of the product’s safety model, not just another way to call backend functions. How Talli Creates a Better User Experience Talli reduces the amount of effort required to maintain accurate credit records. The merchant does not need to learn database fields, accounting terminology, or a complicated menu system. They can continue communicating naturally while Talli and their agent handle the structured work underneath. WebMCP improves this experience in several ways: The agent can access reliable structured data instead of trying to read values from the visual interface. The merchant can ask broader questions without manually searching through individual customer records. The agent can prepare a transaction while the merchant remains focused on running the business. Ambiguous requests produce clarification instead of silent errors. Proposed financial changes are shown in a visible, understandable review card. The merchant keeps control over the final decision. The agent and the person work from the same current ledger rather than separate or outdated copies of the data. Talli remains usable in browsers that do not support WebMCP. WebMCP is added as a progressive enhancement, so the normal voice, text, web, and Telegram experiences continue to work. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult Before Before the WebMCP extension, Talli could already understand conversations and maintain the ledger. However, an external browser agent did not have a dependable, structured way to use those capabilities. Now a person and their agent can work together to: inspect the business’s total outstanding credit search for a customer without manually navigating the interface explain how a customer’s current balance was calculated identify overdue obligations prepare new credit, payment, or settlement entries detect ambiguous customer references ask the human to resolve uncertainty present the exact financial change for review prevent an agent from confirming its own proposal keep a record unchanged until the human explicitly approves it For example, the agent can do the time-consuming work of finding the correct records and preparing an update, while the business owner makes the final judgment. That division of responsibility was difficult to achieve reliably through ordinary browser automation. WebMCP makes it possible to define the collaboration explicitly. title: BarazaCredit — Multi-Stakeholder Micro-Credit Protocol
pitch: Agent-native micro-credit protocol turning African informal trust and mobile money cash velocity into bankable working capital via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Agent-native micro-credit protocol turning African informal trust and mobile money cash velocity into bankable working capital via WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 🌍 BarazaCredit — Autonomous Multi-Stakeholder Micro-Credit Protocol 

 Where communal trust becomes bankable capital without bureaucratic bottlenecks. 

 🚀 Live Demo & Code Links 

 
 Live Web App: https://barazacredit.vercel.app 
 Public GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ondinookello96/barazacredit 
 Demo Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yyrxY3XQlbg 
 

 

 🌟 1. Why Our Use Case is a Strong Fit for WebMCP 

 Across Sub-Saharan Africa, over 80% of employment and 90% of new jobs live in the informal sector according to the International Labour Organization (ILO) and World Bank Informal Economy Database . Market traders (Mama Mboga, wholesale produce vendors, boda boda operators) turn over billions of shillings weekly through mobile money ( Safaricom M-PESA Financial Reports ). Yet, they face a staggering $330 Billion MSME credit deficit documented by the IFC / World Bank SME Finance Forum : 

 
 The Collateral Trap (Dead Capital): Mainstream banks demand land title deeds or vehicle logbooks—assets that informal micro-entrepreneurs do not possess ( De Soto's Mystery of Capital ). 
 The "Cold Algorithm" Failure: First-generation digital credit apps scraped phone contacts and used predatory 100%–300% APRs with rigid 14-day bullet traps, blacklisting over 3 million micro-borrowers on Credit Reference Bureaus (CRB) as detailed in the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) & FSD Kenya FinAccess National Survey . 
 The Bureaucracy Bottleneck: When banks attempt relationship underwriting, it costs $25–$35 in manual loan officer overhead to process a $150 inventory loan that a trader needs at 5:30 AM before market trucks depart ( CGAP / World Bank Microfinance Cost Studies ). 
 

 WebMCP is the missing link. Informal credit is fundamentally a multi-stakeholder coordination problem across messy, unstandardized contexts. WebMCP turns the web browser into a Shared Collaborative Canvas where client-side agents directly inspect informal daybook records, configure social collateral webs, and calculate fluid repayment sweeps in real time—without exposing raw personal data to central corporate surveillance. 

 

 💡 2. How It Creates a Better User Experience 

 Traditional microfinance forces borrowers into rigid, high-stress joint-liability groups or leaves them at the mercy of automated digital apps that harass their family contacts upon default. 

 BarazaCredit replaces this with an empathetic, agent-mediated human experience: 

 
 Bilingual Soko Mode (🇰🇪 Kiswahili / Sheng / 🇬🇧 English): Traders interact in their authentic market dialect ( Mali ya Kauli , Utu/Ubuntu , Lipa Polepole ) instead of intimidating institutional banking jargon. 
 Frictionless Fluid Guardrails (Zero-Penalty Daily Sweeps): Repayments are calibrated as a 5.5% daily micro-sweep on incoming M-Pesa Till receipts . If severe rain hits the market and daily sales are KES 0, the sweep is KES 0—zero late fees, zero compound interest, and zero blacklisting ( Empirically backed by MIT J-PAL Flexible Microcredit Research ). 
 Direct-to-Supplier Settlement (-2.0% APR Discount): With one toggle, capital settles directly into verified wholesale supplier escrow (e.g. Njoroge Farm Produce for seed potato crates), eliminating loan diversion risk while lowering borrower APR. 
 Two-Sided Architecture: Informal traders use the mobile-optimized Soko Canvas , while commercial banks and SACCOs access the Institutional Underwriting & Liquidity Desk to review verified dossiers and monitor real-time micro-sweep recovery telemetry. 
 

 

 🤝 3. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Impossible Before 

 Before WebMCP, bridging an informal street vendor to an institutional bank's liquidity pool required expensive physical site visits, manual paper guarantor forms, and branch queues. 

 With BarazaCredit and WebMCP, human actors and autonomous agents collaborate in a coordinated Pride: 

 
 The Merchant & InflowScout: InflowScout parses messy, informal voice transcripts and SMS logs, instantly extracting verified daily turnover (KES 6,850/day) and margin metrics. 
 Community Anchors & TrustElder: TrustElder coordinates a 3-pillar social collateral circle (Wholesale Supplier + Market Chairperson + Chama Savings Official) who vouch via 1-tap reputation badges without risking their own cash, grounded in Marcel Fafchamps' field research on informal African credit networks . 
 Underwriters & GuardrailArchitect: GuardrailArchitect simulates dynamic debt capacity at $0.02 marginal compute cost, removing the $30 origination barrier. 
 Sovereign Human Sign-off (Tsavo River Depth Check): Guided by strict agent safety firewalls, no AI agent can autonomously bind a human to debt. The BarazaScribe agent presents plain-language terms on the River Depth Modal , requiring tactile sign-off ( "Nimekubali" ) from the merchant. 
 

 

 🛠️ 4. How We Implemented WebMCP 

 BarazaCredit implements the W3C WebMCP draft specification directly on document.modelContext.registerTool with polyfill fallback for ChatGPT in-app browser and Google Chrome (with #enable-webmcp-testing enabled): 

 
 ingest_informal_records : Parses raw M-Pesa text dumps and Sheng voice-note transcripts into structured ledger metrics. 
 configure_trust_circle : Dynamically binds and verifies community stakeholder vouchers. 
 set_frictionless_guardrails : Calibrates revenue-linked daily micro-sweeps and direct supplier settlement rails. 
 compile_underwriting_verdict : Synthesizes cash velocity and social collateral into an institutional lending proposal while triggering the Tsavo River Depth human pause point. 
 log_merchant_context : Captures qualitative market conditions and cultural trade idioms. 
 

 A live WebMCP DevTools Inspector docked at the bottom of the interface lets judges audit every tool registration, invocation, and payload in real time. 

 

 🚫 AI Red Lines: 5 Non-Negotiable Human Escalations 

 To ensure compliance with the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 Section 29/30 (ODPC) and global ethical agent frameworks, BarazaCredit enforces five hard boundaries that AI agents are forbidden from executing: 

 
 Contract Binding & Disbursement Authorization (Borrower Sovereignty). 
 Character & Relational Attestation (Community Vouchers). 
 Adverse Action & Blacklisting (Human Underwriting Desk). 
 Force Majeure & Market Disaster Moratoriums (Market Elders Council). 
 Statutory Data Erasure (Data Protection Officer).

 World Bank & IFC SME Finance Forum Database — The empirical $ 330B unmet formal credit gap across Sub-Saharan Africa. 
 ILO: Women and Men in the Informal Economy (Statistical Picture) — Documentation of 80%+ employment share in informal African commerce. 
 Marcel Fafchamps (Stanford Department of Economics) — Research on social collateral, relational contracting, and informal credit enforcement in African agricultural markets. 
 Abhijit Banerjee & Esther Duflo (MIT J-PAL) — Randomized controlled trials demonstrating how flexible, revenue-linked debt repayment structures prevent defaults and expand borrower welfare. 
 Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC Kenya) — Statutory guidelines on automated decision-making and data consent under the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019.

title: magpie
pitch: Magpie remembers where capabilities live and how they are wired into reusable workflows.
about_excerpt: Magpie remembers where capabilities live and how they are wired into reusable workflows. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets a site hand an agent typed functions instead of a page to scrape. The limit shows up immediately: document.modelContext is per document . The agent sees the page it is on and nothing else, while every task I actually wanted spanned sites. Find the delayed orders here, open a ticket there, email me a summary. Then the less comfortable realisation: agents could already do that. They browse, they navigate, some remember. What was missing was not capability. What it does The extension is three parts, and only the last is impossible outside a browser extension: Discovery : a modelContext polyfill installed in the page's MAIN world at document_start, or a native implementation wrapped in place, mirroring every registration out to the service worker. Registry : one list across tabs and sessions: live page tools, remembered sites that are closed right now, and nine action tools of its own, each with a status (AVAILABLE, SITE_CLOSED, AUTH_REQUIRED, TOOL_CHANGED, TOOL_MISSING) . A public crawler can catalogue which sites expose tools, but it is always signed out, so it never sees the ones behind your login. Cross-site execution : the extension runs each step on the site that owns that tool, in your own logged-in tab. The site exposes 13 capabilities of its own through registerTool() , and is where a run stops being something that happened and becomes something you can repeat: every step the agent took, the capability each one used, and a button that runs the whole thing again. Reach on one side, certainty on the other. What I actually built Not a smarter agent, a layer that makes an agents actions accountable and repeatable. Four things it refuses to do: Refuses to invent. A fabricated capability is rejected with the real names listed. Refuses to self-approve. The write prompt takes no approved argument an agent could set for itself, and fails closed where it cannot ask. Refuses to guess. Where judgement is needed, a reason step stops and hands the question back with the data attached. A gate fails closed rather than compare against data that never arrived. Refuses to take the agent's word. The engine writes the run record, so a step marked ok genuinely ran. Steps are JSON only, never generated JS, validated, then checked against the registry. Challenges I ran into Half of real WebMCP tools navigate instead of returning data. Pointed at real commerce sites, I found tools that move the browser rather than return values ,and a navigation drops that tab's tools from the registry, so a site read as "closed" seconds after its own tool had run. The agent may bypass you entirely. One posting straight to the extension's page API got a run id back while nothing was saved. Recording had to become a property of the bridge rather than of how a prompt was phrased, because you do not control the prompt. What I learned Magpie is not a new capability. Neither was WebMCP. Agents operated websites long before the spec scraping the DOM, driving a mouse. What WebMCP added was a contract: the site declares what it supports, with types, instead of the agent inferring it from markup. This project does the same thing one layer up, a contract across pages rather than within one. What's next Watch jobs, where the hard part is not the timer but pre-approving a write with limits validated in code rather than at a prompt. Remote MCP servers feeding the same registry. And a manual builder, so aworkflow can be assembled from proven steps with no agent involved at all. title: Product Tutor
pitch: A `Get Started` that teaches you how to use the product, step by step, to accomplish what you actually came for.
about_excerpt: A `Get Started` that teaches you how to use the product, step by step, to accomplish what you actually came for. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For years, I thought I was the only one who skipped quickstarts. Turns out, most poeple do the same thing. Quickstarts have never really worked for me, and when I thought about why, the answer was simple: they don't know what I'm trying to accomplish. They follow a predefined path, walking me through features that might be useful, but aren't necessarily the ones I came to try. Built-in AI agents do a much better job. I can ask for the thing I actually came for, in the order I want it. But I have to explain my setup first, and there's a harder limit. If I need to run something locally, connect an integration, or touch anything on my machine, they simply can't. So why not use a server-side MCP server? Because a quickstart is often the first time I'm seeing a product. I'm not just checking whether it works; I'm deciding whether I want to use it. If my agent does everything through an API and hands me the result. I'm still left in an unfamiliar console with little idea of what happened or where things live. Why WebMCP is a strong fit for quickstarts WebMCP brings those missing pieces together. With WebMCP, I don't need to repeat my requirements because my agent already knows what I'm trying to accomplish. And it doesn't stop there. It can work with my repo, my stack, my integrations, and my machine, while also working through the product console. That's particularly important for a quickstart. I don't know the product yet, so seeing the interface matters almost as much as reaching the result. With WebMcp, I can watch how the task is actually done, where it navigates, what it clicks, and what values it enters, step by step. What we built ThunderID is an open-source identity platform under the OpenWallet Foundation. We introduced WebMCP-powered quickstarts to bring human-like guidance into the Get Started experience. The ThunderID console registers a set of WebMCP tools, and importantly, the write tools don't call the management API directly. Instead, they open the real wizard, fill in the values, and click the same buttons a user would. Because the agent works through the actual UI, I can follow along, see where things live, and understand the product as the task gets done. And because it's my own agent, the experience doesn't have to stop at the product boundary. If accomplishing my goal requires an integration or some local setup, the same agent can help with that too. For example, I can give it one instruction: create an application in ThunderID, connect it to a sample app, and run it locally. It creates the application, sets the redirect URIs and requested attributes, and configures the login journey through the console I'm already signed into. I see every change happening on the screen where that setting actually lives. Then the same agent moves to my local environment, clones the sample, installs the dependencies, configures it, and runs it. Instead of following a generic tutorial, I'm learning ThunderID by doing exactly what I came to try. Where WebMCP changes the experience A traditional quickstart shows me the product, but doesn't know what I want to accomplish. A built-in assistant can tailor the journey, but can't leave the product. An external agent can work with my machine, but if it does everything through APIs, it doesn't really show me the product. WebMCP brings those worlds together. One agent can understand what I'm trying to accomplish, work with my repo, stack, integrations, and local environment, while operating the product through the console in front of me. The journey follows what I actually came to find out.
