title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Intelligent Markdown-Driven Process Diagrams
pitch: It may look like an ordinary diagramming tool, but under the hood it's a markdown-driven agent friendly security, governance, and process improvement machine powered by WebMCP!
about_excerpt: It may look like an ordinary diagramming tool, but under the hood it's a markdown-driven agent friendly security, governance, and process improvement machine powered by WebMCP! Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I've found that giving agents structure and tools greatly enhances how they operate. A process diagram can look complete while hiding the complexity in simple steps. I wanted to make diagrams something people and AI agents can inspect, test, and improve together. What it does This project turns a process map into an interactive workspace for human-agent collaboration with a massive amount of context behind each input, action, output, and relationship by adding markdown to each point in the process. An agent can read all of this structure context to draft a new process, inspect steps and connections, and test scenarios by simulating outcomes that expose possible gaps. Proposed repairs appear as suggested change that a person can review before approval, adding to the collaborative feel between you and the agent. The included demo explores an AI evaluation process: what happens if a sandboxed agent decides it wants to escape? Our agent can identify a missing review step and propose a repair before the infrastructure is ever built. How we built it I gave Codex the challenge page url and described my idea 🤓 Challenges we ran into I ran into several issues along the way with actually using the WebMCP tools, troubleshooting the chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing config and finally realized I had to use the embedded browser in Codex instead of ChatGPT browser extension. Also took me forever to realize I couldn't use Luna with webMCP I'm happy to share more specifics if you'd like added feedback. Codex summarized our struggles below: WebMCP tools registered on the page but were not visible in every browser session. Native WebMCP testing required browser support, enabled settings, and correct host headers. Tool registration needed reliable retry, cleanup, and discovery checks. Tool inputs and outputs needed strict validation and clear safety annotations. Repair proposals needed exact graph and evidence references to reject stale requests. Agent-proposed drafts and repairs had to remain pending until human approval. Accomplishments that we're proud of Just finishing the challenge - everything feels SO busy lately. AI tools have made me so much more productive but I also find myself just working more as well. So taking the time to really dig into webMCP as a new capability was great. There's so much value in allowing web users to bring their own agent instead of trying to build AI into my own pages. I think it'll be a totally new unlock for web browsing, not just an agentic augmentation of the UI. What we learned I learned about webMCP from the ground up. I had never heard of it before I saw the tweet for the challenge and I was immediately interested. I've built a few websites but adding AI tooling feels like reinventing the wheel. WebMCP solves that by allowing users to BYOAgent. What's next for Intelligent Process Diagrams I'm very excited to get GPT-6 on it. I have a lot of ideas that I think would benefit from a more long horizon model using it and iterating on it. Sol did a decent job of the higher level stuff but veered sometimes. Now that the challenge is over and it's not so rushed I'll polish the UI and remove some of the bloat in the properties panel. I'm a solution architect by day, so I really want to incorporate this in discovery calls and allow an agent to build diagrams in realtime as I talk through customer processes. That's the long term vision for it. Thank you all for putting this on and taking the time to review all of these submissions!! Again, if you'd like any additional feedback on my experience adding WebMCP please reach out. Built With codex magic markdown Try it out ashy-tree-0eb0b0e0f.6.azurestaticapps.net github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Eric Lott Like Share this project: Updates Eric Lott posted an update — Sep 04, 2026 10:07 AM EDT From process diagram to machine-readable intent While reviewing the export format, I realized the diagram can serve a larger purpose than process visualization. I believe the first safety net of agentic alignment is to remove ambiguity from instructions. If an agent is given an INTENT.md contract then agents can act with more clarity around vulnerable or critical systems where more deterministic outcomes are required. In this project, each node, port (node input and output point), and relationship have theirs own markdown and metadata. The result is a structured graph where every part can explain what should happen, why it should happen, what evidence is required, and where authority stops. This opens up a possible use case as an agent-readable intent contract - INTENT.md During the diagram buildout, a model could inspect the complete process to find ambiguous or missing rules, conflicting conditions, unsafe capability paths, and downstream consequences. The current export already provides stable IDs, explicit relationships, decision paths, and human-review boundaries. The next step would be to add typed permissions, prohibitions, invariants, data contracts, and authoritative branch conditions. This goes beyond instructions or skills by outlining a process end-to-end so an agent understands what's in scope and how to get from point A to point B in a safe and repeatable pattern. title: SupperClub AI
pitch: Supper Club AI turns a favorite book into a thoughtful, host-ready dinner party—menu, music, timeline, shopping, and prep included.
about_excerpt: Supper Club AI turns a favorite book into a thoughtful, host-ready dinner party—menu, music, timeline, shopping, and prep included. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Reading and Music Shopping & Prep WebMCP Architecture Host Packet Review Menu and Pairings Workspace Overview WebMCP Tool Map Supper Club AI Live application: thesupperclub.app Public code: github.com/tmoody1973/supper-club-ai Inspiration Ambitious dinner parties are coordination projects disguised as a creative evening. A host may begin with a book, a feeling, or an artist, then need to reconcile recipes, dietary needs, drink pairings, music, a grocery budget, and a kitchen timeline across many tabs and notes. If one course changes, the shopping list and prep schedule can quietly become wrong. We wanted the agent and the host to work on the same plan instead of passing disconnected suggestions back and forth in chat. Supper Club AI is built around that shared surface: the person supplies taste, cultural intention, guest context, and approval; the agent handles research and structured coordination. What it does Supper Club AI turns a cultural inspiration into a sourced, host-ready dinner plan. A Creative Host can ask for a hopeful Parable of the Sower dinner for eight people, including a gluten-free guest, within a $250 budget, with both wine and zero-proof pairings. The agent can create a fresh plan and populate its theme, three-course menu, pairings, soundtrack, shopping list, and prep work in the same browser workspace the host is viewing. This is a strong fit for WebMCP because those are connected decisions, not independent recommendations. The page exposes 28 typed tools, so the agent can read and update the plan's real data model instead of guessing from the UI or describing six separate next steps. For example, a host can reject only the main course; the agent can replace that course, retain the rest of the evening, refresh the affected pairing, and rebuild the shopping and prep work. Every change appears in the Run of Show and in visible Agent Marginalia receipts with sources, provider mode, warnings, and the new plan version. Marginalia means the notes, comments, doodles, or marks that a reader writes in the blank borders and edges of a book page or manuscript The result is a better experience than a chatbot plus a planning site: the host makes one natural-language request and reviews a coherent, editable plan immediately. The agent can coordinate work across food, music, drinks, cost, and timing, while the host can inspect provenance, dietary warnings, and alternatives before deciding what to keep. Finalization and exports still require explicit host approval. How we built it The Supper Club AI website registers 28 WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a focused description, JSON input schema, behavioral annotations, and structured success/error response. The tool set covers creating and reading plans; research and curation; recipe, wine, music, grocery, and timeline changes; pricing; and approved exports. create_party_plan accepts a book, author, guest count, budget, dietary requirements, tone, and wine/zero-proof preferences. It creates a new anonymous plan, activates the returned plan URL, and returns provider receipts for the theme, menu, pairings, and soundtrack. Read and edit tools operate on the same React plan state that renders the workspace. State-changing calls require expectedPlanVersion , so a stale agent response returns a structured version conflict rather than overwriting a newer host edit. Research stays behind a same-origin server gateway; credentials and raw provider payloads never enter browser code or tool responses. Menu courses resolve independently through Spoonacular, then Perplexity Agent API discovery, then a reviewed local catalog. Pairings use GrapeMinds with an X-Wines fallback; soundtrack candidates are discovered through Perplexity, verified against Apple Music, and optionally enriched with Discogs context. The tool response reports the sources, provider mode, and warnings that the UI turns into an auditable receipt. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not producing suggestions; it was making research results safe and useful inside a real plan. Live providers can be incomplete, ambiguous, or unavailable. We designed per-course fallbacks so a failed dessert lookup does not discard a successful starter or main, and we keep successful live results rather than replacing the entire menu with a fallback. We also had to keep agent speed from erasing host control. We added optimistic concurrency with plan versions, source and dietary warnings, and explicit confirmation before finalizing a plan or downloading host, guest-share, and recipe packets. Recipe exports use original functional preparation outlines and retain the authoritative source link rather than copying protected recipe prose or media. Accomplishments that we're proud of A genuine WebMCP workflow: the website itself registers typed capabilities, and the agent updates the exact workspace the host is reading. One shared, versioned plan rather than a chat transcript plus manually reconciled lists. A practical compound action: an agent can create a complete cultural dinner plan from one brief, including menu, drinks, music, shopping, and prep—not merely recommend a few dishes. Visible receipts that make live discovery, verification, reviewed fallback, warnings, and affected sections understandable to the host. Human control at the meaningful boundaries: the agent can research and coordinate, but the host reviews changes and explicitly approves finalization and file exports. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a site has meaningful state and meaningful consequences. A typed tool such as replace_menu_course gives an agent more reliable leverage than browser clicking because it carries the actual plan ID, selected course, validation rules, and version expectation. It also lets the product return structured next actions and evidence instead of burying important caveats in prose. We also learned that trust is a product feature. Sources, fallback modes, dietary flags, and version conflicts are not implementation noise; they are the information a host needs to judge an agent's work. Making that evidence visible lets people and agents collaborate on a creative, high-consideration task without asking the person to surrender authorship. What's next for SupperClub AI Next, we want to carry the shared-plan model from planning into purchase and hosting. The existing grocery-location and recipe-pricing tools demonstrate store-aware package estimates; we plan to add reviewable retailer inventory, wine-shop offers, and coupon-aware baskets while keeping purchase decisions explicitly human-approved. We also want richer collaborative review for co-hosts and an embeddable version for bookstores, independent grocers, wine shops, and cultural venues that want to turn inspiration into a hosted experience. title: Gildongmu
pitch: A Korean navigation app with no map, where screen reader users search places, plan trips and explore their surroundings in plain text, now declared to the browser agent as seven WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A Korean navigation app with no map, where screen reader users search places, plan trips and explore their surroundings in plain text, now declared to the browser agent as seven WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Gildongmu means "traveling companion" in Korean. I started it in June 2026 to fix a small, stubborn problem of my own as a screen reader user: I wanted to look up an address and call a place as fast as possible. Map apps make both slow, because their answers live in an interface built around images. So Gildongmu has no map at all. Everything it knows, it says in words: places, routes, what is around you, and the accessibility details a screen reader user actually needs, such as station elevators, audio beacons, accessible restrooms, stairs-free walking routes and crosswalks with audible signals. Almost all of that comes from Korean public data. When I read about WebMCP, I realized that this had quietly prepared the app for agents. Every sentence a screen reader user hears is a sentence an agent can be handed. This entry is what happened when I handed them over. What it does Gildongmu is a free navigation app for South Korea with no account and no ads, on the web, on iOS, and as an npm command line tool and MCP server. It joins about thirty public and commercial APIs from nineteen organizations and turns them into plain text. As far as I know, it is the first navigation app in Korea where a screen reader user can search places, plan a trip and explore the surroundings with no barrier in between. For this challenge the web app declares seven WebMCP tools to the browser agent: describe_app: what this deployment can do and how the tools chain search_places: places, addresses and web results, with refs to pass on get_place_info: a place by ref; for stations the timetable, accessibility facilities, live arrivals and barrier-free facilities plan_directions: transit, walking and driving summaries for a destination get_transit_route_detail: one transit route in full, including the boarding door for a quick exit get_route_steps: walking or driving steps as a numbered page read_current_view: which screen the app is on and what it shows Ask the agent "Tell me the first train, the last train and the elevators at Gangdong Station (강동역)" and one tool call brings all of it back. Ask "Seoul Station (서울역) to Gangnam Station (강남역): which car and door should I board to get off next to the elevator?" and while the agent answers, the app in the browser tab has already moved to that route, so the user can turn on VoiceOver and check every line. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The answers were already text. Most navigation apps keep their answer in pixels, so an agent driving a browser has to guess at a canvas. Gildongmu had to write every answer as a sentence for VoiceOver users long before it ever met an agent. Those same sentences are what the tools return, and they come from the same code that draws the screen. The agent cannot be told something the screen does not say. Neither a plain browser agent nor a server MCP can do this alone. Behind one station answer are four public APIs, each with its own key, its own response format and, in Korea, its own coordinate system. An agent reading the page cannot rebuild that. A server MCP, on the other hand, cannot answer "where am I standing right now", because it has no browser tab. WebMCP sits exactly in between: the page keeps the keys and the location, and the agent asks in words. Location stays in the browser. A trip starts from the user's current position, which the page already knows. Tool output goes through a list of allowed fields that has no place for coordinates, so the agent's provider receives place names and sentences, never a coordinate pair. Gildongmu has promised since its first release that nothing personal is stored on its servers, and the tools keep that promise. How it creates a better user experience For a screen reader user the expensive part is not reaching a screen, it is exploring it. A transit plan on screen is dozens of items, one swipe at a time. As a tool result it is one spoken answer, and the app has still moved to that same screen, so the user can take over and verify anything. The size of an answer follows the same instinct. A full transit answer came out at 3,700 characters, far past the 1,500 the guidance recommends. Instead of cutting it off, I split it the way I would say it out loud: the recommended route in full, the other routes in one line each, and the details behind a second tool. Nothing got worse for people. The tools press the same functions a person clicks, and a person always wins. Type a new search or close a section while a tool is running and the tool call ends as superseded. If a dialog is open, the tool declines instead of closing it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before "Which car and door do I board so that I get off next to the elevator?" Gildongmu matches a public quick exit dataset to the live route, so get_transit_route_detail returns the boarding door for each leg. No map tells you this. Ask it in the chat, and the app is already sitting on that route. "Does Gangdong Station have an elevator, and when is the first train?" One call to get_place_info returns the timetable, the accessibility facilities, the real time arrivals and the barrier-free facilities. Without WebMCP the agent would open four sections one by one, and it could not call the four public APIs behind them at all. The handoff goes both ways. The agent and the user share one screen: the tools move the app, and read_current_view reads whatever the person did by hand. The agent can set up a trip that the user finishes by touch, or the user can search by hand and then ask the agent about what is on the screen. Before this, asking an assistant and using an app were two separate places that did not know about each other. Honest absence. Every tool tells apart "none", "not known" and "lookup failed", and says outOfCoverage outside Korea instead of inventing a result. A screen reader user cannot glance at a screen to catch a made up answer, so the tools never let the agent guess. The app has followed the same rule for people since version 1.0. How I implemented WebMCP I used the imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool with a name, a description, an input schema and an execute function. Here is how I understand what I built: One set of seven tools, registered once at the app root, because an agent reads the tool list once. A tool that is not configured on this deployment is still declared and answers notConfigured. A tool that needs another screen moves there itself. Each screen publishes a small bridge to a registry, and a tool reads it at the moment it runs. A tool that waits for a screen waits for a specific place id or sequence number, not for a screen name, so a call about place A cannot be satisfied by place B appearing first. Only one tool runs at a time, with a 30 second cap. A place handle is an opaque ref that remembers which search it came from, and a handle from a replaced search returns staleResult with the call that recovers it, rather than pointing at the wrong place. Every output leaves through one function. It keeps only the allowed fields, refuses coordinates, trims to the 1,500 character budget item by item, and pages a long answer with an offset. Calls to paid third party APIs are budgeted per provider. The human sentences come from the same modules the screen uses, so the screen and the tools cannot drift apart. It is covered by 19 test files and 104 tests. I checked the contracts by deliberately breaking the implementation and confirming that the tests caught each break, and I checked the deployed site with Chrome DevTools WebMCP inspection. Challenges I ran into How many tools to expose. My first design registered tools per screen, ten in all (nine on the directions screen, one on the home screen), and along the way I weighed going much further: four screen-specific sets adding up to 31 tools, or simply re-exposing the 24 tools my Gemini chat already had. Research pulled the other way. Real sites declare one to ten tools, and both OpenAI and Anthropic advise a small number of high-value tools. I settled on seven, always on, at the app root. Gildongmu is already screen reader friendly, so browser navigation and tool calls can share the work, and seven is a number an agent handles without strain. Whether to move the cursor. An early tool moved the screen reader cursor to the item the agent had found. I removed it. What a screen reader user wants from an agent is not help exploring the screen but the exact data, fast, without exploring at all. The tools now return answers, and the screen follows on its own. title: Nightstand — a health diary you run by voice
pitch: A local-first health diary you run by voice. On WebMCP, every on-screen action is also an agent tool so people who can't type keep their records hands-free. Zero backend.
about_excerpt: A local-first health diary you run by voice. On WebMCP, every on-screen action is also an agent tool so people who can't type keep their records hands-free. Zero backend. Like Comment Story Updates The home screen — everything you do here, your agent can do by voice. 19 of 19. Entries it logs show "logged by your agent." Track medications by voice or on screen — the same tool either way. Schedules are versioned so past adherence stays truthful. Ask your agent to prepare a doctor summary — symptom trends, adherence, as-needed doses — downloadable as a real, selectable-text PDF. Inspiration The person I built this for has rheumatoid arthritis. Pain and stiffness in the hands make filling in a form miserable — and it's a disease that asks for a log every single day , for a consultation that happens once every three months, when nobody remembers the details. The people who most need to keep a health diary are often the ones who can least type one. So the diary shouldn't be typed. It should be spoken. WebMCP's own explainer names this exact motivation: it can "enable agents to assist users of accessibility technology." I wanted to take that literally — expose an entire app as agent tools, so someone who cannot comfortably type can run all of it hands-free by voice. What it does Nightstand is a local-first health diary you operate by talking to your AI agent. Speaking, hands-free, you can: Log naturally — "My knee hurts, about a seven, and I took my methotrexate" becomes two records from one sentence, with a single confirmation. Correct and undo by voice — "Actually, make it a five." "No, undo that." When you can't retype, the repair path is the product. Adjust the interface by voice — make the text bigger, jump to a section, raise contrast. Prepare a doctor's summary — "Prepare a summary for my doctor" reveals a printable report (symptom trend, medication adherence, as-needed doses), and one large 56 px button downloads it as a real, selectable-text PDF — generated in the browser, no backend. The whole flow is co-browsing : the person watches the screen while the agent acts, so every step is visible and reversible. How I built it WebMCP is the center of the project, not a wrapper around it. True parity, not a hand-typed number. Every capability is declared once — id, tool name, description, zod schema, handler — and from that one declaration come the on-screen control and the WebMCP tool, the published inputSchema , the runtime validation, and the TypeScript types. The "19 of 19" badge reads the registry, and a test compares the on-screen actions against the tools in both directions, so the number cannot drift. Three trust layers — 5 read-only answer tools, plus act and transact tools that change state. Because Nightstand is a co-browsing journey with a human present, it safely spans all three, with undo and explicit confirmations as the guardrails . An untrusted-input boundary. Tool arguments are produced by a language model, so every handler validates them with zod at the edge; past that point the data is typed and trusted, and invalid arguments return a readable error instead of writing a bad number into a medical record. One write path , so undo covers every write — spoken or tapped. You refer to things by name, never by id : the agent is never handed an identifier it can't hand back. Stack: Next.js (static output: 'export' ), React 19, TypeScript (strict), Tailwind 4, zod, idb over IndexedDB, pdf-lib (zero-dependency, lazy-loaded), Vitest. Zero backend — no API routes, server actions, or middleware — and zero outbound requests after load. The privacy promise holds because the repository has nowhere to hide anything. Challenges I ran into Printing is dead in the ChatGPT app's embedded browser. window.print() and Ctrl+P simply don't work there. I pivoted the doctor summary to a client-side PDF download that works both in a full browser and in the app. A page-initiated voice download loses user activation in that embedded browser and is stopped by the browser's policy — proven, not a bug I could fix. So the summary is a button : the agent prepares it by voice, and the person taps one large target. Timezone-correct clinical math. Adherence and local-day logic had to survive DST and non-UTC offsets, or a number handed to a doctor could be wrong. Pinned timezone test fixtures caught real bugs. Honest domain limits. The schedule model understands daily times, not weekly ones, so a weekly DMARD like methotrexate is logged as as-needed rather than scored — the app says so instead of reporting a wrong number. Which agents actually call the tools? I found that ChatGPT's Chrome extension drives the DOM instead of calling the WebMCP tools — while the judged surfaces (ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled) genuinely consume them. Verifying that shaped where the demo lives. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Capability parity that's real, not claimed — enforced by a test that gates every commit. Privacy by architecture — verified zero outbound requests three different ways. Accessibility as the reason the app exists — WCAG 2.2 AA, 56 px targets, a Lighthouse accessibility score of 100 . Independently validated by Google Chrome Labs' official webmcp-evals harness: 11/11 tool calls pass against the live deployment — real WebMCP calls, not DOM automation. What I learned WebMCP's value for accessibility isn't enabling voice — a DOM-driving agent can operate a site too. It's making agent operation reliable, safe, correct, and portable for something as sensitive as medical records: a typed contract with validation and undo, a smaller data footprint than screen-scraping, and one tool surface that works for any agent — in-browser or headless. And a design rule I'll keep: never hand the agent an identifier it cannot hand back. What's next Weekly and complex medication cadence, so DMARDs are scored for adherence. More entry types and languages. A caregiver mode: the same tool surface, operated by a headless agent someone sets up for a person who can't.
